items.title: Canadian Cyclo-cross National Championships: Sidney McGill wins elite women's title
items.author: Lyne Lamoureux
items.content:
Sidney McGill (Materiaal-Lastig) claimed her first elite Canadian women’s cyclocross title with a commanding solo victory at the 2026 Lazer Canadian Cyclocross Championships in Oro-Medonte, Ontario. The 27-year-old, who previously won the elite Pan American title in Missoula in 2024, reached the top step after finishing second and third in the previous two editions. McGill dominated the race, crossing the finish line with a lead of more than four minutes.

McGill started her cyclo-cross season by taking three UCI victories and finishing on the podium of all but one of 11 UCI races.

 Sarina Daigle (Passion Project) crossed the line 4:39 later to take silver, while Siobhan Kelly (Black Dog Racing) followed two minutes later to round out the podium.

Last year’s winner, four-time national champion Maghalie Rochette, was absent from the race as she is expecting a baby.

Nico Knoll took a solo victory to win the Under-23 title crossing the line 48 seconds ahead of her closest rivals. In a battle with her Caledon Hills Armada teammate, Aislin Hallahan claimed the silver ahead of bronze medallist Eli Clark.

Earlier in the day, Alexa Haviland (Shredders Race Team) claimed the women's junior title with a solo victory, finishing 76 seconds ahead of silver medallist Anna Christensen (Shredders Race Team). Claire MacKinnon (Stimulus Trek Racing Team) rounded out the podium in third.

Held at Hardwood Ski and Bike, a four-season outdoor recreation centre just north of Barrie, Ontario, the race featured an approximately 3km course that challenged riders with natural obstacles, sandy sections, tight corners, and steep run-up climbs.

items.title: Tadej Pogačar reveals three fractured vertebrae after Vuelta crash: “I’m just happy to be alive”
items.author: Lyne Lamoureux
items.content:
Tadej Pogačar revealed that his injuries sustained in his crash at the Vuelta a España were more extensive than first reported. Initial reports stated that the five-time Tour de France winner had suffered a concussion, fractures to his left collarbone, a stable C7 cervical fracture as well as various cuts and bruises. But weeks after his crash, further exams showed that he had broken two more vertebrae.

“There’s actually a funny story,” Pogačar began the interview with . “Two weeks ago, I was in Slovenia and I went to do another CT scan. I knew I had a C7 fracture, but then we saw I had two more broken vertebrae, the T1 and T2.”

“At that moment, I was happy I didn’t do the European Championships, which had been my initial goal. When I saw I had three broken vertebrae? I’m just happy to be alive, actually, or just to be standing.”

He added that he has largely returned to his normal routine, although he is still taking precautions as he continues his recovery.

“I don’t have discomfort anymore,” Pogačar said. “I have to be careful not to crash on the bike, or do some heavy lifting with my left arm or with my neck. But I can do basically everything normal now.”

The UAE Team Emirates rider admitted that the two weeks post-crash were difficult, with concussion-related nausea and dizziness affecting his coordination and forcing a delay in getting back onto his bike, or at a minimum, on the rollers.

“For the first two weeks, I was really mentally not OK. I was really down. I was not a fun person to be around. I don’t think Urska [Zigart] was happy to see me around the house, because I was just, like, depressed. You know, just not feeling anything.”

Everything changed once he got back into training.

“When I started to get on the home trainer, to go to physio every day, then I started to feel better — also in the head. But it was a day-to-day fight.”

“Now, in Monaco, I go for runs, swum a few times — it’s important to build a really good base now through the winter. Actually, it’s not winter yet here — I was in shorts today riding outside. But I‘m feeling like I’m getting back into the proper rhythm of training and recovery.”

items.title: 'They’ve destroyed cycling' - Bardiani-CSF-7 Saber boss gives scathing assessment of the UCI after Italian team unable to race Giro d’Italia in 2027
items.author: Dan Challis
items.content:
Veteran team boss Bruno Reverberi has called the UCI “incompetent” after his Bardiani-CSF-7 Saber team finished outside of the UCI’s top-30 rankings in 2026, making them ineligible to race a Grand Tour next season.

Reverberi said that it is likely that Bardiani-CSF-7 Saber will shutter due to the current regulations, which he says are making teams at the ProTeam level increasingly fragile, with no guarantees of invitation to the world’s biggest races.

The long-standing team has raced every edition of the Giro d’Italia since 1982 and is well known for its attacking style. Bardiani-CSF-7 Saber has been a fruitful breeding ground for Italian talent over the years, including the team’s last Giro stage-winner, Giulio Ciccone, who won in Sestola in 2016. Sonny Colbrelli and Giulio Pellizzari are two other names to have emerged through this system.

The team has also been involved in several doping scandals over the years, with the likes of Emanuele Sella and Stefano Pirazzi banned during their time on the team.

“Our project is to stop,” Reverberi told the “How can you spend €5 million and not have the right to race? There is no future, and cycling has no future. We have already thought about closing in two years. In fact, we have taken four or five new riders and made them sign for only one year.”

“You don’t even have the courage to go to the sponsor and ask for money,” he said, despite signing a “multi-year agreement” with Uzbek clothing company 7 Saber at the start of this season.

Reverberi’s main charge towards the UCI is its points system, which he believes is encouraging teams to race for top-10s rather than chase glory in the breakaway.

It is perhaps the team’s reticence to play the game as other teams have done which left them languishing down the UCI points rankings, 121 below Euskaltel-Euskadi, who travelled to Algeria and Panama in the last weeks of the 2026 season in their search for points.

“Our way of racing was to break away,” he said. “Now you don’t even break away, because you try to keep the rider there to sprint for tenth place for those damned UCI points,” he said.

“The UCI is incompetent. They’ve destroyed cycling,” he concluded, suggesting that while the top of the sport explodes in its popularity and financial investment, the lower-level is breaking apart.

“We’ve reached a bit of a peak with Pogačar in some ways, but everything is falling apart underneath,” he said. “Cycling is disappearing, and nobody’s looking at it.”

items.title: 'It really feels like a victory' - Belgian cyclo-cross champion returns to training following surgery for cardiac arrhythmias
items.author: Dan Challis
items.content:
Two-time Belgian national champion Marion Norbert Riberolle has restarted training after the opening to her 2026/2027 cyclo-cross campaign was halted due to a cardiac arrhythmia.

The Crelan-Corendon rider opened her season in Dendermonde and also raced the Kermiscross on the 15th of October before undergoing surgery to address the issue that was causing her heart to beat with an irregular rhythm.

After several sessions on the indoor trainer, Norbert Riberolle has now resumed training outdoors. She is being closely monitored by her team’s medical staff, and a decision is yet to be made regarding her return to racing.

“After several successful sessions on the rollers, she has now also taken to the road for the first time again. Our staff is monitoring everything closely so that it can be determined later when our Belgian champion can make a restart.”

In Norbert Riberolle’s absence, Lucinda Brand (Baloise Verzekeringen-Het Poetsbureau Lions) has been dominating on the 'cross field, already taking three victories this season.

Born in France and originally racing under a French license, Norbert Riberolle switched allegiances in 2021. She won the under-23 cyclo-cross world championships in 2020 and claimed three victories last season, including her second Belgian national title. The rider born in Troyes also races on the road for Fenix-Premier Tech’s development team.

“I am doing very well and I feel that I have recovered well. The rest has done me good,” she said.

“The first training sessions on the rollers went without problems, and in the meantime, I have also completed my first ride outdoors. It really feels like a victory. I was incredibly happy to be back on the bike and to be able to train outside.”

items.title: 'I still need some time to analyse what I really want' - Tadej Pogačar to return to the UAE Tour, but 2027 race calendar still undecided with Tour de France the main target
items.author: Dan Challis
items.content:
Tadej Pogačar has already confirmed his main ambitions for the 2027 race season; a sixth Tour de France title, a fourth world title and a shot at redemption at the Vuelta a España. In the coming weeks, alongside the management team at UAE Team Emirates-XRG, his race calendar leading up to those objectives will be finalised.

According to the Slovenian, on the cards is a return to the UAE Tour, a race he won in 2021, 2024 and 2025. He skipped the race of his team’s homeland in 2026 and began his season at Strade Bianche.

Speaking on a virtual community ride on MyWhoosh, the UAE-owned training platform which sponsors his team, Pogačar said that there was a “big chance” that he will then return to the Spring Classics, with that elusive victory at Paris-Roubaix surely a focus.

His comments will come as a blow to the organisers of the Tour Down Under, who have said that they are “doing everything we can” to bring Pogačar to Adelaide in January. This option appeared more likely due to Pogačar’s early season ending after his crash at the Vuelta a España. It is also one of just a handful of WorldTour stage races that Pogačar is yet to win.

The 28-year-old raced five one-day races and the Tours de Romandie and Suisse ahead of claiming his record-equalling fifth Tour de France title in 2026. Pogačar then competed in the Vuelta a España for the second time in his career, crashing out on stage 8 while in the leader’s jersey and concluding his season.

A final judgement on Pogačar’s race schedule will be made during a team training camp in December.

"There's like three options that I can do. The team gave me three options of my calendar, but it's a big decision," he said during the community ride.

"I think I still need some time to really analyse what I really want for next year. And I think the final decision will be done in December, where we have another training camp.

"There's a big chance I come back to Classics for sure, and also UAE Tour, and obviously Tour de France. There's no hiding in this, I think, so we will see."

Speaking to at a charity golf event two weeks ago, Pogačar stated his central ambitions for the season. "The goal for next year would obviously be the World Championships, combined with the Tour and the Vuelta. Even though I'd rather ride the Giro, I'll have to tick off the Vuelta at some point too. I think that will be the goal for next year," he said.

While his season will once again orbit around success at the Tour de France, Pogačar admitted that he had not yet looked at the route for the 2027 race, which was presented on the 22nd of October.

"I didn't check a lot the route yet of the Tour. I was not there for the announcement,” he said. "Obviously the Tour is always three weeks long, and there's always big mountains, flat stages, tricky stages, some crosswinds, time-trials. So you always have everything.”

"No matter which cities host the start or finish, it's always more or less the same and the toughest race in the world. You need to be ready for everything."

items.title: 'I think things could have been done better' - Visma-Lease a Bike departee regrets slow development on Dutch team as he drops to continental level for 2027
items.author: Dan Challis
items.content:
24-year-old Loe van Belle is leaving the Dutch squad after three seasons, plus two in its development team. Once viewed as a promising Classics rider and time-triallist, Van Belle was informed in the summer that his services were no longer required.

Speaking in an interview with Van Belle has lamented his development while on the team, suggesting that things could have been done better, both by himself and the backroom staff. Crashes, injuries and an iliac artery flow limitation also played roles in his inability to prove his potential, ultimately leading to his departure.

“I look back on my years at Visma-Lease a Bike with a good feeling,” he told “When you look at the guidance and what you learn there as a rider in terms of tactics, racing style, and preparation for races and training camps, I don’t think you could have a better training ground. I benefited enormously from that, and I appreciate that immensely.

“But when I look at my physical development, I think things could have been done better, both from the team and from myself.”

Van Belle’s ability was clear as an under-23 rider, when he won a stage at the Flanders Tomorrow Tour and finished 9th at the 2022 Tour de l’Avenir. He was promoted to the WorldTour team in 2024 and was utilised as a domestique for the most part, picking up a handful of top-10 results during his three seasons on the team.

While Van Belle is appreciative of the investment that Visma-Lease a Bike gave to him, he now believes that he should have spoken up for himself when it was clear that he wasn’t progressing as planned.

“I want to look at myself first and foremost. I should have been more professional in taking responsibility for my own career.

“I have actually always very politely complied with what others said. That is how I was raised, too. If someone tells you what to do, especially when it is your boss, you do it. You assume that it is best for you. But over the past two years, I have regularly asked myself what I missed out on.

“Shouldn't I have taken more responsibility to get the most out of my career? Shouldn't I have chosen myself a little more now and then, or banged my fist on the table more? Perhaps my situation would look different now. Do I blame myself for that? I think so, actually,” he said.

Van Belle never raced a Grand Tour with the team and has signed for Dutch continental outfit BEAT CC p/b Saxo for the 2027 season. His hope now is to return to the professional ranks in the future, having overcome health issues that have limited him.

Along with a concussion after a crash at GP de Denain this year, which kept him away from racing for six weeks, the native of Zoetermeer had an iliac artery operation in 2025 - a procedure to ease a lack of blood flow, which is common for cyclists.

“I had probably been riding around with that for three and a half years. After that surgery, it felt like a mental brake was released. Finally, I could race freely again, without constantly being afraid that I wouldn't be able to continue after just one effort,” he said of his iliac artery issue.

“That blockage was huge, not only physically but also mentally. Together with the team, we tried to figure out what was going on. But precisely during that period, in hindsight, I perhaps should have taken more responsibility myself. I will take that lesson with me.”

After the surgery, Van Belle made progress on the bike and hoped for a renewed contract for 2027. However, Visma-Lease a Bike decided to let the rider go, bringing in British rider Mark Donovan from Pinarello-Q36.5 and Belgian Matisse van Kerckhove from the development team.

items.title: Wahoo CEO talks finances, artificial intelligence and the company's 'next big opportunity'
items.author: josh.croxton@futurenet.com (Josh Croxton)
items.content:
Wahoo Fitness has returned to year on year growth following its recapitalisation in 2023, CEO Gareth Joyce has revealed.

Speaking exclusively to , Joyce opened up on a broad range of subjects, including why it took so long to update the Kickr Core despite growing the Kickr to its sixth iteration, why it launched a treadmill, the reasoning behind its partnership with Coros, and why 2038 is going to be a heck of a busy year.

He outlined a business very much with cycling still at its centre, but explained that running taking increasing amounts of importance. And he explained that there’s a busy product roadmap ahead, with "seven or eight" launches in the pipeline for 2027 following a year spent reorganising development

Joyce, an engineer and keen cyclist and runner who joined Wahoo in 2024, had never worked in the bike industry before and admits he wasn’t an obvious candidate for the CEO role, but that his then-recent experience talking a company through Chapter 11 bankruptcy made him perfectly qualified given Wahoo’s financial turbulence at the time.

He sees his role as bringing a sense of corporate structure to a startup business. He explained that Wahoo’s foundations were built on innovation, but its scale no longer supports that model of working.

"It’s no longer just a startup," he said. "We’ve got a large customer base that you have a responsibility to."

Asked whether the changes following Wahoo’s recapitalisation are working, Joyce’s answer was pretty conclusive.

"We’ve had very strong growth coming out of that," he said. "We have a great brand, great product, very committed customer base, and there were some things we needed to fix in the business which we paid attention to early on.

"We’ve seen growth year over year in all of the years since the recapitalisation, and I expect this year to be the same."

Naturally, he declined to provide any actual figures, so the extent of Wahoo’s profitability will have to remain unknown, but he affirmed that key "operational changes" are key to the business’s newfound momentum.

Among those changes was burying the hatchet with Zwift, with whom Wahoo was in a year-long lawsuit, after Wahoo claimed the Zwift Hub smart trainer infringed on its patents.

"If we work together, we can grow the industry," he said. "That was what Eric [Min, Zwift co-founder and CEO] and I set out to achieve."

The ball had already begun rolling on this before Joyce’s appointment. The lawsuit was settled in September 2023, the Kickr Core Zwift One launched in March 2024, and Joyce was appointed in April. But he says working with Zwift - and other brands - is now central to how Wahoo should expand. An example of this includes Wahoo’s partnership with competitor brand Coros.

Product plans and clearer priorities

Joyce argued that Wahoo’s innovation and its ability to come up with good ideas can make it difficult to decide which to pursue.

"You tend to become a little chaotic with your product strategy because every idea is a good idea," he said. "When you try and make every product that you think is a good idea, you end up distributing your resources and a distributed focus."

His solution to this was to revisit the company’s mission of "building the better athlete in all of us" and judge product ideas against it. Cycling remained – and still remains – the foundation, with indoor trainers, GPS computers and surrounding accessories supplying the data an athlete needs, but this is underpinned by software. The new Wahoo app was quietly rolled out this year, after a long period of beta testing.

The revised strategy also meant an overhaul of its product launch cycles, which explains some of the recent quiet on the launch front.

"This year was a pretty lean year of releases for us, which was by design," Joyce explained. "Last year, when we kind of reset the product strategy, we then had to reset the engineering program."

He expects the results to become more visible in 2027.

"Next year we have a pretty healthy set of product launches. I think we have seven or eight in the pipeline," he says. "I’m currently testing three of them as we speak. In fact, some of them are lying on my desk."

Unfortunately he turned down my invite for a game of show and tell, despite me awkwardly presenting the Wahoo Elemnt Bolt 2 that was lying on my desk.

Alongside that reset is a longer-term change to Wahoo’s product cycles and release cadence.

I asked why the Kickr Core went from 2018 to 2025 without any update, while the flagship Kickr trainer grew to its sixth iteration – seven if you count the Kickr Move.

"There was no rational reason for that replacement cadence," Joyce conceded. "The market was not demanding changes that quickly."

Wahoo is now working around different cycles for different categories: roughly three years for bike computers, four for indoor trainers, and six for heart rate monitors and treadmills.

I joked that he’s going to have a busy 2038 when those cycles overlap in their 12th year, to which he was keen to re-emphasise the use of the word "roughly" and affirmed that those are loose assumptions, rather than a fixed calendar.

The slowed approach also reflects his view on indoor cycling, and the slowing nature of the technology’s innovation.

"I think it’s now entering that phase of iterative development rather than disruptive technology," he said. "That’s not to say it’ll never happen, but just right now, there’s not something that we see on the horizon of, let’s say, five years, that would be disruptive in nature."

He immediately qualified that by adding "that doesn’t mean we’ve thought of everything."

Wahoo didn’t cut its teeth in running, but in 2024, Wahoo launched a treadmill known as the Kickr Run. As Joyce explains, the plan was to take the formula that saw Wahoo transform indoor cycling, and apply it to another sport.

It’s not quite had the same uptake in the 2.5 years since it launched as the smart trainer, but nevertheless Joyce sees it as an important growth category, and one where there’s plenty of opportunity for innovation and disruption.

"Treadmills, for a very long time, have been terrible products," he says.

And to that end, the Coros partnership adds weight to Wahoo’s move into running, but also demonstrates where Joyce believes Wahoo should avoid spreading itself thin.

The Elemnt Rival smartwatch can’t hold a candle to the quality of launches from market leader Garmin, nor can Wahoo keep up with their annual release cycle. Instead, rather than invest in a complete watch range to compete directly, it chose to work with Coros.

"To develop multiple SKUs is a very big investment, takes a lot of time, and would distract our attention from the rest of the strategy," he explained.

The goal is to provide access to products for cycling and running, indoors and outdoors, developing those products in house where possible, and partnering with others where not.

Connecting indoor and outdoor training

Joyce recognises that many of its customers aren’t exclusively doing one sport, nor are they only doing it indoors or out.

"That boundary is no longer in and out of your house. It’s just cycling," he explained.

And that’s where the Wahoo software offering comes into play. Wahoo has had multiple apps running concurrently for years, one controlling hardware and another providing training solutions, and Joyce is relieved at the recent consolidation.

"If our mission is building the better athlete in all of us, and I can’t tell you whether you’re becoming a better athlete or not, then it’s kind of hard to make that brand play."

If he can reduce the number of apps, or streamline the way in which the heart rate monitor, GPS computer and smart trainer all talk to third party suppliers, efficiencies can be found.

Two approaches to artificial intelligence

When asked about AI, Joyce separated Wahoo’s use of the fast-growing tech into two buckets: internally, how the brand uses it day to day, and externally, i.e. what AI integration might offer customers. Within the business, AI is already used extensively across software, firmware and hardware engineering.

"We’ve seen significant acceleration in our development cycles of products, particularly software," he said, pointing to faster app updates as one example.

He also said AI is being leveraged to help his Customer Service team resolve issues more quickly, while remaining entirely human.

However, for consumer-facing features, such as the AI Coach revealed by Zwift this week, or the AI-based adaptive training used by TrainerRoad, Joyce is more cautious. He believes customers may prefer to use AI services they already pay for, whether that’s the aforementioned, or a direct account with Claude or Chat GPT.

Voicing that customer’s perspective, he said: "I don’t want five licences for AI accounts. I want you to be able to pass me the data where I want it."

That helps explain why Wahoo has yet to commit to a consumer AI offering, despite the fast pace of the industry. Where Joyce does see an opportunity, however, is in Wahoo’s enormous database of accumulated workout data.

"We have records of workout data that goes back over a decade. We have the capability to translate that data into meaning, which is the next big opportunity we see, which we’re now starting to work on using machine learning and AI."

And for that database of workout data, Joyce’s data is as prevalent as any others.

"I love cycling. I love my running. To be able to go out on a Saturday and do a long ride and test stuff... yes, you could technically say that’s work, but for me it’s not."

items.title: 'A contract is about more than salary' - The Cyclists' Alliance 2026 rider survey finds financial insecurity, health and safety issues among the main concerns of the women's peloton
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
The Cyclists' Alliance, a leading labour organisation in women's cycling, has released the findings of its 2026 rider survey. Financial insecurity beyond the Women's WorldTour level and health, welfare and safety issues are the top concerns among 127 riders (118 road riders) surveyed.

The 'State of the Professional Women's Peloton 2026' report found that the sport is currently "creating opportunities" while still leaving riders lacking "the financial security, care and development pathway they need."

The six priorities for women's cycling based on the responses gathered, according to the TCA, include financial security, race safety, health and welfare, safeguarding, development, and broadcast visibility.

The financial aspect of the report found that 75% of the 52 Continental racers who responded to the survey receive no salary from their team, while 52% reported uncovered travel costs. Of riders at Continental level, 73% cited financial pressure as the main factor in considering quitting the sport.

In response, The Cyclists' Alliance has asked the UCI to revise and strengthen its model contract to ensure riders' "essential racing costs" are covered, as well as verifying teams can meet their commitments.

"A contract is about more than salary. Riders need to know what protection they have, and where the gaps are; if they face injury, pregnancy, illness or a change in their team’s plans. TCA members can access independent contract and legal advice before signing and when problems arise," said TCA legal and ethics officer, Judith van Maanen.

On the issue of rider safety, over 60% of respondents cited road furniture, rider behaviour, poor road surfaces, and unsafe final kilometres as concerns.

Only 17% of Continental respondents have access to regular medical screening, compared with 90% of riders in the Women's WorldTour, while 23% of respondents reported negative or toxic team environments as a factor in considering quitting the sport.

The Cyclists' Alliance has requested that the UCI establish RED-S screening in mandatory medical monitoring, safeguards for riders recovering from injury, more "female-specific research" into the health demands of the women's peloton, that riders be able to access "confidential, independent support", and that more stringent verification of staff qualifications and safeguarding credentials be put in place.

"You don’t have to wait until something becomes misconduct to ask for help. If a comment, request or relationship makes you uncomfortable, or simply doesn’t feel right, talk to us to understand the situation, your boundaries and your options. You will be listened to," said Van Maanen.

Elsewhere, development pathways for young riders were raised as an issue, with the cancellation of the 2026 Tour de l'Avenir Femes and the switch of several races from 1.2 to 1.1 highlighted as examples of roads to the top of the sport being closed.

Full coverage of the biggest races on the calendar, such as the Tour de France Femmes and Paris-Roubaix Femmes, was also raised by 49% of respondents, with greater coverage leading to bigger audiences, higher sponsor value, and more investment in the sport.

items.title: Indoor cycling is boring, discuss – A for-and-against debate on the sport's most polarising training tool
items.author: josh.croxton@futurenet.com (Josh Croxton)
items.content:
It’s Indoor Cycling Week here at , a week in which we centre our tech content on the fast-growing world of virtual cycling.

We’re all different, so this article is going to explore the other side of the virtual coin.

Even here within the editorial team, there’s a broad range of opinion. I personally rather enjoy cycling indoors. It’s convenient, structured, safe, and I can know what time I’ll be finished with to-the-minute precision, making planning it into my day perfectly easy.

But others here hate it. On one recent call, one of my colleagues’ immediate replies was: “I’d rather pull my nails out.”

That, and other things mentioned below, are a few of the opinions that have been flying around amongst the CN Team this week, so we thought we would package them up for you to enjoy. They might ruffle some feathers, but balance and honesty are important in journalism, so hopefully we don’t upset too many people.

Indoor training doesn't make a peloton-ready cyclist

When I was racing, I had a love-hate relationship with my indoor trainers. This was before Zwift and the gamification of cycling, when riders only spent time on the trainer if they had broken an arm, had to work during the short daylight hours, or it was snowing. When I had to ride indoors, it was usually one focussed hour of intervals.

Maybe it's because I was a competitive swimmer as a kid and was used to counting minutes of effort and seconds of rest without outside entertainment - but some loud music or an old Paris-Roubaix replay on the TV for inspiration was more than enough.

I miss the days when indoor training was a much-loathed necessity

I've done my time on Zwift, and the gamification aspect can inspire riders to make impressive aerobic fitness and strength gains. However, for me, it de-emphasises what is the best part of being a cyclist is: being immersed in the flow of the peloton, learning etiquette from the more experienced riders, getting fit together and then pushing faster and further than you could ever do on your own.

I remember doing a 'century' (100 miles/161km) in the flatter part of eastern North Carolina with a well-disciplined group of about 20 riders, just pace-lining, no attacks or other hijinks, and finishing in four hours. No stops, no rest, just beautifully efficient at 40kph.

But then came the apps, and dudes started showing up at group rides with impressive fitness from a winter of Zwift, with all the confidence of a member of the masochist club, absolutely no idea how to ride in a group, and zero interest in learning. They were an absolute menace in the bunch: hostile to any advice, frustratingly resistant to being flicked out the back, disrupting the flow completely with attacks, and totally ruining the vibe.

Yes, I'm a curmudgeon, but I really miss the days when indoor training was a much-loathed necessity and road cycling was an in-person collective effort, not just a chance to show off your watts/kg on the no-drop group ride. I think the beauty of a peloton moving like a murmuration at speed is an essential part of cycling culture - and one that an app just cannot teach.

'I don’t hate it as much as I used to'

Let’s get this straight: indoor cycling is not my happy place, but on the other hand, I don’t hate as much as I used to. For me, cycling is about being outside; it might be a cliché, but I enjoy the wind in my face, experiencing the day whether it’s warm or cold, feeling the tyres rolling; it’s all so much better than staring at a closed garage door. It’s a bit sad that someone my age sees every ride as an adventure, but I do; when I ride, I’ve been somewhere and done something.

It’s also about joy. But joy is not clattering into potholes in the dark, and riding in the rain is one of the least joyful things I’ve ever done voluntarily. I won’t ride in the rain; I own a rain jacket, but I’ve only worn it three times in six years. This is where the turbo trainer comes in.

I’m not going to race again, and I can’t remember the last time I did an organised event, so I’m not ‘training’, but I want to continue enjoying outdoor rides and maintain my overall fitness; a bit of exertion stops me getting grumpy, too. So when the days are short, or the weather is bad, you will find me on the turbo.

Back when ‘dumb’ trainers were the only option, I hated it and set a limit of 30 minutes, but a smart turbo and indoor apps make it doable, and much better. Picking one of the workouts on Zwift helps me add some structure, and more importantly, some interest to my indoor riding. It’s also time-efficient; I get a decent workout from an indoor ride, and sometimes it’s even fun as well as productive.

But for me it’s a solo affair. Maybe it’d be better with all the groups, chats and messages, but I’m not interested, partly because I’m a little antisocial and partly because I don’t wear my glasses as they steam up. I won’t notice if you’ve given me one of those thumbs-up Ride On things because unless it’s a very easy session, I just can’t see.

Indoor cycling isn’t going to make me a better bike handler; I won’t have any meaningful social interaction, and it can’t replicate the richness that riding outside creates in my soul. But it does help my fitness and provides a close enough facsimile of the real thing that I get genuine satisfaction out of it. I am now off to ride Zwift for a while; I just won’t see you if you’re there.

Give me a training plan, an erg mode workout and make me follow a line on a graph and I can pluck up the motivation, so long as I know there’s an end goal being pursued. Put me in a virtual world and ask me to ‘free ride’, and I’ll be bored in 10 minutes. I know it’s basically the same principle as ‘free riding’ outside, but the flow state I experience with steering, wind and tyre noise, cars passing, route planning and so on, just doesn’t come when it’s a virtual avatar pedalling awkwardly through a pixelated landscape. Even with the advent of in-game steering and the noise of the fan, I get bored.

Invariably I open YouTube or Netflix, or I get off the bike.

That’s not to say indoor cycling is bad. It can definitely serve a purpose, and to have helped more people be more active, I’m all for it. But it’s not fun. Not the type 1 variety anyway.

I love riding bikes outside, but I also used to get a perverse satisfaction from my old school, wheel-on trainer in combination with a stopwatch, a towel, and somewhere to be sick. It got me very fit for racing cyclo-cross, and while it didn't replicate the fun of riding outside it was efficient, and masochistic in a way that pottering about up a pretend volcano can never replicate.

The thing I love about outdoor cycling is the effort in combination with all of the lovely sensations, but in the absence of those lovely sensations of cornering, wind, a snotty nose, the spray of leaf mulch on my shins, and the abominable noise of modern freehubs, I just want .

Modern indoor training isn't rubbish because it doesn't replicate outdoors well enough, it's rubbish because it puts too many barriers between me and getting my heart rate up to something approaching maximum while I listen to Bullet For My Valentine. I don't want to log into an app, realise the WiFi connection is spotty, dig out the extender, pair my trainer and heart rate monitor with the laptop, update nine different firmwares, choose a course, realise that bit of the map is locked, choose a different course, wait for it to buffer.... and finally ride. At each of those steps the risk of me just giving up in frustration becomes higher.

I just want a machine to provide resistance and a brick wall to stare at. I don't want to race a man from Finland. I know it's still possible, but it's becoming much rarer.

The contrasting (positive) opinion: Indoor offers almost everything I need from cycling

For me, cycling is not about the wind in my hair, an in-the-moment adventure or finding the path less travelled. It’s about being competitive, racing, testing myself and sprinting for the finish line with a chance of victory.

Riding outdoors teaches a part of that: bunch etiquette, handling, tyre grip limits and so on. But once you’ve got those skills, they don’t need much refinement. And without a good foundation of fitness, those skills aren’t particularly useful anyway.

And riding outdoors is fine for building that foundation of fitness, but I can do it much more quickly and comprehensively on a smart trainer with a machine forcing me to ride at a set power output. It also means an hour of riding takes about an hour and five minutes. Unlike riding outside in winter, where an hour’s ride takes close to two hours, once you factor in getting changed twice and cleaning the bike.

A few years ago, I spent an entire summer training indoors for the British Gravel National Championships. Knowing the route wasn’t technical, and knowing I had bunch etiquette down from years of racing on the road, I don’t think I did more than four or five rides outside before the race. I finished fourth.

items.title: USPro criterium star Luke Elphingstone, 'a Michael Matthews kind of rider', among three national champions featured in younger Project Echelon Racing squad for 2027
items.author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
items.content:
Three national champions feature on a leaner roster for Project Echelon Racing in 2027. The team are adding five new riders to a lineup with eight returning teammates, three of those having performed as stagiaires last season.

The trimmed roster of 13 riders moves the average age from 25.5 to 22.6 years, in what the team called a "big transition year", their fifth at the UCI Continental level. Seven familiar faces depart, including Eric Brunner, Ricky Arnopol, Stephen Bassett, and Laurent Gervais, who have been with the team for the past three or more years.

"These guys have been with me for a long time and helped me build a really strong legacy with Project Echelon. Retiring or just moving on, the majority of the guys were going to be leaving, and I wanted to give them an opportunity to leave on their own terms and move on to a different phase of life," Eric Hill, Project Echelon Racing team director and non-profit co-founder, told

Arnopol and Gervais are retiring, while others were "just taking a different direction", such as Bassett, a former USPro criterium champion, and Brunner, a three-time US elite cyclo-cross champion who was expected to begin his 'cross season at Cycle-Smart Northampton Cyclocross UCI C2 races in Massachusetts. Caleb Classen, Quinn Felton and Ethan Craine also bid farewell.

Hill was excited to have consistency with "cornerstone" riders back, such as Tim McBirney, who was third overall at the 2026 Tour de Beauce, as well as versatility with Brendan Rhim and Colby Lange, who have been with the team for four and five years, respectively. Second-year riders Elphingstone and Gauthier will showcase their national jerseys with the team's international calendar.

"He's a Michael Matthews kind of rider. If it's a straight-up drag race sprint, he's going to be in the mix," Hill said about the 23-year-old Elphingstone, who performed well in stage races with stage wins at the Tucson Bicycle Classic and Tour de Bloom, then a podium at the Tour of Samsun in Turkey in the back half of last season.

"Jérôme's just an absolute grinder, and you know, when things are uncomfortable, and people want to start giving up is kind of when he shines," Hill added about the 22-year-old Canadian.

Gauthier finished second at the UCI 1.2 Gran Premio New York City and scored 4 top 10s at Tour de Beauce, including a podium on the final day in Saint-Georges, to win the youth classification. However, it was at Canadian road nationals, where he won the elite road race and, with it, also secured the U23 title, that exhibited that true grit.

"It was cold and raining and windy and miserable, to the point where they had to take down the finish banners because it was too windy and postpone the podium celebration. He just thrives in that type of gritty environment, and he made it happen for himself."

A trio of stagiaires return to the squad on one-year contracts: 19-year-old Canadian Jacob Roy and 20-year-old US talents, Ben Boroff and Noah Shelton.

Boroff caught attention for a stage win at the Tucson Bicycle Classic and then held the points competition lead in the American Criterium Cup for several weeks until he went to Turkey to race for Project Echelon. Shelton was also on the late-season swing to Europe and impressed with a stage podium at Tour of Istanbul.

Two 19-year-olds debut Project Echelon: Canadian Arnaud Lajoie, who moves from Team Skyline and US rider Garrett Beshore, who rode with Roy and Kreikemeier at Meridian Racing.

Kreikemeier made his big step this year at USPro Road Nationals, winning the U23 ITT. He rode the last three seasons with small Spanish squads, his best season in 2024 in national stage races, sixth overall at Vuelta a Ávila and second on GC at the Vuelta Zamora.

The final two new riders are Dylan Fluckiger, 24, who has a US collegiate medal in the time trial, and Jesse Maris, 22, a native of Washington in the Pacific Northwest who had a breakout ride at the Volta a Portugal U23 stage race, placing in the top 10 in all four stages and finishing third on GC.

The team starts 2027 with a camp in Southern California at the end of January and will transition for racing and more training in Arizona with Valley of the Sun and Tucson Bicycle Classic stage races. They will travel in the spring to Croatia, Spain and Portugal for racing before a swing back for Redlands Bicycle Classic, then to Tour of Norway.

They'll have a long North American campaign through the end of June with the back half of the year in Europe. A special focus will be on three US races – the Armed Forces Cycling Classic, Battenkill, and Philadelphia Cycling Classic.

"To have this kind of resurgence of some of these one-day classics in North America, and to be able to end our season with all of these, is really important to us. Especially these guys that are retiring [and were] at Philadelphia this year, Ricky and Laurent, was really cool to see."

items.title: 'Unfinished business' – Vuelta return more likely for Tadej Pogačar in 2027 than Giro, says agent Carera
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
Tadej Pogačar's agent said the sport's top rider has "unfinished business" with the Vuelta a España after crashing out while leading the race on stage 8 back in August, making a return in 2027 to the Spanish Grand Tour look more likely.

While no confirmation of Pogačar's racing schedule will be announced until the team's training camp media day in December, his agent, Alex Carera, has pointed to an immediate return after a high-speed crash prevented him from completing the set of Grand Tour GC wins. Having suffered fractures to his collarbone and neck, and a concussion, Pogačar's season came to an abrupt end.

The route for the Giro will be announced on November 3, with the Grande Partenza in Trieste expected to venture into Slovenia. Even considering that, Carera was of the belief that the Vuelta will be prioritised, having already won the pink jersey in 2024.

"Tadej clearly has unfinished business with the Vuelta, and he doesn't like having unfinished business," said Carera on RAI programme 'RadioCorsa'.

"However, the final decision on which stage races he'll compete in 2027 will be made in December, when he'll be in the United Arab Emirates with the team for a collective training period.

"Tadej will sit down with all the UAE sports directors, with general director Mauro Gianetti and technical director Joxean Matxin Fernandez. That will be the moment when it will be decided which race he will compete in in 2027. Then, if I had to make a prediction, the chances of him returning to the Vuelta a España are higher than those of him starting the Giro d'Italia."

"The desire for next year would of course be the World Championships combined with the Tour and the Vuelta," said Pogačar.

"If the Vuelta somehow didn't work out this year... Even if I would rather go to the Giro, I will have to check off the Vuelta at some point. I think that will be the goal for next year."

Pogačar will have just five days to recover from returning to the Worlds in France before the start of the Vuelta on September 4 – moved back to accommodate the early 'super' Worlds in Haute-Savoie – and with such a back-loaded calendar, appearances in the early season look unlikely.

There is talk of him making a first return to the Tour Down Under in January since his WorldTour debut seven years ago, with race director Stuart O’Grady admitting last week that he is "doing everything" to try and get Pogačar to start in Australia. But this would mark a change from his past few seasons, which have mostly either started as late as March or at the UAE Tour in mid-February.

What Classics and Monuments he returns to in 2027 also remains unknown before December, but the Worlds and the Tour – where he will be chasing a record sixth yellow jersey – look all but certain.

Carera also commented on the route, which was revealed on October 22 in Paris, after there was some talk of it resembling an 'Anti-Pogačar' route, with the duo of 30km+ time trials being more in favour of his closest competitor from this past season, Remco Evenepoel.

"I don't know if you can call the TDF 'anti-Pogačar'," Carera said.

"I'll just say one thing: if every rider interviewed gets asked about Pogačar, if organizers are changing their routes to make things interesting against Tadej, and if sponsors keep referring to him, it means he matters enormously to cycling. Whether these time trials will put him in difficulty or not, we'll see. He's still the man to beat."

items.title: Wind tunnel tested: The UCI-illegal Merida Reacto One was designed to beat the wind tunnel tests – it failed, but that's only half the story
items.author: josh.croxton@futurenet.com (Josh Croxton)
items.content:
By every objective measure, the Reacto One isn't a groundbreaking bike, but subjectively it's brilliant. A really enjoyable bike to ride, and I love that Merida went a bit wild. Progressive spec.

Comfortable ride with confident handling.

Value for money is pretty good, when compared to others of this level.Sub-par aero performance despite having an unfair advantage.

Heavier than competitor bikes of similar aero performance.

UCI-illegal bars could cause issues if you want to race it.72%

The Merida Reacto One is a bike that confuses me. It sort of proves you can't always judge a book by its cover. But then again, it sort of proves you can.

With its narrow handlebars, one-by (Classified-equipped) groupset, deep wheels and aero tubes, it looks as if it was designed to 'win' the wind tunnel tests performed by ourselves and other media.

It should have been a prime candidate for the top spot in our aero bike wind tunnel testing, but it fell remarkably short of the current leaders, Factor's One and Cervélo's S5, landing a disappointing result; the details of which are below.

It was better than the older Reacto we tested in 2025, but despite being a full-house bingo card of go-faster tricks that make it UCI-illegal and are undoubtedly an unfair advantage compared to other bikes, it barely scraped the top 10.

But then when I climbed aboard it and rode it in earnest, I liked almost everything about it. The position was great, the handling was superb, it was plenty responsive under power, and it was decently comfortable.

  • £9,500.00 / $N/A / €11,000.00
  • 7.73kg (no pedals, computer or bottles).
  • 3XS, 2XS, XS, S, M, L, XL
  • Shimano Dura-Ace x Classified Powershift, Rotor Aldhu crank
  • DT Swiss Arc 1100 65mm
  • Red/Silver, Silver/Black
  • 32mm (with room to spare)
  • 52T chainset x 11-30 cassette as tested, plus Classified Powershift

The Merida Reacto One is the black sheep in the wider Reacto range. All of the other Reacto Models are 'normal' in that they come with two-by groupsets from Shimano or SRAM, and handlebars that are UCI-legal in their width.

The One – not to be confused with the Factor One (or even the Trek Mad(One)) – is a showcase of what the product team can create when they're let a little loose.

The Taiwanese brand partnered with some revered European brands to kit the bike out with the set menu from the aero playbook. DT Swiss supplied its ARC 1100 Dicut 65mm deep wheels, Continental supplied the Aero 111 front tyre, and Classified chipped in its Powershift rear-hub gear system, which in turn meant Rotor could supply a 1x aero chainring alongside its InSpider power meter chainset.

Perhaps most pertinent of all, though, is that Vision supplied a super-narrow, special edition Merida Team CW 1P cockpit that measured a grand total of just 22.5cm between the Shimano Dura-Ace hoods. And no, I've not got the hoods set up tilted inwards like a 2022 WorldTour pro.

It's an off-the-shelf version of what I think I'd build for the type of crit racing that suits me best – flat, fast and tightly packed, rather than hilly or too punchy. Deep wheels, one-by groupset, big chainring, small cassette, narrow bars and aero frame. The Classified groupset is a nice touch, and one that means you get the aerodynamics of one-by without compromising on gear range or steps, meaning you can actually live with it and ride it at the weekend without messing about with swapping wheels or cassettes around. I like it. It's well thought out.

Notably, and this perhaps goes some way to explain why it didn't storm to victory in our wind tunnel test, that narrow cockpit is mainly achieved through a massive flare from the tops to the drops, as the outside-to-outside measurement down there is actually 42cm.

When we test in the wind tunnel, we do so with our hands in the drops, meaning the narrow bars didn't really have an opportunity to shine. If I'd performed the same test in more of an aero position with hands on the hoods, horizontal forearms and elbows bent to 90°, the narrowness would have probably made a difference.

It would have also been less comparable to other bikes and thus, less of a fair test.

Also, I can't hold that position for more than a few minutes at a time, and I'm going to bet that not many others can either. On the flip side, it only takes a few minutes at a time to make the difference in a race sometimes, so you can spin it that way if you prefer.

Elsewhere, the bike promises 32mm tyre clearance front and rear. The 29mm Aero 111 tyre up front measured at exactly 29mm on the DT Swiss wheels, and the clearance measured amply at 12mm either side, so you could easily go wider if you wanted.

At the rear, the 30mm GP5000 S TR tyre measured at 31mm, with 6mm of room to spare on either side according to our calipers, so you could probably get away with a little more than claimed, but not much. Perhaps 34mm if you're in need of cobble-smoothing comfort.

And while I'm on the subject of measuring, the Reacto One tipped our scales at a not-bad-but-not-excellent 7.73kg (weighed without pedals, computer mount, or bottle cages).

Okay, I've dallied long enough. Time to get stuck into the stuff you're really here for.

As with all our wind tunnel tests, we took the Reacto to the Silverstone Sports Engineering Hub, tested it back-to-back against our baseline bike (as well as a handful of other competitors on the same day), to measure how aerodynamic it is. Using its comparison against that baseline bike, which remains unchanged between tests, we can also measure it against bikes we've tested in years gone by.

We test every bike in three separate setups: the bike on its own first, then the bike with a rider, then finally we swap in a 'control' wheelset to isolate the differences found in the frame/fork and cockpit.

We test each of these setups across seven distinct wind angles – -15°, -10°, -5°, 0°, 5°, 10°, and 15° – for a total of 21 different measurements.

And we test at a wind speed of 40km/h, for either 15 or 30 seconds per measurement, depending on whether it's with or without a rider.

Everything that can be controlled remains unchanged between tests, including the tyres, the bottles, the clothing and so on, and we do our best to ensure the bike setup and rider position are the same across all tests, no matter what bike is being tested.

Starting with the raw measurements for the two tests without a rider. This doesn't tell us too much, aside from that the DT Swiss Wheels tested slightly faster than our Enve SES 4.5 control wheels, especially at higher yaw angles. Hardly a surprise given the depth difference.

From here, as we do with all our tests, I've run some calculations and applied weightings to land on an average that's relevant to real world conditions. From here, we can then see how many watts the Reacto One saves against our baseline.

As suggested at the top of this review, I'm pretty disappointed to see it down in 11th place. Don't get me wrong, that's still a reasonable result and one that puts aero bikes like the Giant Propel, Canyon Aeroad and X-Lab AD9 to shame, not to mention its own predecessor, but I was expecting more for a bike that pulled out all the aero tricks.

The Reacto One is exactly four watts behind the Factor One, and very much on par with the new Enve Melee v2, which is much more of an all-rounder in its design.

Next up, things don't really get any better when we swap in our control wheels…

We only introduced the control wheel test in 2025, so some of the older bikes are missing, but the Reacto is still mid-table, approximately five watts behind the Factor One. The Cannondale SuperSix even climbs ahead, which is another all-rounder.

We're splitting hairs, of course; it's still 35 watts better than our baseline bike, but I can't help but feel disappointed with its result.

Next up, let's check what happens when we chuck a rider on the bike.

At first glance, things start to look a little rosier here. At certain wind angles, the Merida is actually faster than the Factor One, which remains our benchmark (even though the Cervelo S5 snuck ahead by a fraction once the weightings had been applied).

But this only really happens at the wider yaw angles, which we know aren't seen anywhere near as commonly in the real world. Therefore, when we get to the averaged result, the rankings are as follows.

The big caveat to this data is that our error margin is bigger than many of the differences between the bikes, so the Reacto lay claim to a victory, but it be right near the bottom of the table.

But taking the results as they come, the Reacto One is once again around five watts behind the leaders, in 10th place.

When it first arrived at HQ, I was reluctant to test the Reacto in our wind tunnel test at all. Clearly it's a bike designed to be aero, and part of me feared it would win the test and I'd forever have to caveat that "of course it won, it was specced with 22cm handlebars." But when it came to measuring up, the bar width at the drops was no narrower than our baseline bike. 42cm outside-to-outside.

The 1x groupset is still a bit sneaky, but Merida does sell the bike like this, so why should I leave it off the test? Factor was radical and progressive when designing the ONE, and we tested that. Merida kept things relatively sane when designing the Reacto frame, but then applied that progressive mindset to the spec. Two routes to a similar end goal, really.

If the Reacto One stormed to victory, I would be caveating this write-up heavily, saying you could also just fit a 1x groupset or narrow bars to any other bike, so the test was unfair and so on.

And, well, you can, and that's pretty damning for Merida. Despite having a significant spec advantage, the Reacto still didn't challenge the top spots.

But – and this is a very large but – I don't care.

As it happens, I went from reviewing the Factor One straight onto the Merida, and while I appreciate I'm probably a bit boring for saying this, I'd take the Merida almost every time.

Objectively, by a true performance yardstick, the Factor does most things better, particularly power transfer, sprinting, aerodynamics, steering directness, and holding pace when tanking along flat ground. But, subjectively, I still preferred riding the Reacto. I had a much nicer time on it every time I rode it, and whatever performance I was probably giving away didn't really feel worth stressing about.

Power transfer felt plenty enough, albeit this is what stood out the most when comparing the two, mainly because it's so insanely good on the Factor. The narrow cockpit was easy to get used to, despite my inability to hold an aero-hoods position for more than a few minutes. The comfort through the bars made it a much better bike to ride, so I was more confident on descents, and I was able to ride for longer without feeling beat up. I couldn't go more than an hour without aches and pains on the Factor, but I did multiple four-hour rides on the Merida without issue.

This isn't a head-to-head between just two bikes, but even compared to other bikes I've ridden lately, which includes the Tarmac SL9, the Merida is the one I've enjoyed most. It strikes a solid balance between being race-ready, something you can ride to the cafe at the weekend, and something you can do your intervals on after work in the evenings.

It wasn't completely without fault, though. For one, I had a terrible time with the Aero 111 tyre up front, puncturing three times in a single ride and five times overall in my two months of testing. It's hard to say whether that's due to the narrowness of the DT Swiss wheels, the fragility of a TT tyre, or just a coincidental streak of bad luck.

I also struggled to get on with the Classified Powershift drivetrain, which wasn't running as smoothly as I'd experienced before. The shift itself is instant, but there's still a small delay after you press the shift button. I found that sometimes it didn't register the click, and during that small delay, there's no feedback to confirm whether it's registered. So it was a case of click, wait, nothing, click again, shift! It's a first-world problem, but it was annoying no less.

The one problem I can actually attribute to Merida, though, was that the plastic cap that sits over the steerer tube and cockpit bolts didn't fit properly. On one fateful trip over a cattle grid (aka Texas gates for those outside the UK), it came off and went on a little journey to the wrong side of the road, where it was duly run over by a passing car. I retrieved it, but you'll see how bent it is in the photos.

And finally, to round off the negatives, the little metal grills that Merida insists on putting over its brake calipers are, to put it nicely, the devil. I have scars on my left ankle from repeatedly catching it. The best thing about them is that they're removable, and should be the first thing you do if you buy this bike. Sorry to the Merida designers reading this, but in your defence, it's a small thing to find so irksome, so the rest of the bike must be pretty good.

At £9,500, for a bike with a progressive top-spec build, competitive (albeit not quite leading) aero performance, and a reasonable weight, I don't think you can complain too much, given the price of the aforementioned competitors.

Here in the UK, it's £2,499 cheaper than a top-spec S-Works Tarmac SL9 - currently £11,999. Or £2,699 less than the Factor ONE (£12,199).

It's still an inordinate amount of money to spend on a bike, but if you're in the market for a top-tier bike, it's a pretty good option as long as you're not going to want to upgrade your wheels anytime soon, as the Classified Powershift hub locks you into using the DT Swiss ones specced.

It's not the cheapest in its class, though. For a comparison in the other direction, you can get a Canyon Aeroad CFR with Dura-Ace and very similar DT Swiss wheels (the same but 55mm instead of 65mm) for £1000 less. Having not ridden the latest Aeroad, I can't comment on a direct comparison, but it is a more 'normal' build with UCI-legal bars.

Overall, I really liked the Reacto One. I like that a brand known for being safe, good value – dare I say boring? – has the wherewithal and panache to sell a bike with a UCI-illegal 22cm handlebar, rather than just selling it as a frameset and forcing people to make their own fun.

And in execution, I think it has pulled it off. It's a bike that sits in a nice sweet spot between everyday liveable, race-day ready, and a little bit mad.

Maybe, just maybe, I'm seeing a bike that's otherwise a little underwhelming through rose-tinted glasses because of its aero-ification and the factor that it brings. It's hard to say whether I'd have enjoyed riding the 10K or Pro models, with their more common specs, as much as I did this.

But I think sometimes the objective comparison is allowed to give way to the subjective opinion. Aerodynamically, the results are okay. Top ten, not bad. Nothing to write home about, but the Merida Reacto One is a good bike.

Testing scorecard and notes

Deep wheels, aero tubes, 1x chainset, narrow bars. It looks fast standing still, and the paint scheme complements it

7.7kg for a deep-everything aero bike isn't bad, but there are others with similar wind tunnel credentials that come out much lighter.

A competitive result, but in the context of the spec, it's pretty underwhelming, and had it been specced 'normally' with 38cm bars and a 2x chainset, it probably would have languished in the bottom half.

This is where it shines. Comfortable, confidence inspiring, fun, and well rounded. It didn't shine in any one area, but didn't feel like a let down either.

£9.5k for a top-level, progressively specced bike is pretty good value, even if it's still a lot of money. It's not quite Canyon Aeroad CFR good, but it's impressive nonetheless.

items.title: Will Wout van Aert race cyclo-cross this winter? Even he's not sure yet
items.author: Matilda Price
items.content:
Wout van Aert is continuing to be coy about his possible return to cyclo-cross this season, saying that his calendar is not yet decided but that he is "already getting the itch" to race in the mud.

Whilst Van der Poel has not given all that much hope of him spending much time on the CX bike this winter, Van Aert has given his fans more reasons to be hopeful, particularly with the World Championships taking place in Belgium in January –

It's the first time in six years that Worlds have been in his home country, and the first since 2016 that spectators will be allowed, with the 2021 Worlds taking place with no crowds due to the Covid pandemic.

"I'm already getting the itch," he admitted to . "But for me it is important to wait long enough and make a well-considered choice, because the road season follows immediately after the cyclo-cross season, for which I am ambitious."

Having raced the Vuelta a España and Road World Championships, Van Aert has only recently switched focus to cyclo-cross, which is why he's hesitant to commit to a schedule just yet, despite the 'cross season being well underway.

"I've only been training for a week. The focus is still on the basics, and I haven’t done any specific work yet," he said. "Give me another three weeks to see what my fitness is like and how much more training I need before I'm race-ready. For now, nothing is set in stone."

He confirmed that he will stay in Belgium until the start of December, and is then due on Visma-Lease a Bike road training camp on December 8.

If that pattern of the last five years is to be repeated, Van Aert's debut – if he decides to race – is likely to come only towards the end of December, with a short but sweet campaign probably all that is possible before he must focus on road preparation, with his main goals at the Spring Classics coming only a few weeks after the conclusion of the 'cross calendar.

Last year, he made his CX debut at the World Cup in Antwerp on December 20, and had intended to race through to at least mid-January, but his season was cut short when he injured his ankle at Exact Cross Mol on January 2.

He could be tempted to lengthen his season this winter, though, with the World Championships taking place at home in Oostende at the end of January.

"A World Championship on home soil is more appealing than a World Championship that is far away," he said. "I already rode a World Championship in Oostende in 2021 without spectators, and I would love to get a taste of it with a large crowd."

items.title: Bahrain Victorious welcome third bike sponsor in three years as Factor returns to the men's WorldTour peloton
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
Bahrain Victorious are the latest team to announce a major equipment chance for 2027, swapping to Factor bikes after just one year on Bianchi machines.

Factor has retained a place in the men’s peloton, with US ProTeam Modern Adventure riding the brand’s bikes – and the brand will step up as a title sponsor in 2027 – while Women's WorldTour team Human Powered Health have been riding Factor since 2024, a partnership which will continue into next season.

The length of Bahrain’s deal with Factor is unspecified, with press releases from both the team and the brand stating "from 2027".

Factor have been around for 10 years and recently launched their new Factor One, which is highly likely to be Bahrain’s bike of choice, though they will also have access to the brand’s climbing bike the Ostro VAM, with the One SP for time trials. And should they follow Modern Adventure's example from this year, they may even choose the Monza for Paris-Roubaix.

"We have found a fantastic partner in Factor, a brand that shares our performance ethos and our ambition to be the best," said Bahrain Victorious managing director Milan Eržen.

"Factor is continuously innovating on the bike, with a huge focus on performance, which will enable our riders to have one of the best setups in the peloton.

"For us, it was important to find a partner that shares the same drive to continuously improve. We believe that by combining Factor’s engineering expertise with the knowledge and feedback of our riders and performance team, we can push the boundaries of performance together and give our riders every opportunity to win at the very highest level."

Rob Gitelis, Factor's founder, also expressed his pleasure with the partnership, saying: "At Factor, we have always believed that racing at the pinnacle of the sport is fundamental to who we are. It’s where our ideas are challenged, where our engineering is tested, and where we continue to push ourselves forward.

"Bahrain Victorious shares our ambition and our belief that performance comes from challenging what is possible. We see this partnership as much more than supplying bikes to a professional team. It’s an opportunity to work together, to innovate, and to compete against the very best. We are incredibly excited about what we can achieve together from 2027."

Bahrain’s one-year partnership with Bianchi yielded only nine victories for the team, their fewest since the Covid affected 2020 season, so Matej Mohorič, Lenny Martinez and co. will be hoping for more success atop their Factor steeds.

items.title: 'In recent years, I put too much pressure on myself' – Failed search for a new team ends in retirement for former La Flèche Wallonne winner Dylan Teuns
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
Former La Flèche Wallonne winner Dylan Teuns has announced his retirement after 12 years as a professional. At 34, the Belgian puncheur also won two stages of the Tour de France, a stage of the Critérium du Dauphiné, and GC titles at the Tour de Pologne, Tour de Wallonie, and the Arctic Race of Norway.

After stints at BMC, Bahrain Victorious, Israel-Premier Tech, and most recently Cofidis, Teuns had confirmed before Il Lombardia that he was looking for a new team in 2027, not yet wanting his career to end.

But on Thursday evening, Teuns confirmed that the search for a new squad was over and that he would be hanging up his wheels.

"What a ride it has been! It is time to say goodbye to the professional peloton," read a post from Teuns on Instagram.

"I look back with immense pride and gratitude on a career in which I was able to fulfil my absolute childhood dreams."

He explained the situation he found himself in during the summer to the Flemish press, having been without a confirmed contract before July for the first time in years. Despite meeting with three WorldTour teams in the subsequent months, Teuns was unable to find a place, and admitted that he didn't want to move to a smaller team just to extend his career.

"I had known for months that I was in a difficult situation. My spring didn't turn out the way I had hoped. As a result, I ended up in a contract situation I had never experienced before," he told .

"The Tour had already started, and I hadn't signed anywhere yet. That caused extra stress. Almost every team repeated the same mantra: 'we need to rejuvenate'. Eventually, I held intensive talks with three WorldTeams and two ProTeams. The talks with those WorldTeams came to nothing.

"When I was told by Lotto-Intermarché last Friday that they had no place for me, I consulted with Elke [His partner, ed.] and my parents. It was already clear in my mind at that point, but together with them, I weighed all the pros and cons once again. The conclusion was that I wouldn't be happier by choosing a smaller team."

Teuns didn't want to reveal which two ProTeams he'd been in contact with, saying. "I would rather not reveal that. Out of respect. Because those teams are doing excellent work with limited resources, and I do not want to speak ill of them."

But he was honest in stating how he still believed he was good enough to compete at the WorldTour level, despite his struggles to perform in recent years and match his stunning 2022 season form.

"I really wanted to continue for another two years. With a team, WorldTour or WorldTour-worthy, that performs. Because I felt I still have the potential for it," he said.

"The responsibility of leadership was no longer a must. I was perfectly happy to act as a lead-out man for a puncheur or contribute to the team in the top classics from a free role.

"The fact that I haven't been able to show that potential over the past two seasons gnaws at me. In recent years, I put too much pressure on myself. I had high expectations. But because the results failed to materialise, the pressure only increased. And even when I did have a good moment, I received little appreciation from the team involved."

Having to accept his situation, Teuns could only look back on his best victories, singling out: a specific 20-day period from July 24 to August 13, 2027, when he took his maiden victory as a pro and eight in total as he burst onto the scene with BMC, his two Tour stage wins atop La Super Planche des Belles Filles and Le Grand-Bornand, and his triumph on the Mur de Huy ahead of Flèche Wallonne master Alejandro Valverde in 2022 as his career highlights.

|I am proud of the versatility I was able to show: from a time trial victory in the Ruta del Sol to completing all five Monuments and all three Grand Tours," said Teuns.

"To all the fans, teammates, and staff members who have backed me all these years along the road and in front of the screen: thank you! But a special thanks goes out to my parents, close friends, and girlfriend for having my back during the highs and the lows.

"Deep gratitude for my loyal, steady entourage over the years. Without you all, this dream would have never become reality. It is time for a new chapter, but the love for the bike remains forever. Merci!"

items.title: Paralympic champion cyclist Thomas Peyroton-Dartet provisionally suspended after positive EPO test
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
The International Testing Agency (ITA) have announced that French cyclist Thomas Peyroton-Dartet has tested positive for Erythropoietin (EPO).

41-year-old Peyroton-Dartet returned the adverse analytical finding on September 5 at the 2026 UCI Para-cycling Road World Championships in Huntsville, Alabama, USA, where he won gold in the C3 road race two days later.

"The ITA reports that a sample collected during an in-competition testing mission conducted by the ITA on 5 September 2026 during the 2026 UCI Para-cycling Road World Championships in Huntsville, Alabama, USA, from French rider Thomas Peyroton-Dartet has returned an AAF for EPO," the ITA announced on Friday, adding that Peyroton-Dartet has been provisionally suspended from racing as a result.

EPO is a well-known substance in cycling, having come to prominence during the 1990s. EPO stimulates red blood cell production, increasing an athlete's oxygen-carrying capacity, and so is incredibly effective in endurance sports such as cycling. The EPO test was introduced at the 2000 Olympic Games in Sydney and was first carried out in road cycling at La Flèche Wallonne a year later.

"The rider has been informed of the case and has the right to request the analysis of the B-sample," continued the ITA statement.

"If the B-sample analysis is requested and confirms the result of the A-sample, the case will be considered as a confirmed anti-doping rule violation. If the B-sample analysis is not requested, the case will also go ahead as a confirmed anti-doping rule violation. The rider will have the opportunity to present his explanations for the result."

Peyroton-Dartet's gold this year wasn't the first medal of his career. He won the C3 road race at the 2022 and 2023 UEC Para-Cycling European Championships and took road race silver at the 2025 Worlds. His biggest triumph, however, came in 2024 at his home Paralympic Games in Paris, where he scored gold in the C3 time trial and silver in the C1-3 road race.

Peyroton-Dartet has been competing in para-cycling since 2021, when he hit a car while on a training ride. Since then, he has suffered from cerebellar ataxia, a neurological condition resulting in a loss of balance, poor coordination, and difficulties with speech and eye movements.

As well as competing in para-cycling events, Peyroton-Dartet has raced on the road with the EuroCyclingTrips-CCN Continental team at races around the world, including the Chrono des Nations, Tour de Taiwan, Vuelta Asturias, Tour de Beauce, and Tour du Maroc.
