items.title: Is virtual racing 'real' racing? – Our team weighs in on whether esports is 'legit' or 'just a fitness contest'
items.author: cyclingnews@cyclingnews.com (Cyclingnews)
items.content:
Back in the day, the prospect of an indoor turbo trainer session (that's what we called them before they got smart, kids) would generally unite cyclists, who pretty much unanimously agreed that they were a great way of getting a quality session in, but they were hard and generally a means to an end, that being improved fitness and form.

With the rise of smart trainers and everything that comes with them, from virtual mountain climbing to intense virtual e-racing, opinions on the latter seem to be a bit more skewed.

Some riders, particularly in winter, get stuck into virtual racing to maintain fitness, whilst others shun any sort of virtual world and simply head out in the wet and cold to train.

Virtual racing has only grown in recent years; there's a rainbow jersey for it now, and the inaugural UCI Esports World Championship took place back in December 2020. It can also be incredibly lucrative, with big prize pots up for grabs on a regular basis.

But does virtual racing really count? It's Indoor Cycling Week at , and the team got together for another editors' roundtable for a healthy exchange of views on the legitimacy of racing indoors.

Here are our thoughts, but let us know yours too. Is virtual racing real racing?

Is there a treadmill world championship? No, exactly.

I could probably stop there, as I think that summarises my point quite well. To me, indoor racing lacks all of the things that make cycling truly competitive. It's a test of fitness, sure (and a difficult one at that; I don't doubt indoor athletes are incredibly strong), but the element of tactics, gameplay, positioning and, to be frank, racing skill is so minimal that it feels very far removed from actual racing.

It's also more or less completely useless as a spectator event, which I think is a key element of being a sport – there has to be a degree of entertainment.

To me, indoor competition is more akin to the Hyrox world championships or a fitness contest than real bike racing. Challenging and a big achievement for the competitors, yes, but a real sport that the public need particularly pay attention to? Not really.

Virtual racing, as Matilda already pointed out, is racing in the way a swim meet is racing. But if rubbing is racing, it's definitely not.

You can't throw an elbow, dive the inside of a turn, latch onto another team's lead-out train or use your descending skills to get away from your competition (see Chris Froome/Col de Peyresourde, Matej Mohorič/Sanremo, Marianne Vos/Giro).

Real racing takes skill, tactical nous, teamwork and luck – all aspects absent in virtual racing. But if you consider a VO2 max test to be 'real racing', then, sure.

Of course, virtual racing is real racing.

I haven’t raced a bike for real in a very long time, and there’s no way I’ll go back to it. I wasn’t very good – though I did once win a race – I’m no longer very fit, and even in veterans racing, the variation of ability in the real sport is huge.

With online racing you actually race against others of around the same physical ability, which suits me. That said, I’ve only done it once, and then only to test a power meter, but it was short, sweet, incredibly hard, great fun, and Zwift awarded me a new FTP after I came second.

And for all those efforts on the road or in any other indoor session, I can never push myself as hard as when there’s the thrill of competition.

I’ll certainly give it another go, maybe in the next month or so.

No. In much the same way that rowing on an erg machine in the gym doesn’t give you the spray of delicious river water (or sewage, depending on which water company’s area you’re operating in), riding indoors totally fails to offer anything close to the experience of riding and racing outside.

Can I take that corner faster, or will the tyres slide? The wind has changed direction. I can’t see; there’s too much grit in my eyes. Indoor racing is sanitised nonsense, and I’d be just as happy having a test to see who has the highest FTP and be done with it, as bike racing without bike handling is just a fitness test.

Of course it's real racing. The finish line might be made out of pixels, but if racing on Zwift isn't real racing, then neither is Mario Kart, and I think we all know that it is.

Sure, it's not the same as outdoor racing, and it's not a spectator sport. But when I'm being dropped from the lead group on a climb, that feels pretty damn realistic.

Can indoor bicycle racing be considered real racing? The 'indoor trainer' remains just that: a fitness tool, not a race machine. Akin to my lovely NordicTrack, which still gets used occasionally, there is no virtual classic cross-country skiing championship, or skimo or even biathlon (can you imagine?).

I do think the training apps that allow people to test their skills against each other bring the feel of a peloton, but it is not a real race. Besides, the true definition of 'peloton' – a group moving forward – just doesn't ring true for stationary bikes.

Indoor racing is real racing.

Indoor racing can be shockingly hard; suffering and pushing as hard as you can whilst sitting on a stationary bike indoors is really tough. Indoor racing and efforts demand a special kind of suffering, and it definitely counts.

I see indoor racing sitting off to one side; I’m never going to love it or see it the same way as I see road, or any other kind of real-world racing, but I have respect for the world's best indoor racers; they are putting out incredible numbers and performances indoors, and that takes a certain type of rider and skill set. The effort is very real.

Indoor racing also has nuance and tactics that can’t be overlooked; it’s improved as online platforms and technology have developed over time.

Indoor racing is legit, but don’t count your indoor kilometres as real ones – they don’t count!

The appeal of the bike for me is intrinsically tied to the outdoors, with the unpredictability and sense of discovery of the world around me crucial to my enjoyment of the sport, both as a rider and spectator.

That means even track cycling fails to connect in the same way, and virtual racing takes that to a whole other level. Still, while I'm not drawn to virtual racing and struggle to connect with it, I can't dismiss it. The effort and competitive sensations are all real and also I can see how virtual training and racing can be such a valuable tool to close some of the vast chasms in opportunity.

The clincher for me is that Australians Jay Vine, Neve Bradbury and Emily Dixon are unquestionably real racers, and they gained their opportunity to enter the pro ranks , despite the geographical hurdles they faced, via a virtual training and racing platform.

It's hard to question the validity of a racing medium where talent like that rises to the top. So, yes, virtual racing is real racing, but just please don't make me watch it.

If the objective is to get from point A to point B first, then I will call it a race every single time.

Yes, virtual racing is real racing. It certainly lacks elements and variables compared to racing on the road, trails, track, etc., but it requires training in strength, endurance, tactics, and skill - even if it is taking place inside of a gaming world.

For a lot of athletes, racing is largely a mental battle that is won in the mind first, with drive, focus, confidence, visualisation and the ability to push past limits while under pressure, whether it's on the road or a virtual platform.

While there is no treadmill World Championships (yet), there is treadmill racing; ask Eric Min, who caught me right on the finish line for third place in a Zwift race … I'll get him next time we line up on the starting line.

items.title: Who can compete as a gravel pro in Unbound? Organisers of Life Time Grand Prix establish new 'Pro Number' qualification process
items.author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
items.content:
A 'LT Pro Number' will now be required for riders to compete in the professional category across Life Time events, from the Sea Otter Qualifier in April to individual events that are part of the Life Time Grand Prix off-road series, including Unbound Gravel 200.

Many athletes will receive automatic approval for a LT Pro Number, based on past results in Life Time pro events, the Life Time Grand Prix series, as well as status with national and world championships, related to mountain bike or gravel.

Life Time, which owns and operates more than 195 athletic country clubs across the U.S. and Canada as well as endurance, cycling and running events, also outlined factors considered by a selection committee which will look at results in age groups and races outside the Life Time family.

Safety was the driving factor to implement the new criteria, based on results as well as past experience. The process was also seen as a way to "further professionalize the sport", as the Life Time Grand Prix enters a sixth season in 2027.

“We love that our events bring together athletes of all ages and abilities, and create opportunities for people to challenge themselves. At the same time, mass participant events like Unbound and Leadville are fast and can be tightly packed, particularly at the front of the field.

"Establishing clear, performance-based criteria for the Pro start helps ensure riders competing at the front have demonstrated the experience and ability to race safely at that level, while providing a transparent pathway for athletes to earn their place," Michelle Duffy, director of the Life Time Grand Prix, stated in the announcement on Thursday.

Concerns about the scramble for positioning at the front of the elite fields had been raised in the past by athletes themselves, especially at the two most demanding races - Unbound Gravel 200 and Leadville Trail 100 MTB.

During the Unbound Gravel 200 two years ago, there were several crashes involving less-experienced riders with Grand Prix contenders in the first six miles. The new protocols will help ensure riders have "demonstrated the ability and experience to compete at the front of the fast-race starts" before they line up, according to Life Time.

This new vetting system requires each rider to register online, with one approval covering all events for one year. The LT Pro Number does not guarantee entry, with registration or lottery request still required.

For LT Pro Qualifier races, such as Sea Otter Classic Gravel 60, Sea Otter Classic Fuego XL, Lutsen 99er and four other events, the races are open to all participants and no LT Pro Number is required. With good results, a rider can earn an LT Pro Number in order to complete registration for LT Pro events.

Life Time noted that the entire process would be transparent, with all cut off times and qualifying places posted publicly for athletes to track.

items.title: Best mountain bike lights 2026: Top MTB lights reviewed and rated by our expert off-road testers
items.author: Guy Kesteven
items.content:
Why are you wasting hours of potential riding fun in winter when the best mountain bike lights mean you can ride the rowdiest trails right through to dawn?

Even affordable mountain bike lights are bright enough to push the pace on tasty trails for an hour or more, while more expensive sets will give near daylight conditions for several hours. Helmet lights put their power exactly where you look, so even the tightest corners or steepest drops don't catch you out.

Even so, riding at night will put a whole new spin on your rides, with everything seeming faster and totally fresh – even on local trails you ride day after day. As well as being huge fun, night riding is a great way to maintain hard-won summer fitness into the new year.

The great news is that after huge advances in lithium-ion battery, LED and display tech, light development has slowed down recently. That means proven, reliable designs at every price point, rather than troublesome tech that's been rushed into the after-dark arms race.

So scroll down our list of the best mountain bike handlebar and helmet lights from under £100 to over £500 to find the perfect products for taking your XC, trail, enduro and riding 24/7. If you want to check out our pick of models better suited for on-road use, see our guide to the best bike lights.

Exposure incrementally improves its lights on a regular basis, and its latest Six Pack Mk15 is its most powerful front light yet - but that's not the biggest news.

The Six Pack now has a maximum output of 6,000 lumens (peak power in Reflex mode) from six white XPL2 (W3) LEDs powered by an internal 20,000 mAH Li-Ion battery that's 17.6% bigger than the last model. The run time ranges from just over two hours to a day and half, depending on which of the seven pre-programmed settings are selected.

Three of those programs use Exposure's Reflex 2.0 technology, which uses onboard accelerometers to calculate when you’re riding downhill or rough terrain and will automatically boost the light's output to max. It will then automatically go back to its regular output when things calm down and dim significantly if you stop.

Self-rationing run times are also slightly easier on the Mk15 thanks to a new colour OLED screen on the back of the light (previous versions had a monotone LED display). The displayed run times (Reflex is by its nature something of a lottery) are actually accurate too, which isn't always the case with other lights. The screen background colour also changes 'traffic light style' as your remaining runtime ticks down.

The big practical news for this update is that the SixPack 15 swaps its bespoke charger and plug design for USB-C. That means it can be fast-charged (minimum claimed time is five hours) from any appropriate socket/plug setup. The light can also be used as an emergency power bank for other USB-C devices.

Exposure has also introduced a new handlebar bracket. The hinged clamp with clip-in inserts for 31.8 or 35mm bars is definitely easier to fit than the previous jigsaw design, and the forward-projecting arm that holds the light is longer for improved clearance on crowded bars. Our test sample had wobble in the projecting arm bolt to start with, but that was sorted by tightening to the maximum torque of 6Nm (it's not marked on the clamp, but we checked with Exposure). Both the steel arm and bar band bolts screw into alloy threads, so be sure to use a torque wrench so you don't strip the threads.

Other mounting options come in the form of stem bolt and GoPro-style mounts available separately from Exposure, but the sheer bulk of the Six Pack means they won't work on some bikes. Whatever mount you choose, the triangular shoe on the underside of the light that engages with the QR mount is a potential weak link. The connection is again a short steel bolt into alloy threads. That creates another torque tightrope between security and stripping, and we'd advise regular checks that it's tight.

Mounting issues aside, the light output from the multiple LED's is excellent with the Six Pack's seven preset programs. Program 1 provides the brightest illumination and benefits from the Reflex 2.0 technology. The 4240-lumen output in the High setting is very impressive, providing a broad beam pattern to capture all the trail features directly in front of you. This gives at least 25 meters of illumination down the trail and a good spread to the sides. Once the onboard sensors have detected you’re heading downhill, the output seamlessly increases to the maximum 6,000 lumens. That's more than enough for most trails, though, so I generally run the light in lower power settings (Program 2 or 3) to avoid any run-time anxiety.

Exposure's quoted run times are actually around 10 percent short of what I got in testing. Even once the counter runs to zero, the Six Pack still gives 30 minutes of low-power 'Reserve' light to limp you home too.

The customer support from Exposure has a reputation for being equally helpful with reasonably priced repairs and spares, as well as a generous warranty program. I even know of several Exposure lights still in circulation literally decades after being bought, which is a big plus in terms of value.

There’s no avoiding the fact that the Six Pack is expensive, but the beam is outstanding for a self-contained light. The new screen and USB-C functionality are useful upgrades, and long-term customer support is top-class.

Premium lightweight UK made race light but not without niggles

2,650 (Reflex mode) | 222g / 7.8oz | 8,000mAh | IP67 (dust-tight, fully submersible in water up to 1m) | USB-C | Min run time (triple tested): 1hr 5mins

Great beam quality for speed
Useful screen and USB-C charging upgrades
Excellent customer service
Expensive for middling power
Beam too focused for tech trails

✅ You want a fancy, focused, lightweight light with lots of features: Great speed beam for the weight with new colour screen wins. You want excellent customer service: Exposure typically look after their products and buyers for decades.

❌You want maximum lumens for your money: You can get the same peak and practical power much cheaper.You want 100% reliability on all features : My sample would get stuck in peak Reflex mode ruining battery runtimes.

The Race is a lightweight, focused beam light that has been in Exposure's range for decades. This Mk19 is the lightest (222g) and most compact (107mm long and 41mm in diameter at the bright end) version they've made. It still uses their trademark machined alloy cylinder design with carved ribs for cooling, two LEDs at the front and a new coloured OLED screen at the back. Exposure has also introduced USB-C charging on all their latest-generation lights and you get a high-quality fast charger included with the Race.

Peak output is 2,650 lumens in the brightest of the three automatic movement-sensing, self-dimming Reflex+ modes. That drops to 1,800 lumens in the brightest of the four manual modes. The relatively narrow 14-degree spot beam flatters those numbers in terms of distance you can see on simple, straight trails. The sharp cut-off and lack of peripheral coverage can get 'Blair Witch' very quickly on more twisty tech though. That means you'd be better off with the Toro, MaxxD, or the Six Pack (see above) for trail use.

While the brighter colours make reading runtimes easier, the OLED screen on the back of the light is still harder to see than a top-mounted screen. While it's hard to read the digits as you ride, you can't miss the background colour changing from green to yellow to red as your remaining runtime ticks down.

The Reflex+ mode on my sample light would only dim after being totally stationary for several minutes though, rather than when it sensed smoother/slower riding. That meant the claimed three-hour run time dropped dramatically to around an hour. I've had better luck with Reflex on other Exposure lights though, and Will didn't experience issues with his Race sample during testing.

I did have the same potential wobble and bolt-strip concerns with the new bar bracket with the Race as I did with the Six Pack. Although the much lighter weight of the Race means it's all stayed put OK so far.

Looking at the other options in this list from Lezyne, Ravemen and Magicshine will underline the Exposure price premium you're paying for a light that isn't perfect. They are made in the UK with a three-year warranty though. Plus, Exposure has an excellent reputation for repairing faulty lights or refreshing batteries, etc., at reasonable prices, even decades after they've been bought, which is worth factoring in when deciding which light to go for.

Outbound proves quality of light beats quantity on tech trails

2,200 | 276g / 9.7oz | 10,000mAh | IP65 (dust-tight and withstands low-pressure water jets) | USB-C | Min run time (triple tested): 1hr 45min

Excellent broad beam pattern
Low profile, centralised design
Very clever Adaptive Mode
Excellent reliability and warranty
Lots of custom mount options
Very expensive shipping outside USA
Basic battery communication
Switch can be hard to use in gloves

✅ You want excellent tech trail illumination: Multi LEDs and smart optics mean superb light quality for reading upcoming trouble.

✅ Excellent practical performance: Low-profile design, solid mount, excellent reliability and simple operation.

❌ You want max lumens for your money: Outbound concentrate on quality of light not quantity.

❌ You don't want to pay hefty import charges: Delivery charges are high outside the USA and there's currently no established UK distribution.

US firm Outbound Lighting is relatively new but is already floating on a raft of rave reviews from users. The Trail Evo is the flagship design of their 'broader is better' philosophy. Translating medium numbers on paper into outstanding night vision on the trail.

The secret lies in the nine double-row LEDs and broad, ribbed flood optic, which spreads light really well across the trail. The carefully curated (and extensively tested) multi-point light delivery means the 3D representation of the trail is excellent, rather than it being flattened by concentrated light.

While it's brighter in the centre for reasonable reach, it dims progressively to the periphery just as your own vision does, and the colour temperature is very natural too. There are no bright spots, dark spots, or other optical glitches to distort your read of the trail either. That all means that while the headline lumens are relatively low, the 'feels like riding in the day' result is outstanding, even compared to much brighter lights.

The transverse rather than inline (torch style) design mounts the battery across the back of the lights. Critically, they're separated by cooling airflow from a big chin scoop so the LEDs and battery stay efficient rather than cooking. Once you've got it bolted into place and learned the clip-in knack, the light is held centrally in front of the stem and it's totally wobble-free too. There's even an optional cable clip to make sure all your control lines stay out of the way under the light.

The final cunning trick is the default Adaptive mode that starts the light at full power and then throttles it back to medium as your eyes adapt. That keeps actual vision levels the same but extends the run time by an hour. Alternatively, you can 'epic up' your Trail Evo by using a plug-in USB-C battery to pass-through charge while you're riding.

Compared to the screen-equipped lights, the four LED 'traffic light' battery communication is basic, and there are only three modes to switch between. That's all you really need, though and the reliability and run time gains from a simpler system are a real practical bonus. My tested run times were 10 percent longer than Outbound claim too, which is a nice change.

Considering it's handmade in the US and the customer support is outstanding by all reports, pricing is excellent, and they offer bundle deals on helmet and handlebar combos too. Unfortunately, shipping to the UK and Europe is expensive, so be sure to factor that into any buying decisions.

Decent beam with excellent display and reliability

2,400 | 304g / 10.7oz | 8,000mAh | IPX8 (fully submersible in water over 1m) | USB-C | Min run time (triple tested): 1hr 40mins

Easy to read, accurate screen
Decent beam with sensible modes
Outstanding waterproofing
Pass-through charging or power bank options
Adequate not amazing run times

✅ Excellent tech for the price: Great screen and loads of Smart Control and charging features.

✅I've used several sets for years without a glitch and the waterproofing is outstanding.

❌ You want the longest run times: Extra tech means the internal battery life is relatively short.

Ravemen's PR2400 has been my top value choice for a decent beam with really useful smart tech and outstanding reliability for years.

Illumination comes from one powerful central refracted LED and four corner spot lights. The MTB mode uses all of these LEDs to give a good balance of width and reach in three 2,400 to 600 lumen outputs. There is a slight central hot spot if you're being picky, but it's not enough to be distracting and the three modes mean you're covered for crazy, cruising and crawling. There's also a road bike menu which just uses the diffused central LED four 900 to 100 lumen outputs. These are all controlled through two central top side buttons which are easy to use with gloves, but you also get a wireless remote switch included too.

A simple but bright OLED screen gives accurate run time and charging information. This is invaluable for rationing the adequate but not amazing run time, so in reality, 3-hour mixed terrain rides aren't an issue. You can also plug a power bank (or e-bike) into the back of the light to boost run times or use the light itself as a power bank.

Sturdy metal flaps over the charge ports give class-leading IPX8 waterproofing and in several years of using several PR2400s intensively, I've never had a single reliability issue. Battery life has stayed decent too, so they're obviously using quality cells.

The previous downside of a round bar-only mount has now been sorted with an optional 'universal' band-on strap for flat/aero bars. Either way, you can slide the light on and off and leave the mount in place so you're not resetting angles and tightening clamps every ride. That leaves only the lack of a top lip/peak as a potential dazzle hazard if you're climbing out of the saddle, but that's a really niche niggle.

The result is an absolutely outstanding all-round, on- or off-road light with a very well-proven reputation at an excellent price.

The most powerful MTB light you can buy turns night into day

12,000 | 1,197g / 42.2 oz (including battery) | 10,000mAh | IPX6 (withstands high pressure water jets) | USB-C | 2 hrs 10mins

Fully customisable light modes via Magicshine app
Not quite as bright as claimed
Flimsy light angle adjustment

✅ You want the brightest light available: 12,000 lumens is still the biggest output around. You want max lumens for your money: You always get a lot for your cash with Magicshine.

❌ You're worried about weight and bulk: 12,00g is a chunk of weight and the battery isn't always easy to find a home for on your frame. You want quality of light over quantity: Max power is overkill for most situations and the beam isn't as smooth and 'readable' as some

If you want maximum trail illumination, then the Magicshine Monteer 12000 is the light for you. As the name suggests, it kicks out a huge 12,000 maximum lumen – which is more than twice as much as any other light in this article.

The twin clamps on the lamp are designed for 35mm bars, but you get shims in the box to fit thinner diameters, while the separate battery pack has Velcro straps for mounting to your top tube.

The light can be toggled between four different output settings – 12,000, 6,000, 3,000, 1,000 lumen – with claimed 2.1, 7, 11.5, 37 hour run-times respectively. In testing, we mostly used the light in its 6,000 lumen setting on the trail, as the highest setting was so bright, light would bounce back off trees and other nearby objects making it more difficult to see. But on fireroads and open sections, the full power beam extends further and wider than anything else we've used.

Our reviewer, Paul Burwell summed up the Monteer 12000: "With this much power on tap, you can ride as fast at night as you do during the day. And at under $500 you’re doing it for less too."

Simple but super effective and reliable 'strap on and ride' lighting

2,400 | 335g / 11.8oz | 9,600mAh | IPX7 (fully submersible in water up to 1m) | USB-C | Min run time (triple checked): 2hrs 26 mins

Excellent light fill for tech trails
Race mode is handy for easier power switching
Standard modes are fiddly to swap between on the trail
Battery level indicators are not very accurate
Light wobbles on rough terrain due to its rubber strap

✅ 'Fill rather than far' beam is great for MTB.Simple design means nothing goes wrong.

❌ You want a fancy display: A simple 'traffic light' is all you get for run time and recharge.Rubber strap can waggle a bit, but it'll fit anything.

My top-rated, top-value grab-and-go light for years now, the Lezyne 2400+ is a great example of why simple can sometimes be best.

Simple doesn't mean low quality, though and the five LEDs (three medium, two big), built-in battery and CNC-machined casing are all top gear. The output is concentrated on well-graded fill rather than focused for far too, so it's great for twisty, techy trails. There's even a top lip to shield your eyes from glare when you're out of the saddle.

While there's four steady (300 – 2,400 lumen) and four flashing (700 – 20 lumen) modes in the default setting, selecting between them is a nightmare to navigate on the trail.

Race mode is much better; this toggles between 2,400 lumen full power for the sketchy sections or 700 lumen cruise with a single button push. It'll remember if you had it in 'Race mode' when you switch it off/on again too, so you don't have to reprogram each ride.

Extensive fins and efficient design mean I had no issues with ‘thermal throttling’ either. So it keeps running bright as long as you need, rather than dimming to protect itself from overheating.

Charge/discharge communication is limited though. There’s no set up app or wireless/ wired remote options, and the milky 'orange' half-full light actually comes on at 65 percent of run time left. Even after you've emptied the red warning segment, there's still a limp mode that adds 25 minutes of emergency crawl. The high-capacity 9,600mAh battery works as a power bank, and you can 'pass through' charge the light from a USB-C power pack or e-bike battery. As always, that will reduce the otherwise excellent waterproofing rating.

While the rubber strap mount will fit on any bar shape or even a stem/fork leg, it does allow some wobble on really rough terrain. If you find this distracting, then it's definitely worth getting the more secure round bar band mount.

Powerful but tiny light with iconic mount

1,200 | 125g / 4.4oz (incl mount) | 4,000mAh | IP67 (dust-tight, fully submersible in water up to 1m) | USB-C | 1hr 40mins

Superlight, compact design
Excellent customer support
TAP tech is potentially great
Small size means short run times

✅ You want a super-light, premium-quality light: Bright enough with barely noticeable weight and a brilliant mount. Excellent customer support: Exposure has a loyal following for good reason.

❌ You want max power for your money: The lumen to price ratio is half (or less) than that of some competitors.You'll need an extra power pack for epic adventures.

Meet a serious UK mountain biker at night and they'll almost certainly have an Exposure light of some sort on their helmet. And while the range has now been expanded with the more powerful Diablo and Zenith options, the 105g, 1,200 lumen Joystick is still the lightweight icon.

As it's a dedicated helmet light, the beam uses a single high-power LED behind a focused optic to maximise targeted reach. There's still enough peripheral coverage to stop it being disorienting in complicated trail situations or disrupting the fill from a bar-mounted light though.

The ultra-low weight means it basically disappears on your helmet in terms of neck strain. The ingenious double-disc vent clamp now gets a GoPro-style joint for better articulation too. You will need to check that your helmet has a suitable central vent to mount it symmetrically; otherwise you'll need a glue-on base plate.

Run-time and recharge communication is still through a single traffic light LED system, but the 18th version of the Joystick introduces super-fast USB-C recharging.

You can also run the light with a power pack attached, which is super useful for extending the inevitably short run times of the internal cell.

Run times can be managed through the six different 'OMS+' mode menus. The 'tap the light' mode change tech is theoretically great for switching between modes too. You need to set it to the appropriate sensitivity level for your riding though, or it can start self-switching on rough sections of trail – which is the last thing you want.

I've found button operation of this Joystick - and other Exposure lights can be niggly and unit reliability can be variable. But you can always rely on Exposure to look after you in the event of an issue. So while initial cost might seem very high for the bare performance figures, you should factor the long likely lifespan of your light into the value equation.

Awesome, low weight, helmet targeted trail illumination

1,650 | 190g / 6.7oz (including mount) | 5,000mAh | IP65 (dust-tight and withstands low-pressure water jets) | USB-C | Min run time (triple tested) : 1hr 30mins

Exceptionally clear trail illumination
Clever cooling for efficient running
Very clever Adaptive Mode
Excellent reliability and warranty
Relatively short run time
Hefty import duty if buying from the UK

✅ You want excellent all-round illumination from your lid: Multi-LED design seems way more powerful than the numbers suggest. Super clever compact design: Low front-of-helmet mount gives great vision and tree clearance.

❌ You want maximum focused reach: The Hangover is the Outbound light you want for more focused depth of vision.You don't want to pay import duty from the US: Great USA Outbound value gets hammered when the products cross the Atlantic.

Outbound Lighting offers two US-made helmet lights, but the Portal tested here is the one you want for standout illumination of technical trails.

That's because the five-LED array behind the super-smart optics gives an outstandingly natural and easily interpreted 'read' of the terrain in front of you. Not just from the '3D render' effect of the multiple light sources rather than a shadowy single point source, but also because of the carefully calibrated colour temperature of the LEDs.

The LEDs also operate at a lower current density than most designs for higher efficiency and less heat. A small fin radiator under the chin also chills things out to extend run times from the relatively small battery, so actual tested times were significantly longer than claimed.

If you're riding alone (so that no one can overshadow you from behind), the Adaptive Mode is really smart. It starts with five minutes of high beam before a gradual 30-minute dim to medium as your eyes adjust to the darkness and I genuinely struggled to notice the difference until I blipped it to full power – which then seemed overkill.

Battery and mode communication is via a four micro-LED traffic light strip with an additional low battery flash warning for the 20 min 'get you home' limp mode. Counterintuitively, the sheer size of the stiff top button can make it hard to recognise with winter gloves at first. The need for a hefty press reduces the risk of it switching on accidentally in your kit bag etc. A wireless remote is in the pipeline too.

The low-profile design and rear-mounted 'action camera' style mount keeps the unit low on your lid so there's less chance of catching it on branches and it's very stable too. The Portal is light enough for the forward mount not to strain your neck noticeably either.

Finally, Outbound run their entire operation from design to building and customer service in the US. This includes a three-year warranty with an extended "don't-be-a-jerk" reduced cost repair service policy that covers everything - including gnarly crashes - as long as you have a great story behind it!

US manufacture does mean a hefty import duty price hike if you're buying from elsewhere though, so either find a local distributor (there currently isn't one for the UK) or buy one of Outbound's bundle deals to save a bit of money.

Top value torch style design that works great as a helmet light

1,600 | 184g / 6.5oz | 5,000mAh | IPX7 (fully submersible in water up to 1m) | USB-C | Min run time (triple tested): 1hr 40 mins

Easily replaceable battery
Great reliability and warranty
Simple, effective adjustable mount
Very focused beam isn't the best for tech trails
Button can easily be pressed accidentally

✅ You want a super bright spot beam at a great price: 1600 lumens for under £100 is great value.You want indefinite battery life: Just take reload cells if you're feeling epic.

❌ You want a broad beam for handlebar use on tech trails: While there is some peripheral shine, most of the power goes straight down the line.

❌ You want a fancy display: The Fenix does all its charge communication with a single, not entirely intuitive LED.

Fenix produce all sorts of high-value, high-power lights, but their compact, powerfully focused BC26R is a particularly great option for helmet use for a whole load of reasons.

Firstly, the single LED is tightly focused for a seriously impressive reach down the trail, which works great in a helmet-mounted context if you use the strapped 'action camera' style mount. You also get a really good, secure, angle-adjustable QR handlebar mount included, which works great for fast, simple gravel-style trails or road work. The lack of wider peripheral coverage reduces context and overall awareness, as well as 'see round the corner' performance on more twisty tech trails though.

My actual tested run times were half what Fenix claim, but they're still good for the size and weight. In warm weather use, the thermal throttle will often cut in to stop overheating and extend run times anyway. There are also 600, 200 and 50 lumen lower settings to eke out your energy.

As a nice practical touch, the flash mode requires a button hold rather than just a press, so you won't strobe yourself silly accidentally. However, the easy-to-press button can turn on accidentally if you chuck it in a kit bag, but on the plus side it's easy to use with winter gloves.

An accidental 'on' is easy to get around by unscrewing the end cap and pulling the single 21,700 rechargeable battery cell out too. Being able to remove and swap the battery also adds the huge advantage of being able to reload the light as many times as you have spare cells for unlimited epic potential. At under £30 a battery, that's awesome value compared to a power bank, and it doesn't compromise the excellent waterproof rating like a power bank does either.

It's worth noting that the light indicator on my sample needed some learning though, as while the green level started flashing very early, it lasts until 50 percent charge. From there, it's red until it starts flashing very shortly before it gives up entirely. Once I'd learned that, reliability has been flawless through two intensive use years. Fenix also offer a limited lifetime warranty and free five-year repair service, which improves already impressive value even more.

How many lumens do you need for mountain biking at night?

With advancements in LEDs and batteries, it's possible to buy bike lights that are several times more powerful than car headlights. Lights are rated in lumens but it's an imperfect measure because the calculation is based on the LED power and battery charge in ideal conditions. In the real world, lights deal with limitations created by circuitry, and thermal rollback – that is, when a light automatically reduces its output to prevent it from bursting into flames.

Most lights designed for trail riding are rated to a minimum of 2,000 lumens, and the lowest-power bar light we've recommended here is 2,200 lumens. That said, if you're using a bar and a helmet light setup, you can get away with less.

Are bar or helmet-mounted lights better?

In a light system, bar-mounted lights should provide the majority of the lumens, flooding a wide beam down the trail. Mounted below your eye line, this light creates shadows helping you to spot rollers, rocks, and roots as well as creating some depth perception.

Helmet-mounted lights shine where you're looking, helping you see around corners, over rocks and anywhere your bars aren't pointing. This light doesn't need to have the power of the sun and should have a tighter beam pattern than your bar lights.

If possible the best option is to have both helmet and handlebar-mounted lights simultaneously to get the advantages of both setups to illuminate as much of the trail as possible.

When we talk about lights, lumen count usually grabs the headlines, but the beam shape is equally, if not more important. Ideally, you want something that will have a smooth transition from flood to spotlight with no dark spots or hotspots as this can distract from the trail.

If you're doing lots of high-speed riding and your trails aren't all that curvy, a narrow spotlight beam will suit, but if your local singletrack is twisty and more technical, look for something wide and bright.

What type of battery is best?

Pretty much every light will use a rechargeable lithium-ion battery. Some lights will be completely self-contained, while others will use a separate battery pack.

Self-contained lights eliminate the awkward cables and cumbersome battery packs, however, they are usually bigger and considerably more substantial.

For lights that have a battery pack, consisting of the head and the battery; you'll need to find somewhere to put the power pack, either on your bike or in a backpack. As batteries degrade over time, external packs can be replaced or upgraded, and some brands offer options with different capacities.

How much battery life do I need?

A light that won't last the entire duration of the ride is about as useful as a puffer jacket in the middle of summer. Take into account how long you're planning to ride (keeping in mind that you're probably going to be slower in the dark) and factor in some extra time.

Also, keep in mind that many batteries are affected by temperature, and the cold can have a severe effect on run time. If you live in an area where nighttime temps go below freezing, consider buying a bigger battery or storing it somewhere that's insulated from the cold.

Knowing how much juice your light has left is also vitally important. Some lights have rudimentary green, orange, and red battery indicator lights, while others will show you the time or percentage remaining. Some of the lights in this guide have an in-built backup 'limp mode' that will give you just enough light to get you home if you do get caught short.

Rear lights for mountain biking are less important as you don't need to be visible to traffic while on the trail. However, if you do need to ride on the road, whether as a connection between trails or in case of emergency, you will need a rear light so that cars can see you in the dark. Rear lights are also a nice safety feature for riding on the road in the daytime. A rear light will make you more visible to drivers.

A rear light doesn't need to be as bright as your front and we recommend looking for a 70-lumen rear light for general countryside and city riding. All rear lights will have at least a constant and flashing mode these days although different brands will offer various power modes and flashing patterns that are designed to increase visibility. Daylight modes differ from standard night modes as they rely on disruptive flash patterns to attract attention.

Fitting commonly uses silicon straps to mount lights to a seatpost, and is easy to attach or remove quickly. While most lights will accommodate a wide range of seat post sizes it is still worth considering fitting options. Especially important if you have a dropper seatpost or are looking to mount your light to seat stays, helmet, or saddlebag. See our main best bike lights guide for rear options.

If riding muddy trails, don't forget to wipe your light down before hitting the roads. Your rear light is in the firing line for getting covered in crud!

Every light I've recommended here has been put through its paces for months, if not years. I've also tested generations of most of the lights featured in this buying guide. Which means the information here is not only bang up to date, but also properly trail-tested in all weathers.

Testing means beam patterns assessed at speed on tight, twisty, tree-lined singletrack as well as open moors – not just pointed down a garden. Mounts that have been rattled (and sometimes rattled loose) down the roughest descents, and crashed hard when lumens and luck have run out.

All the run times are the averaged results of multiple tests in realistic air-cooled conditions, not just pulled off manufacturers' websites or run without cooling so they overheat and throttle back. Which is why our numbers and conclusions may well differ from other results out there.

For more on testing, see our How We Test article.

items.title: Tadej Pogačar and Demi Vollering top Vélo d'Or nominations – Who would get your vote?
items.author: Matilda Price
items.content:
A few days after Harry Kane and Alexia Putellas won the Ballon d'Or for excellence in football, the 2026 Vélo d'Or nominations were revealed with the season's biggest stars leading the shortlists for the men's and women's awards.

The Vélo d'Or – 'Golden Bicycle' in English – is a prestigious award that is handed out by France's with the winners decided by a jury of international cycling journalists.

There are two main awards, the Vélo d'Or for men and women, which is given to the overall best road rider of the year. There are then a number of sub-categories, including Classics rider of the year, sprinter of the year, rookie of the year, French rider of the year and paracyclist of the year.

The shortlists for all of the categories were unveiled on Thursday, a month ahead of the awards ceremony on Saturday, November 28, in Paris, with nominations full of the year's standout racers.

Three-time winner Tadej Pogačar is once again nominated for the men's award after taking his fifth Tour de France title, with his teammates Isaac del Toro and world champion Brandon McNulty also making the list. The two other Grand Tour winners of the year – Jonas Vingegaard and Enric Mas – also earned nominations, alongside Paul Seixas, Remco Evenepoel and Felix Gall.

Only two Classics specialists are up for the main award: Mathieu van der Poel and Wout van Aert.

On the women's list, Demi Vollering is surely a favourite to win her second Vélo d'Or, with last year's winner Pauline Ferrand-Prévot perhaps surprisingly not receiving a nomination after a lacklustre year on the road, though she is nominated for French rider of the year.

Tour de France Femmes stars Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney, Marlen Reusser and Elisa Longo Borghini all make the list, as did revelation Paula Blasi, Antonia Niedermaier, Juliette Berthet, Anna van der Breggen, Kim Le Court-Pienaar and sprint sensation Lorena Wiebes.

Matthew Brennan, Jakob Omrzel and Paul Seixas are up for the men's rookie of the year, with Paula Blasi, Célia Gery and Isabella Holmgren earning the women's rookie nominations.

items.title: Zwift reveals higher subscription tier with AI coach, adaptive training plans and real-world video
items.author: josh.croxton@futurenet.com (Josh Croxton)
items.content:
As indoor trainer season starts gathering momentum faster than an avatar down a virtual mountain, product updates and new launches are coming thick and fast.

MyWhoosh came with zombie chases, Tacx dropped the Nera smart trainer, and Zwift teased a few more Californian routes, but today’s announcement is one that’s sure to shake things up good and proper.

It comes in the form of Zwift Plus, a new higher-priced premium subscription tier that, certainly at first glance, appears to borrow features from a number of its competitors, no doubt closing the feature gap in a bid to capture a greater share of the market.

The first part is the integration of adaptive training and an artificial intelligence ‘Zwift Coach’ that can help you set a goal, analyse workouts, and adapt as time passes in line with progress.

The second part is the unveiling of new real-world video-based routes, as opposed to the virtual worlds – or digital recreations thereof – which Zwift has committed to and relied upon thus far.

Adaptive training and Zwift Coach

AI is the buzzword of the year, and it’s no surprise to see Zwift, whose headquarters lie just a stone's throw from Silicon Valley, lean into the technology.

Zwift says there’s a strong correlation between consistency and fitness gains, including three main claims:

  1. Those who ride twice a week are 2.8x fitter than those who ride once every two weeks
  2. Those with a 12-week streak see an increase of up to 12% in their FTP.
  3. Riders on a training plan see their FTP grow by 4.15%, versus 1.97% for those without one.

The Zwift Coach, therefore, aims to get more of those people onto a plan and riding consistently, setting a plan that aligns with goals set from the outset, and then “adapts to life” in real time, as sessions are completed, failed, or skipped.

The integration of video is the second major upgrade exclusive to Plus subscribers, and despite some of Zwift’s competitors – and indeed its new subsidiary, Rouvy – offering footage filmed by users, Zwift will use footage obtained exclusively by an in-house team of videographers.

The feature will launch with 21 routes across the following destinations:

  1. The French Alps: Col du Galibier, Cime de la Bonnette
  2. Mallorca: Sa Calobra, Coll de Femenia
  3. Western Cape: Chapman's Peak, Bains Kloof
  4. Lofoten Islands: The Midnight Sun Road
  5. Southern Utah: The Hogsback, Arches NP
  6. The Scottish Highlands: Glen Etive

The routes will include digitally created finish line banners and blimps in the sky, bringing a touch of the familiar Zwift gameplay to users, but will ultimately bring more destinations to the Zwift world.

The new subscription tier will be priced at a £9 / €10 / $10 / AU$15 upcharge over the current price, meaning a monthly subscription will be £26.99 / €29.99 / $29.99 / AU$44.99.

Annual subscriptions allow users to get 12 months for (almost) the price of 10. These are charged at £269.99 / $299.99 / €299.99 / $449.99.

The existing Zwift tier is still available, and the prices for that remain unchanged.

items.title: 'This shouldn't happen' – Paul Seixas joins calls for greater rider safety following death of Finlay Tarling
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
Paul Seixas has continued the call for better safety in the peloton following the death of British rider Finlay Tarling at the Volta a Portugal in August, who was killed after colliding with a non-race vehicle that had entered the course.

These included Coppa Bernocchi – where a DHL delivery van driver turned onto the course – and Tre Valli Varesine – where a police motorbike hit two Pinarello Q36.5 riders – two of the Italian Autumn Classics that serve as the build-up to Il Lombardia, where Seixas made history as the youngest-ever winner.

The young French superstar got emotional as he emphasised the need for better safety standards once more, having raced against Tarling several times, including at the junior World Championships and junior Liège-Bastogne-Liège as they both developed towards professional careers.

"Honestly, it's terrible. The problem is, he's not the only one," said Seixas.

"What's more, I raced with him, and it really affects me. It really affected me at the time, because what's terrible is that we'll be thinking: 'This is yet another cyclist who has died in a race this year.'"

The protest at Il Lombardia came about through a WhatsApp group with Tom Pidcock and Ben Healy spearheading the idea, which was kept quiet from teams and the CPA – the rider union – and coincided with a statement being released en masse by riders on social media.

Seixas didn't mince his words as he detailed how serious the call is for greater safety, admitting just how scary bike racing can be when incidents like what happened in Portugal are still possible.

"I think it really affected everyone, all the riders. That's when you realise that sometimes there are real organisational problems; the organisers do their best, that's not what we're saying, but sometimes there should be more strict standards," he said.

"We protested about it at Lombardia, at the beginning of the race, for five minutes. What happened is extremely serious. Families are affected. It's very serious that it happened during a race. A professional organisation, riders losing their lives; it's frightening."

Seixas talked about how while he hasn't had a major crash himself, the risks of racing can enter a rider's mind at the most dangerous parts of a race, and while noting that accidents and crashes are unfortunately part and parcel of professional bike racing, a death like Tarling's simply should not happen.

"Let's just say that sometimes you get a little stressed, but you don't think it's for your life either. When you're in a peloton, there's a false flat downhill, and you're going 80 kph, sometimes you're still a little scared," said the Frenchman.

"You think to yourself: 'Now, it could be… Serious', but you must not think about it; that's the thing. And you know that everyone else is aware of it too, so they're not going to do anything reckless either. Then, sometimes there's nervousness; that's what can make everyone tense and create danger.

"When there are falls, yes, you get injured, but on the road, I've never had a fracture or a sprain; I've never had anything. Scratches, that's happened to me, several times, many times even. But you always come out of it well. Afterwards, there have been very serious falls in history, but riders who find their death like that in a race, that shouldn't happen."

items.title: 'You try to survive' – Esmée Peperkamp adds her name to the criticism of the culture at Picnic-PostNL
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
After spending five seasons with Picnic-PostNL, Esmée Peperkamp has added her voice to those criticising the management and support structures at the Dutch team.

In an interview with Dutch broadcaster , Peperkamp said her health and form deteriorated during her time with Picnic, described the medical support at Picnic as "substandard" and alleged she was told to train through injury.

She also stated that all the riders and staff she worked with have contractual clauses preventing them from publicly criticising the team, even after they have left.

Peperkamp alleged the team is guilty of negligence, saying: "You are never listened to and that things are decided for you that are ultimately not good for you."

Now in the middle of a two-year deal at VolkerWessels, Peperkamp arrived at what was then Team DSM in 2021, aged 23, as a promising climber. She left at the end of the 2025 season with only six top-10 placings to her name.

Peperkamp was one of several riders NOS spoke to anonymously in their original story about the culture of the team, but she has now decided to go public, so she can both help others and explain her continuing poor health.

"My health is still deteriorating because I still do not produce enough hormones," she told . "I haven't had a period since 2021, and I have RED-S, relative energy deficiency in sport. I contracted that during my time at DSM and later at Picnic-PostNL."

"Whether you got your period, for example, was never a question. It was never checked whether my hormone levels were in order, even though there are annual health checks. This could have been prevented."

After suffering a concussion at the 2024 Vuelta a Burgos, she alleged she was left unsupported, adding: "They handled it very casually. For example, they left it up to me whether I would train the next day."

Peperkamp also explains that she suffered from irritable bowel syndrome and a lactose intolerance, which meant she struggled with the nutrition provided by the team, though she was not allowed a substitute.

"I became very sick. So nauseous that I couldn't eat anymore. I was vomiting too. I could feel sick for days and therefore ate very little. I just had to get used to it, they said. I sometimes had kind caregivers who gave me bottles with regular isotonic drink, or water.

"You try to survive, to get yourself noticed by other teams, to keep your dream alive."

Having moved to VolkerWessels this season, Peperkamp has not raced since failing to finish Liège-Bastogne-Liège in April.

While Peperkamp is one of several former riders to have criticised the team, others have come out in support, with John Degenkolb questioning why voices like his were not included in ’s reporting.

In response, the team have appointed lawyer Professor Marjan Olfers to lead an independent enquiry into the team’s culture. Olfers has a long history working in professional sport, leading the investigation surrounding Michael Rasmussen’s presence at and exclusion from the 2007 Tour de France

Picnic-PostNL issued the following statement to : "We regret that a member of our team experienced matters such as those you describe. As previously announced, we will have an independent investigation conducted into this matter.

"For various reasons, we cannot comment on individual cases as outlined by the NOS. Firstly, it concerns an anonymous complaint, making it difficult for us to respond specifically.

"In addition, we do not share information about individual team members with third parties, even when we suspect who is involved. This policy is partly aimed at safeguarding the privacy of the (former) riders mentioned by you, as well as the privacy of the many team members, on and off the bike, who work or have worked together (intensively), and thus to prevent them from feeling unsafe due to the sharing of such information."

items.title: Thibau Nys to kick off cyclo-cross campaign at Koppenbergcross after challenging road season
items.author: Matilda Price
items.content:
The Koppenbergcross has been run 36 times, and almost a third of those editions have been won by a member of the Nys family, with Sven winning nine times in the 2000s before his son Thibau Nys took up the mantle in 2023 and 2025.

Nys junior will be hoping to make it 12 wins for the Belgian cyclo-cross dynasty this weekend as he kicks off his campaign at Koppenbergcross – officially the Oudenaarde round of the X2O Badkamers Trofee – on Sunday.

Given he has already won this iconic event, with takes in the famous cobbled Koppenberg climb in Flanders, Nys is targeting nothing less than victory in his first race back on the mud this season.

"Otherwise, I cannot be satisfied," he told as he trained on the course on Wednesday, with his father and a smattering of fans in attendance.

"I am very well aware that it will not be easy, perhaps the most difficult edition of the last few years for me. But on the Koppenberg, I cannot be happy with a podium finish."

The main reason Nys expects a tougher edition than usual is that he's had a particularly short preparation period for his cyclo-cross season. That's because he raced the Vuelta a España in September and then the Road World Championships, giving him only a few weeks to switch to CX training.

"Because everything had to be crammed into three weeks, I was unable to do quite a few important training sessions," he said. "And those are precisely the sessions that can provide a confidence boost. So we’ll have to make do with it and hope it’s enough."

Starting with possibly the most important race for him personally seems like both throwing himself back in at the deep end and a way to ensure he hits the ground running, with chasing his father's record of nine wins something of a career goal for the 23-year-old.

"I want to win that race as many times as possible in my career, more than, for example, wanting to become European Champion," he said, though he has won the stars-and-stripes jersey before, and will be in the team in the Netherlands in mid-November.

"That doesn't mean I prefer the Koppenberg over Zeddam [host of the European Championships] in two weeks right now, but after my career, I would rather be able to say that I managed to win on the Koppenberg seven or eight times than that I became European Champion seven times."

There is also perhaps extra pressure on Nys to put together a successful 'cross campaign this winter given how tough his road season was. He underwent knee surgery in March, which required a long period away from racing – he missed the first six months of the year – meaning he could only fit in 30 race days and had no wins.

He took third on a stage of the Vuelta, but was then a DNF at the Road Worlds. But with his knee seemingly in full working order again, he can hope to stand on the top step of a podium again soon – as soon as this weekend, he hopes.

items.title: The best indoor cycling accessories for under £50 / $50
items.author: Tim Perkin
items.content:
One of the big misconceptions regarding indoor cycling is that creating a suitable training space is expensive.

Purchasing a high-end smart trainer can be costly, but once you have it, the additional purchases that add the real value and make the biggest differences are surprisingly affordable.

Ultimately, a well-thought-out indoor setup is about more than just the bike and trainer. Comfort, cooling, and bike protection all help you train consistently and maximise every session.

Here are five useful, practical accessories priced under $50 that are worth investing in and will make your indoor cycling experience more enjoyable.

A bike mat is one of the first purchases to consider when setting up your indoor training space, particularly if you're mounting your outdoor bike on an indoor trainer.

The bike mat protects your carpet or flooring from grease, grime, or oil from your drive chain.

The bike mat also protects your flooring from sweat that accumulates during your sessions, as well as preventing deep indents in your carpet.

The mat can help contain sweat and make post-workout cleanup easier, and it's far less expensive to replace a mat than new carpet!

There is a range of mats on the market; it doesn't have to be a cycling-specific mat, and they can be found for under $50.

To protect your flooring, you may want to purchase some interlocking foam floor tiles. These are a popular option that can be laid on top of your carpet or garage flooring, creating a more level, stable base, depending on the flooring.

Effectively, it helps create a solid base on which to lay your bike mat and the best platform for your smart trainer and bike.

A pack of 12 can cost $49.99, with each tile measuring 24 in x 24 in, which totals 48 square feet.

A suitable fan is a must-have item for indoor cycling. Without the natural airflow you experience when riding outdoors, staying cool during indoor cycling can be a challenge, and things quickly get pretty uncomfortable.

A fan is essential for improving airflow, helping regulate your body temperature, and reducing the risk of overheating.

Choose a fan that suits your training space and budget. There is a range of fans available, but Amazon offers a basic fan for under $50 that would serve its purpose.

A small, foldable camping table is a useful item to purchase. This may seem slightly unconventional but is highly practical and very useful when undertaking long rides, races, or intense training sessions where you can place additional bottles and snacks within easy reach.

If you aren't within easy reach of a worktop or table, an extra table makes perfect sense; supplies can be lined up and kept close when needed. The small table also functions as a place to hold a secondary fan.

When you have finished your ride, simply wipe down the table and pack it away until your next longer session.

Prices vary, but there are plenty of options available for under $50.

Muc-Off offers an Indoor Training Kit, which normally retails for slightly over $50 but is currently on sale at $23.99 (usual price is slightly over $50, but such good value it’s worth including).

The Indoor Training Kit includes everything you need to keep yourself and your bike in top condition during indoor cycling sessions.

The kit features Antibacterial Equipment Cleaner to keep your training equipment fresh, Luxury Chamois Cream to help prevent chafing, and Sweat Protect to help protect your bike against sweat-related corrosion.

C3 Ceramic Dry Lube keeps your drivetrain running smoothly, while the Microfibre Cloth is ideal for cleaning and polishing your bike.

To complete the kit, a Muc-Off Tote Bag provides a convenient way to store and carry all your essentials.

Building a great indoor cycling setup doesn't have to cost a fortune. A few carefully chosen accessories can make your training sessions more comfortable, protect your flooring, and help keep your bike in good condition throughout the indoor season.

A bike mat and fan are excellent starting points, while protective floor tiles and a foldable table can make your training space more practical. Add a maintenance kit to the mix, and you'll be better equipped to handle everything from short weekday workouts to long indoor rides.

You don't need to buy everything at once. Start with the accessories that address your biggest needs, then upgrade your setup as your training demands grow. The goal is to spend wisely on products that make indoor cycling more enjoyable and hassle-free.

items.title: Primož Roglič's options for a 2027 contract narrow as two teams drop out of the running for his signature

The Slovenian has reached the end of his three-year stint at Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe and has been linked with a host of other teams for 2027.

have reported that Roglič did indeed hold talks with Visma in recent weeks, but on Wednesday stated the talks have been called off.

Talks with Lotto went further as the Belgian team, who this winter are waving goodbye to two leaders in Arnaud De Lie and Lennert Van Eetvelt, offered Roglič a contract. However, according to , he has declined their offer.

Roglič's future remains open, then. All three teams previously linked with him do have roster space open for him, while the prospect of retirement remains on the table.

items.title: Will Van der Poel and Van Aert race, Brand's dominance, and Van Empel's return – The storylines to follow this cyclo-cross season
items.author: Matilda Price
items.content:
The road season is over, the clocks have gone back, and the temperatures in Europe are dropping, which can mean only one thing: cyclo-cross is here.

The 2026-27 season is actually well underway by now, with the action kicking off in the US and Europe in September, but most of the main series are just starting or yet to begin.

The HG Cross series, formerly known as Exact Cross, is underway, while the Telenet Superprestige kicked off in Overijse at the weekend. The X2O Badkamers Trofee begins with its most iconic round, the Koppenbergcross, this weekend, whilst the headline series, the UCI Cyclo-Cross World Cup, will start on November 27 in Czechia.

The busy season, with series crowns up for grabs, plus national, Pan-American and European titles, builds towards the World Championships, which this season will be held in Oostende, Belgium at the end of January.

Whilst many of the races and protagonists stay the same year to year in 'cross, the plotlines and points of intrigue change and evolve each season, with different and exciting narratives running throughout the season, from the overall standings of each series to the competition building towards Worlds.

From the will-they-won't-they around Mathieu van der Poel and Wout van Aert to the exciting return of the prodigious Fem van Empel, there's plenty of interesting stories already brewing this winter – here's some you should be following this cyclo-cross season.

Definitely no big three, but what about the big two?

For the last decade, most of the intrigue around the men's calendar has revolved around the so-called 'big three': Mathieu van der Poel, Wout van Aert, and Tom Pidcock. They were cyclo-cross stars before they ever made it big on the road, and even as their WorldTour careers have grown, they've almost always made time during their winters to head back to the mud, with their first appearances circled in everyone's calendar.

This year, though, we won't get the big three – and we might not even get the big two.

That's because Tom Pidcock has already confirmed he won't be racing CX this season, and perhaps not in the future either, with road and mountain biking taking up more and more of his time, and the lack of an Olympic slot for CX, it's becoming harder for the Brit to justify adding the discipline to his schedule.

However, whilst we've been getting used to Pidcock doing less and less CX, what might be new this year is that we may not see Mathieu van der Poel in action, either. Wout van Aert has announced his intention to race at least some CX this year, though probably not starting until December, but the eight-time world champion might skip it altogether. He, too, has been doing less in recent years, but the imminent arrival of his first child seems to have only made his return to the fields even less likely.

So could we really be looking at our first CX season in years without the stars that have defined the last decade of the discipline? It certainly looks that way. In some ways, it might be good for the sport, as it opens up opportunities for the specialist to take more big wins, rather than being steamrolled by the blockbuster names when they turn up for a few races. But for the casual fans drawn in by Van der Poel and Van Aert, it might make for slightly less enthusiastic viewing.

Fem van Empel is back, and doing things differently

In women's CX, the biggest story of the season is undoubtedly Fem van Empel's return to competition. Still only 24, Van Empel was a prodigious force in the discipline, winning practically at will for several seasons, but she stepped away last winter after repeatedly struggling with her mental health and motivation for racing.

No one knew then when she might return – if ever – but the Dutchwoman has found her groove earlier than expected, and is coming back to the sport this winter with Specialized TMRW, FDJ United-Suez's new off-road branch.

Formerly a prolific winner, it would be easy to expect Van Empel to return to those heights straight away. Instead, she and her team are doing things differently, making sure they don't repeat the mistakes of before, and that's really refreshing to see. For the moment, Van Empel is only racing a maximum of once per week, limiting the pressure on her and trying to enjoy being back first and foremost.

Of course, Van Empel's talent is such that even a gentle start has seen her already take fourth and fifth in her first races back, and it seems probable that she will return to winning ways this winter. But the important thing is that the pressure and tension is off, and Van Empel seems to have found the freedom to rediscover what she loves about racing. A winning Van Empel was good, but a happy one is even better.

Lucinda Brand just can't stop – but she will be challenged

Lucinda Brand has raced cyclo-cross since she was a teenager, and though she didn't start winning regularly at the top level until her sixth year as an elite, since then she's been a prolific victor and one of the most consistent riders on the circuit. So far this season, she's already won three of five races she's started, and she'll be chasing the whopping 20 victories she took last winter.

With the power of the rainbow bands, only the second time she's been world champion in her career, she's sure to be on another fantastic run, with zero signs of slowing down as she enters her final 18 months of professional racing.

However, if the races so far are anything to go by, it's not going to be a walk in the park for Brand, with other riders really stepping up to challenge her already. The returning Fem van Empel is an obvious candidate, but so are the likes of Blanka Vas and Shirin van Anrooij, who are changing teams this winter and returning to cyclo-cross with renewed motivation.

Among the specialists, Ceylin del Carmen Alvarado looked stronger than ever last winter and so far this year, while the likes of Denise Betsema and Aniek van Alphen haven't been much behind Brand either. Luxembourger Marie Schreiber seems to be finally finding a real groove, too, taking a big win at Nacht van Woerden, so the world champion certainly can't rest on her laurels.

Make way for the specialists

The upside to the absence of some of the big multidisciplinary stars this winter is that it will make room for more of the pure CX specialists to shine. These riders who commit their whole year to the discipline are sometimes outshone when the part-timers make their appearances, but with less of that on the cards this year, the series and big events should be contested more by the specialists.

On the men's side, Michael Vanthourenhout looks primed to step into the position of the season's dominant rider, and will perhaps be dreaming of a possible world title at the end of it, whilst riders like Cameron Mason look to be right on the verge of a first major level win. With younger riders like Niels Vandeputte and Witse Meussen on the up too, the men's series could be the most competitive we've seen in years, with plenty of chances of glory for the riders who make this discipline their bread and butter.

Who is going to have a breakout season?

And finally, on that topic, we'll be following closely to see who is going to make 2026-27 their breakout season, with plenty of talent rising to the top right now. There are a few names we have our eyes on already, but actually, the exciting thing is that there are a multitude of riders who could find that breakthrough result this year – the fun is in watching it happen, not trying to predict it in advance.

With the Belgian and Dutch riders naturally dominating the CX scene, even to this day, it's interesting to see who is coming up from outside the 'cross heartlands. US riders Mia Aseltine and Kaya Musgrave are both looking really strong on the European circuit, racing for Competitive Edge Racing, and Czech rider Kristýna Zemanová is on the cusp of a really big win – perhaps in one of the two World Cup rounds in her home country this November?

items.title: 'I can still win this day' - Alison Jackson recovers from mechanical to win middle stage at seven-day Gravel Burn
items.author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
items.content:
Alison Jackson (St Michel-Preference Home-Auber93) ignited the fourth day of racing at Nedbank Gravel Burn as the elite women contested their first bunch sprint, and the Canadian scored the unexpected victory after recovering from a mechanical.

Jackson returned for her second appearance at the weeklong 750km South African gravel stage race, where she finished 11th overall last year, and was looking for her first stage win.

“I approached this year differently; last year I had a surf camp ahead of the event but this year I kept riding, so I had no excuses. The first few days didn’t go to plan with crashes and mechanicals, but you never give up," Jackson told organisers.

Jackson began the opening day of racing from Graaff-Reinet in the lead pack, which was split with 49km to go on the climb of Conical Peak, where Nele Laing (Canyon DT Swiss ATR) accelerated away. Jackson suffered a crash and then struggled in the chase on the hilly 90km route, finishing 7:30 off the pace to begin the week in seventh overall.

The next two stages combined for 242km and nearly 2,000 metres of elevation gain as the race moved south into the Great Karoo, a vast desert-like landscape that translates to 'land of thirst'. The GC standings settled into place with Laing in the lead, South African gravel champion Hayley Preen (ChemChamp Honeycomb) in second place and Clara Koppenburg (Tudor Pro) in third, with Jackson into eighth.

During the loop route Wednesday through valley roads and then a climb back to Merino, Jackson dropped out of the lead group to deal with a battery mechanical on the rear derailleur. As the race camera caught her working on the bike at an aid station, she said, "I can still win this day", and this proved to be a true statement.

She worked her way back on the loose gravel and dry dirt to catch the lead pack, and then surged from the 12-rider group in the closing 500 metres to win the stage.

"I know I can sprint – a sprinter can always sprint at the end; it doesn’t matter how tired you are,” the former Paris-Roubaix champion confirmed after the win. She's had a number of top 10s on the road this year, including stage 4 of the Giro d'Italia plus the time trial and road race at Canadian Nationals. At the UCI Gravel World Series event, The Gralloch, earlier this year, she finished sixth.

Laing comes to the race for the first time fresh off fourth place at UCI Gravel World Championships. She finished safely in the bunch behind Canyon DT Swiss ATR teammates, third place going to Larissa Hartog, who was also third at UCI Gravel Worlds for the Netherlands, and Carolin Schiff in sixth, and Jade Treffeisen going 10th. The German took the first orange leader's jersey with the opening stage win and now has 56 seconds on Preen and 4:14 on Koppenburg.

The men's division saw their second sprint finish of the week so far, stage 4 with 13 riders going to the line in a cloud of dust, with South Africans Travis Stedman (Toyota Specialized Imbuko) and Ryan Gibbons (RoadCover SunGod) going one-two and USA's Cole Davis (SpeedStudio) in third.

GC leader Matthew Beers (Toyota Specialized) let the breakaway go and finished 2:41 back, marking his rivals, with second-placed Filippo Colombo (Scott-SRAM) 32 seconds back and third-placed Tristan Nortje (Toyota Specialized Imbuko) at 51 seconds.

The final three stages take the riders to Gwanishi and the southernmost point at the Shamwari Private Game Reserve in the south. Beers seeks a second consecutive GC title, while defending women's champion Axelle Dubau-Prevot (EF Education-Oatly) has work to do to move from 13th position and 8:23 from Laing.
