items.title: 'He's now one of the big stars in cycling' – Can Visma fit British rider Matthew Brennan into Tour de France plans alongside Vingegaard and Van Aert?
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
With the Tour de France Grand Départ taking place in Great Britain in 2027, and a likely sprint into the Carlisle stage offering up the first yellow jersey, Matthew Brennan (Visma-Lease a Bike) represents the best chance at an opening day home winner. But will the rising British star even be present?

Riding for the same team as Jonas Vingegaard and Wout van Aert means that any kind of stage-hunting opportunities are going to be limited, but Brennan has shown throughout 2026 that he can be relied upon for victories, and as a perfect accompaniment to the Belgian star's talents.

Throughout the Vuelta a España, Brennan and Van Aert combined perfectly as Visma dominated the flat and punchy days, winning a third of the 21 stages – five for the Brit and two for the Belgian – across sprints and breakaways.

"It's my first Grand Tour, but also to be as successful in this first Grand Tour is a really nice step into the ambition to try and win in the first few stages in the Tour de France next year," said Brennan.

"I've seen the first and also the second stage [of the 2027 Tour, and the third is quite hard, but there are definitely opportunities to do something within my strengths.

"I would really like to be on the start line. I also understand that the best squad has to go with the ambitions the team has, but I think that for the moment, with being successful as a team, we can probably use myself in different ways to help Jonas bring out his strengths even more and play the cards.

"But that's also just something the team will discuss in the future, and there has been no decision made, so we just take it as it comes and go from there."

With the full route confirmed in Paris earlier this month, it confirmed more than just two or three chances for Brennan on home roads, but a Tour filled with flat days and punchy finales, where he can potentially challenge the top sprinters and the likes of Mathieu van der Poel and Tadej Pogačar.

Visma are considering Brennan, and team boss Richard Plugge couldn't deny that the Brit was going to make up a big part of their plans in 2027, having taken the same number of pro wins as Vingegaard this past season: 12.

"He's entered a small group of very big riders, I think. And when he came to the team, we already knew when he started sprint training, etc. We thought, 'Whoa, what is happening here?' And you see how he climbs here with the best punchy climbers on a parcours like this, then it's really promising for the future," Plugge told at the finish of the last stage in Granada.

"But it's also his first Grand Tour, and I told him just now to just be really proud: five stage wins – that's incredible, but also finishing your first Grand Tour will only make you stronger and your motor bigger.

"Let's wait and see for the Tour… Let us evaluate and make plans for next year. Obviously, he's part of our plans also with Wout and with Jonas [for 2027], so we will discuss with the whole team like we always do in the coming weeks, and then in our training camp, when we have a media day, we will tell you."

Visma's media day will arrive on December 17, when the full schedules for their big leaders will be revealed, alongside provisional squads for the Tour, which Brennan will desperately hope he's on.

Plugge and all of the management at Visma will have the main goal of winning back the yellow jersey from Pogačar, as they did in 2022 and 2023, but there is little harm in including one stage hunter in Brennan to the ranks.

He's already shown his versatility as a winner and helper for Van Aert, so he would be more than willing and capable to support Vingegaard on the punchier days where victory isn't potentially on the cards. Plugge has some deciding to do, but Brennan signing his future with Visma until 2029 suggests he's confident he'll get the opportunities he wants, even with the Dutch squad's other priorities.

"Matthew knocked very hard on the door there," he told , referring to the Brit's five stage wins from the Vuelta. "You know that he is now one of the big stars in cycling. And this is the biggest race. So we are certainly going to consider it."

items.title: 'It feels like coming full circle' – Australian DS Matt White rejoins EF Education-EasyPost 16 years after departing
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
White, who hung up his wheels as a racer in 2007, began his directing career at the team, staying there for three years before being dismissed over a breach of policy. He then completed a long stint at Jayco-AlUla.

"It feels like coming full circle. I started my career as a sports director here back in 2008," said White.

"I've obviously spent a lot of time away, but it's a team that I've always kept very close to my heart. It's exciting to come back to a team that has so many talented young riders and a lot of ambition to develop this group over a long period of time."

White, who will join an EF DS team that includes Charly Wegelius, Ken Vanmarcke and Tom Southam, said he's excited by the team's attacking ethos and added that he's looking forward to working with the young riders at the team.

"I think the beauty of going for stages is that it's all or nothing. You're all in for the day, then you might have a day or two when you're not, and then you're all in again. Especially in a Grand Tour, I think that's a really exciting mindset and way to approach a race," he said.

"The most exciting thing about this group is that it's such a young, talented team. You just don't know what these athletes are capable of on any given day.

"Nurturing those guys and getting the best out of them, both as individuals and as a group, is an exciting challenge for me. Working with riders who don't yet know where their ceiling is, and helping them discover what they're capable of, is something that gets me up in the morning."

Ben Healy and Neilson Powless will lead the team next season, while Iván Sosa, Tao Geoghegan Hart, and Lorenzo Milesi are among six confirmed additions.

White said that success for him and EF next year will be measured by featuring throughout the season and getting results at the biggest races of the calendar.

"My passion is getting the most out of people. Cycling has changed a lot, but there's one thing that hasn't changed: you're dealing with human beings," he said.

"Getting the most out of people is something I really enjoy. I think if, in 12 months' time, we can sit back and look at the season and see that we've featured prominently throughout the year, especially at the pointy end of the races that matter, then that's a measure of success. And those races are the three Grand Tours and a lot of the Monuments."

White rode as a professional between 1996 and 2007 before joining what is now EF, and was then Garmin-Chipotle, for his first directing role in 2008. That stint with the team lasted only three seasons, before he was dismissed for breaching team policies by referring a rider to an outside doctor without reference to the team's own medical staff.

items.title: Netcompany Ineos to use AI-based aero testing app from 2027
items.author: josh.croxton@futurenet.com (Josh Croxton)
items.content:
Netcompany Ineos are set to reveal a partnership with digital aerodynamics app, AiRO, which will see it use a consumer-available app and artificial intelligence for its aero testing in the 2027 season.

The AiRO app, which launched a new AI-based CFD simulation tool called Vayu on Wednesday, promises to bring aero testing to a broader audience via bike fitters across the world.

It was founded just 14 months ago, and already claims to have multiple other WorldTour teams as paying customers.

AiRO confirmed it will be working with Netcompany Ineos in 2027, and understands a fuller announcement of the partnership will be made next week.

Founder, Ingmar Jungnickel – who cut his teeth with the German Olympic team, Specialized’s S-Racing division and the development of the last edition Specialized S-Works Venge – founded the company as a spin-off from a similar project he developed for the USA speedskating squad.

He ran a select group of media, including through the AiRO app, which spans road, gravel, mountain bike, and time trialling.

The app is available to anyone via specialist bike fitters for approximately $200 per session, and works by creating a 'digital twin' of each rider.

Using photographs, specialised software turns the images into a 3D simulation of the rider, which you can use to then run app-based aero experiments, such as swapping helmets or adjusting the rider’s position.

By integrating AI and its new 'Vayu' add-on, Jungnickel explains he has generated a long list of potential benefits.

One of these, which he caveats is a future innovation currently under construction, is the ability to instantly test 20+ different helmets (which have already been scanned into the app) on one rider, each in dozens of head positions, effectively recreating over 400 wind tunnel tests at the click of a button.

If Josh Tarling stops wearing a Kask helmet next year, we may able to attribute that decision to this feature, but there are of course other sponsorship agreements to navigate there.

A second feature is to immediately test over 100 small rider position changes – arms, head, shrug, etc – and order them by the available improvement. Working with the bike fitter, the rider can then replicate these positions to check whether they are actually achievable and sustainable in the real world.

The Netcompany Ineos deal is the brand’s first official partnership with a team, but based on existing work with teams, Jungnickel’s expectation is that the British squad will use it alongside real wind tunnel testing to help with testing the full squad rather than just the top riders, without the increased time and financial commitment that doing so in a wind tunnel would need.

He also says teams are excited by the opportunity to test riders' road bike positions, which he says takes longer and is less repeatable in a wind tunnel or velodrome setting.

Finally, he predicts that by having a digital twin of all the team's riders, the team will be able to quickly and cheaply test ideas, without needing the rider present.

And from there, if a new, faster position is found, but where a biomechanical concern exists, they can work with coaches and biomechanics experts to formulate a plan before the rider makes the switch and potentially causes an injury.

The full scope of the partnership is still being worked out, and details are expected to follow soon.

items.title: 'He has a very long way to go' - 19-year-old Tofik Beshir continues recovery in hospital from horrific training crash as CXD Trek Bikes teammates offer support with 'endless supply of bracelets'
items.author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
items.content:
It has been 20 days since Tofik Beshir went on a gravel ride near his college in North Carolina and was air-flighted to a nearby trauma hospital after being struck head-on by a driver of a motor vehicle. He was allowed to relocate to a Washington, D.C.-area hospital to be near his family, but "there's a long road ahead" according to his cyclo-cross team manager at CXD Trek Bikes.

"I can say he is much more conscious than he has been the prior week. Having Tofik talk back, even with his raspy voice, is just wonderful. I'm looking forward to when he can say thank you to the world," Chris Merriam, founder and team manager for CXD Trek Bikes, told .

Beshir first received medical care at Johnson City Medical Center in east Tennessee, with "injuries consistent with brain shear trauma". Before his parents could travel from Virginia to be at the ICU, Lees-McRae College cycling team coach Timothy Hall and school President Dr. [Herbert l.] Lee King were at Beshir's bedside. He also had Kelly Benefits road team coach and mentor Mark Frazier present. Hall has provided some updates on Instagram, with Beshir's family asking for privacy.

"He was just on a pretty short recovery ride in North Carolina. Both his [Lees-McRae] coach and I were expecting calls from him that night," Merriam recalled. "One of his teammates was actually able to ride to where the sirens were [heard that day] and kind of put everything in motion. Lees McRae and their support system jumped into action, and then we learned about it."

Merriam, who is based in Washington, D.C., said the young riders on his team have been deeply disturbed by the situation. Beshir started with the team as a junior several years ago and opened this season with five wins in six races, sweeping elite races at Charm City Cross en route to winning the USCX Series title and establishing himself as a leader.

Beshir was back in North Carolina for school in early October and preparing for race weekends in Ohio and Indiana, where last year he landed his first UCI elite men's cyclo-cross podiums, including a first UCI elite race victory, at the age of 18, at Major Taylor Cross Cup.

When the news of Beshir's horrific crash was relayed to riders on October 9, Merriam said his CXD teammates wondered if travel and racing in Ohio was "the right thing to do".

"It's a really hard thing to balance going out and racing, just doing the sport, and knowing that our teammate and close friend is lying in a hospital bed. The response from the team [has been huge]. Alyssa [Sarkisov] and Miles [Mattern] in particular, they really led the charge."

He described how team members gathered supplies to hand thread beads onto elastic bands, many in the purple and gold colours for the CXD squad, the day before the race in Ohio. On the first day, he said more than half the field of elites wore the 'Tofik bracelets', including rivals and elite winners Manon Bakker and Andrew Strohmeyer.

"It was thanks to them and Cora Cusack, one of our junior riders, who just made boxes full of them. We were also able to get cards, about 100, so people could send Tofik a note. My wife and I took the cards to him last night, and more from another local race. His mom is helping him work his way through this giant pile of cards.

"I know from him it really means quite a bit the amount of community support he's getting. Whatever people want to call it, prayers or positive healing vibes, he is definitely aware.

"A shout out to Finnley Sonnemann, another one of our juniors. He went to a farmer's market and sold a few hundred dollars of them, which went straight to the GoFundMe."

The GoFundMe page was started on October 9 and has raised $142,157 to date. Merriam said to get the word out right away at Kings CX, the team also created a poster with a QR code, and they hoped to spearhead the crowdsourcing effort into a medical trust for care over time.

"The poster was there when people were coming to pick the bracelets and fill out the cards. It was everybody making donations at whatever level they felt comfortable with, but it made a huge difference. That kind of momentum has really carried forward. It was strange doing what we love, racing, as a team and a family without him."

Trek CXD Bikes will co-host the Pan-American Cyclo-cross Championships in Washington, D.C. on November 7 with the DCMTB club team, the event returning to the Armed Forces Retirement Home. Merriam said a special poster will be created by Marian University cycling alumnus Lucas Stierwalt using a photograph of Beshir popping a wheelie to win a bike race. The posters, as well as "an endless supply of bracelets", will be available at the team tent to continue fundraising efforts.

Merriam confirmed he knew Beshir was healing, though slowly, when the teenager still had his sense of humor.

"I told him that Manon Bakker was racing in Europe with his bracelet, she sent me a message overnight. He said 'I finally get to race in Europe'. So he is internalising all the good feelings."

In addition to the medical trust, his family and collection of teams as that get well cards be sent via US Mail: Tofik Beshir, PO Box 6323, 5636 Connecticut Ave NW, Washington, DC 20015.

items.title: From scandals and scepticism to parasocial belief – I've witnessed cycling's perception of doping shift dramatically over the last decade, but is that OK?
items.author: Andy McGrath
items.content:
"It was the season of Light, it was the season of Darkness, it was the spring of hope, it was the winter of despair, we had everything before us, we had nothing before us." - A Tale of Two Cities

The problem was that his emphatic performance coincided with an all-time low in trust in pro cycling; scandal after scandal, lie after lie, burned its followers.

The next morning, a hundred members of the media crammed into a conference room at the Park Inn Hotel in Orange to bury the yellow jersey with demanding questions, not to praise him.

The bombardment began: "What plan do you have to answer the critics suggesting doping may be behind his performance?"

"Yesterday you said you were 'honoured' by the comparison with Lance Armstrong. How can you be honoured given he got all his titles with doping?"

Sat next to him, Team Sky principal Dave Brailsford was also in the crosshairs.

"Dave, can you provide me with your most compelling reason why we should believe not just Chris but every single member of your team?"

The kicker at the end to the race leader: "Is all this beginning to tarnish the whole experience for you?"

"I just think it’s quite sad that we're sitting here the day after the biggest victory of my life, quite a historic win, talking about doping," Froome said. "Quite frankly, my teammates and I have slept on volcanoes to get ready for this, been away for months working our arses off to get here. And here I am basically being accused of being a cheat and a liar. And that's not cool."

With that, the mild-mannered Briton got up and strode out of the room. That spicy 15-minute press conference was a memorable indictment of the crippling lack of belief in the sport.

There was the same cycle after every scandal: talk of rebirth, springs of hope leading to more controversy and winters of despair. Being a cycling fan, let alone a journalist, who believed wholeheartedly in what they were seeing play out on the road was like outing yourself as someone who also thought the Tooth Fairy, Father Christmas and flying pigs existed.

Back then, the sport seemed irredeemably rotten. Every record-breaking ascent raised eyebrows; many superhuman performances were treated as guilty until proven clean, with the baseline assumption that most racers were on something. Doping talk – pharmaceutical and mechanical – was a constant background thrum, asked about in every long-form interview. And if I had a pound for every time I heard or read the going-through-the-motions answer from a bike racer: "the sport is much cleaner now..."

At the pinnacle of performance, Team Sky, Froome and company preached pristine values and zero tolerance to a crowd of angry non-believers. No wonder it occasionally got ugly.

At times, the racing was like a sideshow to the volatile atmosphere between the peloton, spectators and media. Riders felt the frustration and distrust, sometimes physically: Froome had urine thrown at him, was slapped and spat at, super-domestique Richie Porte was punched, and the Sky team car was battered and rocked by spectators on Alpe d'Huez.

The sport is moving from being mired in doubt and traumatised scepticism to a more protective level of fandom – and one of the reasons for that has little to do with pro cycling.

Not so long ago, a rider's primary means of self-expression was limited to interviews with online cycling media or magazines, perhaps a brief appearance on . A comparatively limited output, a slow-burn way of getting to know them.

The digital media landscape has transformed. Social media and video-sharing platforms allow an infinite scroll of unfettered, unfiltered-appearing access, leading to a closer, more parasocial relationship with the sport’s protagonists.

Consequently, traditional print media is no longer the primary storyteller; control of the message has shifted to top riders, squads and brands. Short-form video is king, whether that’s from racers like Victor Campenaerts vlogging authentically pre-race on Instagram or sizable in-house media teams posting curated content for YouTube and other platforms.

With all the proximity over the months and years, a passive, subconscious background swell of positive feeling washes over some followers, driven by personality and good vibes. Doping never comes up organically in their narratives; why on earth would it? Positivity sells – they want your love, but don’t forget that in a sport bankrolled by businesses, the sponsors or partner cycling brands also want your money – not thorny stories lacking in digestibility.

That shift means the d-word is more likely to be further out of sight and mind, alongside the fact that it has been almost ten years since a seismic cycling scandal. It is easier than ever for doping, the sport’s number one enemy in the 21st century, to slide into the collective mental background.

The sport appears cleaner too. Empirically, there has been a fall in the number of positive doping tests, going from 29 in 2022 to 20 last year. It is over a decade since a rider was thrown off the Tour de France – Luca Paolini, for a cocaine positive in 2015.

Of course, most cycling fans are not naive. They know an apparent lull does not mean doping is a vanquished scourge. After all, it’s only been three weeks since Alberto Bruttomesso (Bahrain Victorious) was suspended for anti-doping rule violations.

Some modern sport fans' battlegrounds have also moved from doping doubt onto personality, beliefs or politics. In the polarised world of social media,where opinions fly around as freely as leaves in an autumn gale, I see both greater warmth and protectiveness towards some racers and a more deeply reinforced negativity against others.

Take Lidl-Trek rider Quinn Simmons, who told me in December 2025 for that certain people have "harassed" him his whole career, but that for every negative comment, he gets ten positive ones. Real life is very different to the online world's vocal, invisible minority: the American champion turned up to a 2026 Tour de France stage start in the town of Aurillac (i.e. the middle of nowhere) and encountered a French fan who had driven six hours to be there, wearing his team kit and impressively recreating his hair, beard and moustache combo.

Can Pogačar and today's peloton make reparations for previous errors?

Figurehead riders or squads tend to set the tone of every era, and Team Sky came to embody a lot of the previous era’s ills, as well as bringing a few of their own. Sharing Chris Froome's 2013 Tour power data with French newspaper – an act which is seemingly more than any leading contemporary team has done – did not quieten the questioning voices. The issue put forward remains the same as now: how do you prove a negative?

Ultimately, the zero tolerance team did not break the toxic cycle orcleanse themselves of the whiff of wrongdoing. In 2018, a British parliamentary committee found that the team "crossed an ethical line" over the use of medical exemptions for banned drugs, related to the jiffy bag farrago.

The drift away from traumatised scepticism has probably been helped by the changing of the guard: Sky is no longer the sponsor, and current incarnation Netcompany Ineos does not rule the roost.

After the transition of cycling power, new bosses UAE Team Emirates-XRG are not so different on the face of things. The probable richest team in the sport, winning Grand Tours repeatedly with a coterie of well-paid helpers, most of whom could be leaders in their own right – check, check and check again, straight from the "Death Star" playbook.

Associations with doping? They have a few. Mauro Gianetti and Matxin Fernández were managers of Saunier Duval, the team embroiled in doping scandals at the 2008 Tour de France. Kristijan Durasek was suspended after being named in Operation Aderlass in 2019, and rider Marc Soler's father Jaume received a (now overturned) suspension in February 2026 for working with banned ex-US Postal doctor Pepe Martí (there is no suggestion of wrongdoing by Marc Soler himself). Some fans may also look negatively upon the team's close association with the United Arab Emirates, a Middle East oil giant with a "dismal" human rights record, according to Amnesty International.

But none of this mud sticks, and that has much to do with the individual who defines this decade in pro cycling. Tadej Pogačar holds a lot of soft power, not just as an exemplar of spectacle and excellence, but as a transmitter of sympathetic feeling and good vibes to his team and the sport as a whole from his own actions and image.

To, if the modern peloton feels like repairmen for their predecessors' wrongdoings, Pogačar is the inadvertent head fixer in this move from embattled past to a present of fragile hope.

Though he has not faced the Spanish Inquisition level of questioning that Team Sky and its leaders encountered, Pogačar has quickly learned to answer challenging questions better than "I’ve never tested positive", his 2021 groan-worthy echo of a Lance Armstrong answer.

He has faced down queries about doping, his credibility and UAE's connections to the sport, never flying off the handle or pouring fuel on the fire like more combative superstars of recent generations. He understands that such inquiries are the lot of every new world-beater in this day and age "because cycling was so damaged in the past, before my time".

Generations change, but professional sport doesn't. Those seeking optimal performance will still use any legal method – such as carbon monoxide rebreathing, grubby but lawful – and some will inevitably go over the ethical and permissible line. Anti-doping agencies are historically under-funded and invariably playing catch-up against the next doping advances. It takes a long time for a culture to alter and, as a product of my time, scepticism is baked into me.

But I think some cycling fans have moved on, allowing themselves to be more cautiously hopeful – to believe again. That’s something to be cheerful about, with a caveat: after a good while without a sport-shaking controversy, the shock and damage will likely be even greater if an epochal racer is caught in the net. We aren’t out of the woods yet, just in a clearing.

items.title: 'He will restart as scheduled' – Egan Bernal more likely than ever to return for the 2027 season
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
Former Tour de France and Giro d’Italia winner, Egan Bernal, is likely to return to the peloton in 2027 after some earlier doubts following the early closure of the Colombian rider’s season.

In that statement, Bernal said he intended to return in 2027, but left the door open to his premature departure from the sport, saying: "I don’t know exactly what the coming years hold, and I don’t think I need to know everything right now."

However, the 29-year-old recently travelled from his Colombian home to a team meeting at Netcompany’s Copenhagen headquarters, signalling his intention to continue racing. And if that wasn’t enough, comments from one of the team's sports directors, Dario Cioni, seem to have gone at least some way to confirming he will remain.

"Egan took a break from the season finale, but he had done the Giro and the Tour, so it’s not something we’ve never seen before," Cioni told .

"It’s clear that Bernal is a winner; he is not happy with finishing tenth. And rightly so, after the Giro and the Tour, he didn't feel he could be competitive, so he chose to end the season early. But he will restart as scheduled in 2027."

Winning the Tour de France at just 22, Bernal was heir apparent to the team’s Grand Tour-winning heritage. He went on to win the 2021 Giro d’Italia, but, despite some glimmers of hope, has never been the same since a career-threatening training crash in Colombia at the start of 2022.

The team gathering in Denmark was an opportunity for riders and staff to meet their new sponsor, Cioni, describing it as halfway between the end of the 2026 season and the start of 2027. Riders had medical checks, while staff had their chance for meetings.

In the interview with Cioni was also asked about the departure of Filippo Ganna to Lidl-Trek, a rider with whom he had worked closely.

"Those are choices in the hands of managers," Cioni said. "On a personal level, obviously I'm sorry, but these are team decisions that must be respected.

"A rider like Pippo [Ganna], who gives 100% towards the goals he sets for himself, pushes everyone to the limit. I think that as a team, until the arrival of Remco [Evenepoel], we were the point of reference in time trials.

"Beating Remco is not easy, but if we look at the collective, we are still at the forefront. We have the best package, certainly not inferior to Specialized, and we got to this point also thanks to a rider like Ganna."

items.title: Lidl-Trek launch women's development team with rising talents from USA and Great Britain among 10-rider roster
items.author: Matilda Price
items.content:
Lidl-Trek are adding a women's development squad to their line-up of teams for 2027, launching Lidl-Trek Future Racing Women with a 10-rider roster packed full of talent.

Lidl-Trek launched their men's under-23 squad in 2024, and will now join the small number of teams to run a women's development squad with their new project for 2027. It will be registered at Continental level and is not strictly an under-23 squad, with some older riders in the roster.

The team will comprise 10 riders from eight different countries, including the USA's Katherine Sarkisov, Great Britain's Kate Richardson, and Austria's Tabea Huys, who has already been riding a stagiaire for Lidl-Trek's Women's WorldTour team this autumn.

Also in the line-up are the Italian pair Chantal Pegolo and Matilde Rossignoli, Liv Wenzel, from Luxembourg, Spain's Ane Zubeldia – daughter of retired pro Haimar – Olympia Norrid-Mortensen from Denmark, Messane Bräutigam from Germany, and Sarkisov's compatriot Ella Sabo.

The launch of the squad marks "an exciting new chapter in the team’s commitment to nurturing the next generation of talent in women’s cycling", the team said.

"Our aim is to give young riders the time, support and opportunities they need to develop," women's team manager Fränk Schleck said.

"The step up to the WorldTour is becoming more demanding, so we want to create a clear pathway where riders can learn, make mistakes and grow without the immediate pressure to deliver results."

Whilst U23 feeder teams are commonplace amongst men's WorldTour squads, it is still only a minority of women's teams that run such a programme, in part down to the fact that there is no dedicated U23 racing circuit for women.

Lidl-Trek will join Canyon-SRAM, AG Insurance-Soudal, Liv AlUla Jayco and Fenix-Premier Tech in having a development arm in 2027, though the total number of such teams will stay the same after UAE Team L'IMAD shuttered their development team this year.

"Now is the right time because women's cycling is growing, and our investment needs to extend beyond the WorldTour team. We also have a responsibility to help develop the next generation," Schleck continued.

"When selecting the riders, we looked beyond the results. Potential, attitude, a willingness to learn and what each rider could bring to the group were all important. We also want to support riders across different disciplines, because there is more than one route to becoming a successful road rider."

Whilst racing will of course be important for the team, Schleck also underlined the team's commitment to preparing riders for life as a professional in general, too.

"The goal is to prepare them for the demands of professional cycling, both on and off the bike. Winning is part of that learning process, but success will also mean seeing riders gain confidence, take responsibility and eventually earn their place in the WorldTour," he said.

Huys, who is one of the older riders on the team at 21, has already been racing in the pro peloton at Continental level this year, taking some promising results that earned her a stagiaire ride with Lidl-Trek and now a place on the development team.

The team have already joined the wider team gathering in Bad Wimpfen, Germany this autumn, with their debut on the road set for 2027.

  • Matilde Rossignoli, 18, Italy
  • Kate Richardson, 24, Great Britain
  • Olympia Norrid-Mortensen, 21, Denmark
  • Liv Wenzel, 22, Luxembourg
  • Messane Bräutigam, 20, Germany
  • Katherine Sarkisov, 22, United States

items.title: From Zwift to the pro ranks – Cofidis sign double Esports World Championships runner-up
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
The Brazilian, who won the silver medal at the 2024 and 2025 Worlds, has joined the French ProTeam on a two-year deal.

In announcing the signing, Cofidis likened the 32-year-old's life to a TV series. A former skateboarder, she moved from Brazil to Germany and then took up mountain biking. In recent years, she took up e-cycling on Zwift, running a YouTube channel charting her racing career, and has become one of the world's top virtual racers.

Guerra took up road cycling last September and joined the German Continental team Wheel Divas. This year, she took part in several one-day races, including Binche-Chimay-Binche, the Women's GP Stuttgart, and the French 1.2 race, the Mirabelle Classic, which she won.

"I'm very curious and really excited about joining Cofidis. I want to find out whether I can transfer my strengths from e-cycling to the road," Guerra said.

"The few races I took part in towards the end of the season gave me confidence and caught Cofidis' attention. It's a challenge I'm really keen to take on. I don't have any particular apprehensions, just a huge amount of enthusiasm.

"I can't wait to start the season, give my very best, help the team and discover the very highest level of road racing. It's going to be a fantastic challenge!"

Guerra joins a growing list of top Esports racers to join the professional road ranks, including Jason Osborne, Jay Vine, Ella Harris, Neve Bradbury, Mattia Gaffuri, and the latest Zwift Academy winners, Emily Dixon and Noah Ramsay.

"We are very enthusiastic and excited to see how Gabriela will take on this incredible challenge," said Cofidis sport manager Raphael Jeune.

"Towards the end of the season, she demonstrated a real determination to succeed, as well as some very promising qualities on the road. Naturally, this makes us really keen to work with her ahead of next season.

"We will do everything we can to help her progress through the ranks and show us the same level of ability on the road as she has demonstrated in e-sport, where she is a world silver medallist. We can't wait to see her compete in her next races in the Cofidis jersey!"

items.title: Why Paul Seixas might not immediately return to the Tour de France in 2027
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
Paul Seixas made history in July as the youngest starter at the men's Tour de France in 89 years, before delivering on his promise as the hottest prospect in the sport to finish fourth on debut. It was huge for cycling in the era of Tadej Pogačar, with a look at his potential heir to the throne, but also for France, who have been waiting more than 40 years for their next home winner in the men's Tour – not since Bernard Hinault won in 1985 has La Marseillaise rang out in Paris as the yellow jersey champion stood on the final podium.

With all that said, an immediate return to cycling's biggest race in 2027 seems incredibly likely, especially given how rapidly Seixas seems to be taking the experience from every race he starts into his next goals. Just look at how quickly he moved on from completely berating himself at the World Championships for cramping to becoming Il Lombardia's youngest-ever winner two weeks later.

Seixas was fourth at the first time of asking, in the longest race he'd ever done, only around two minutes off Isaac del Toro on the podium, and he did all of that at only 19. Now 20, and starting to think about where he can showcase his wealth of talents in 2027, the French star was unwilling to say a return to the Tour was a guarantee.

Speaking on the 'Super Moscato Show' on this Monday, a week after the Tour's 2027 route was presented in Paris, Seixas stayed vague about his schedule.

"I have the general outline, but there are some decisions that are still unknown to me. I'm waiting for the team's opinion. It will depend a lot on what my coach says," he said, which is not uncommon at all for this time of year, with upcoming team training camps in December and January always serving as the place for planning calendars and announcing anything for Decathlon CMA CGM and almost every team in the WorldTour.

What Seixas doesn't hold back on is that he already has his eye on a home World Championships in Haute-Savoie – the department where his grandparents live – next August, and it's the Grand Tour that comes before it which is still up for discussion between him and the team. It's here that the door is potentially open to him not racing at the Tour.

"What's the best option, this or that Grand Tour before the World Championships? I'm obviously going to try to perform well in a Grand Tour, but I need to know how to structure the season around that. Knowing that no matter which Grand Tour I take part in, I'll have high ambitions for it," said Seixas.

"I haven't yet considered what I'm going to do next season. That will come in due time, and quite soon. I can't tell you I'm going to ride the Tour de France if I don't know yet."

Though the Tour route, like Worlds, also passes through Haute-Savoie, with somewhat of a dress rehearsal of the rainbow jersey race on stage 10 to Sallanches, it's not to say that Seixas doesn't to return to the Tour in 2027. He openly admits that: "It passes a lot through Haute-Savoie, near my grandparents' house. It's nice and it makes me want to ride it," but it may not be seen as the best path to success by him or his team.

Even with the end of the Tour coming on July 25 and the road race at Worlds being on August 29 – more than enough of a gap to do both, which the likes of Pogačar and Remco Evenepoel will surely do – there is room for Seixas to potentially make his Giro d'Italia debut instead in May.

Not only would this allow him a full block of recovery and then build-up towards the Super Worlds in France, but it could also put him within striking distance of victory at a Grand Tour in 2027 or at least an expected podium, with the stacked start list at the Tour making anything higher than fourth still seem a tough ask with Pogačar, Evenepoel, Del Toro, and Jonas Vingegaard all likely to be present.

Like Seixas, his team made sure to stay vague about Grand Tour hopes for 2027, with sports director Julien Jurdie choosing to focus on that goal of a top three instead of a specific race when he spoke in the wake of Seixas' Lombardia success.

"His program isn't known yet; we'll finalize that this winter. But Paul loves Strade Bianche, so I think he'll want to add that race to his palmarès," Jurdie told .

"He should once again tackle Monuments like Liège-Bastogne-Liège and Lombardy, and unsurprisingly, next year the goal will be to aim for a podium finish in a Grand Tour. We'll see which Grand Tour he rides."

With two time trials on the route and without an abundance of summit finishes for Pogačar to completely dominate, it's a Tour route that brings Seixas potentially closer to the likes of Del Toro and Vingegaard. However, the Giro should be equally difficult and suited to Seixas, with the rain and cold that can always threaten to affect the Italian race being no problem for the young Frenchman, who thrived in adverse weather conditions en route to his Itzulia Basque Country victory.

How his 2028 contract could change things

Seixas admitted he has grown tired of the whole process, with each stunning performance causing several people to tell him what to do. No decision over his future has been made yet, but it will come in the next 12 months, or sooner if he wants to be "free" of the speculation.

"It's going to become increasingly oppressive. I can't just decide at the last minute, either," he said to . "But perhaps I'll start the [2027] season without making any announcement - I don't know yet. I think there will come a point where I'll want to be free of this."

However, the contract situation could be key to defining which Grand Tour he rides in 2027. While most of his schedule was unveiled in the early months of 2026, Seixas' historic participation at the Tour wasn't announced until May – allowing for months of speculation and anticipation.

If he extends with Decathlon, the Giro and Worlds combination seems more likely, with a real shot at winning the pink jersey, and the best chance at Worlds on home roads and on the last climber-favouring course for a while, with the upcoming World Championships in Abu Dhabi, 2029, Copenhagen, 2029, and Brussels 2030 set to suit the sprinters and Classics specialists. Having just struck gold at Il Lombardia as a Monument winner, Seixas won't want to wait until Trentino 2031 for his next chance at rainbows.

However, if he decides to move teams from 2028 onwards, Decathlon would likely favour putting their big star into his second Tour de France and a final hope of winning cycling's biggest race with a French rider on a French team before he leaves.

Former long-term team manager Marc Madiot sees this as a likely possibility, with success at the Giro and Worlds also potentially solidifying Seixas' position as Pogačar's main challenger for years to come.

"The question is whether he will still be with his current team after 2027 or not. Because if he has a long-term contract with Decathlon CMA CGM, he can make the World Championships on home soil his main objective next year, and go for the win in the Giro before that. But let's imagine he signs with another team. In that case, instead of Decathlon CMA CGM, I would put him in the Tour de France in 2027," said Madiot on .

"After 2027, the World Championship course [in 2028] won't be suited to him. Let's imagine he extends his contract with Decathlon CMA CGM. He could go and win the Giro, become world champion, and thus become Tadej Pogačar's main rival. We would have a showdown at the top in 2028."

Seixas should face off with cycling's top rider in the hilly Classics, and maybe one of the big one-week races, and his team are expecting him to step up even more and provide serious challenges as he did at Liège-Bastogne-Liège. But their main battle may have to wait for Worlds in August if Seixas opts for the Giro as his approach.

"I think everyone now wants to see this battle between Paul and Pogačar. Paul is gradually closing the gap," said Jurdie. "I think on Saturday [referring to Il Lombardia], Pogačar must have watched the race thinking he'd be in trouble soon. He might have thought, 'He's going to give me a hard time next year!' There will be high expectations for Paul in 2027."

items.title: What it takes to make the yellow jersey – Inside Castelli's new partnership with the Tour de France
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
Watch the Castelli video launching their partnership with Tour de France organisers ASO and you’ll see a small boy, his imagination fired, watching the stars of the late 80s and 90s, when the Italian company last supplied the yellow jersey to the world’s biggest race.

That campaign is based on Steve Smith’s experience falling in love with our sport, watching it on TV at his childhood home in Oregon. Now living in Italy, not only is Smith a strong cyclist, but he’s Castelli’s Global Brand Manager, helping launch the company’s association not only with the Tour, but all of ASO’s races.

"When you're a kid you see that and it just strikes you just like it's so big. You know it'd be interesting to see how many hands would be raised today if we asked how many people got interested in cycling because of the Tour," Smith tells .

We’re speaking after the launch event for the new jerseys, eight floors above the city’s hubbub, on the roof terrace of ASO’s Paris headquarters. Listening to Smith, it’s hard to argue with what the Tour can bring to a brand.

"At the most basic level there's just that international exposure," he says. "I mean, 1.6 billion hours of coverage watched around the world, it's insane, what else can actually get that level of coverage?

"And then there's the next level on the product side, it's in our DNA, but this is another push to just make sure that we keep ourselves at the absolute forefront technologically, because clothing makes a big, big difference."

The partnership between Castelli and ASO will see the Italian brand providing jerseys for the men’s and women’s Tours de France and all their professional road races, from Paris-Nice to the Volta a Catalunya. In the one-day races where there are no leaders’ classifications, you’ll see the brand as sponsors.

So we’ll see a lot of the scorpion logo in the next few years – up to nine seasons – which is entirely the point, but while those other events will help the company its products to a wider audience, it’s the Tour which is the golden egg.

Castelli is not new to making leaders’ jerseys for Grand Tours. The brand worked with the Tour de France in the 1980s and 1990s, and while that was an age ago, it has been working with the Giro d’Italia since 2018. Coincidentally, that deal came to an end this year, the same time Santini’s deal with ASO ended, and after 18 months of talks, the new deal was done.

For a clothing manufacturer, the Tour de France is a big deal when it comes to getting eyes on its brand and products, but it also means it has to deliver enough of their best kit to riders performing in the biggest race in the world.

When a rider moves into the lead of any classification, they’re given a variety of kit to see them through any preference or eventuality. First there’s a race jersey, which they’ll be expected to wear with their own team shorts, though there’ll be two weights available to cater for the weather.

Most riders race in one-piece race suits these days, and there are two weights of those available as well, with a new one issued every couple of days if the rider still qualifies to wear it. And on top of that there’s a gilet, short-sleeved Gabba jacket and a long-sleeved rain jacket.

But perhaps the most talked about piece of kit issued to classification leaders is the time trial skin suit. With the perfect fit and a suit’s aerodynamics the subject of much discussion, we’ve even seen conjecture that GC riders might avoid leading a race in order to avoid ill-fitting kit. So how does Castelli hope to ensure its suit is one that helps rather than hinders riders?

"At the top levels now, each rider has spent countless hours perfecting their suit, but if teams are being honest, there's a lot of times you can put somebody into a suit you don't know and it throws up some great numbers," Smith continues. "And our suit at the Tour de France has been consistently very fast across a very wide range of people. So nobody’s going to be racing in a poorly designed suit."

Preparations for next year’s Tours de France can begin now, with the routes published and the company able to begin making educated guesses about who might be in the race lead and need a suit. There is even the chance of the company doing some pre-fitting with likely riders.

"We've been doing this for years at the Giro, where 90% of the guys we can put our standard suit on and it fits them quite well, and we do have a seamstress available if we need to do some modifications," Smith says.

The Tour de France isn’t the only race Castelli will be providing kit for, the agreement includes all ASO’s races, and some of those have different requirements to the Tour. The weather for both Paris-Nice and the Volta a Catalunya, for example, is cooler and often wetter than your average July in France or – as the men’s and women’s Vuelta a España are also on Castelli’s calendar – in Spain during September.

Castelli was around long before its first foray into supplying Grand Tour leaders’ jerseys, indeed, the company traces its history way back to 1876, when Vittore Gianni began his tailoring business in Milan, dressing football teams like AC Milan and Juventus, and even the Milan Ballet.

Its first foray into cycling was on the shoulders of Alfredo Binda, who won the Giro d’Italia five times in the 1920s and 1930s, though the company began concentrating on the sport when Armando Castelli bought the company in 1935. Ever since then, the company has tried to be at the forefront of technological advances. From silk time trial suits for Fausto Coppi in the late 40s, through the road racing skin suit Johan Vansummeren wore to win the 2011 Paris-Roubaix, to freezing, snowy 2013 Milan-San Remo, when half the peloton wore Gabba jerseys with the scorpion logo scrubbed out.

While Assos were first to use Lycra in cycling shorts, Castelli claim "the first aerodynamic Lycra shorts used in racing and sold to the public," producing coloured shorts for the first time a few years later. The company also lays claim to the first windproof jerseys and ergonomically designed seat pads.

With Armando’s son Maurizio at the helm, the company rebranded form Vittore Gianni to Castelli in the early 1970s and their scorpion logo was born. Maurizio died of a heart attack aged only 47, and in 2003 the company was bought out of bankruptcy by current owners, Manifattura Valcismon SpA, joining forces with other cycling brands Sportful, Karpos, Zoot and, more recently Tailfin.

This saw the company move to Fonzaso in the Dolomites where their products are still conceived and designed, before manufacture is completed at partner factories throughout Europe.

As part of the deal with ASO, Castelli recently launched its 'Maillot Jaune' line of kit. It’s not all yellow, and even the yellow they do use is different to that which we’ll see the Tour leaders wearing next summer, but it is a good example of the kind of effort that goes into producing a new consumer line.

"There was an incredible amount of work that went into that kit," Smith explains. "Trying to make it stretchy enough, but not too much because you make it too stretchy, it starts to sag. We've always made jerseys with limited stretch on the back to keep your jerseys or your pockets from sagging.

"But we knew we wanted to fit the widest range of people with the maximum amount of comfort, we wanted to make that fabric more stretchy than we've ever done before, both in width and in length. So we've actually kind of re-engineered the way we engineer the pockets by tightening up the waistband, so we're holding the pockets from below rather than above."

You can have all the striking and innovative designs you like, but any cycling kit company must live and die by how comfortable and durable their shorts are. While Castelli’s prototyping group will put most new items through four or five internal samples, shorts take far longer.

"They have about double the total production time because so many things could go wrong by doing it wrong, we feel it a lot more, so it's obviously quite a bit quicker on a jersey than on a short. But yeah, shorts will take a good year and a half in the production cycle," says Smith, before revealing the as-yet un-released shorts he wore earlier that day went through 14 rounds of samples.

For now at least, the only bits of Castelli kit you’re unlikely to be able to buy are the jerseys the brand will make for the Tour de France and Tour de France Femmes for the next few years: "We don't think there's really that much of a market for it," Smith says.

items.title: Lucinda Brand switches to Canyon-SRAM for the next two years with plans to end road cycling career at Paris-Roubaix
items.author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
items.content:
An "exciting new chapter" for multi-talented Lucinda Brand has been sealed with a two-year contract and a dual rule with Canyon-SRAM Scalable Capital for 2027. She has spent nearly half of her 18 years in the pro peloton with Lidl-Trek and will continue on the Women's WorldTour level through 2028 at her new home.

"It was almost like a new fire had been lit inside me," she said in a press release about her decision being based on more than a change of team.

"I didn’t want this to be just one more year on the bike. I wanted it to be the beginning of a longer-term project, where I could keep contributing to the sport and build on what I’ve already done as a rider. I really feel that this team shares my passion, ambition and philosophy on cycling, which gives me a lot of energy and motivation for this next chapter, and for what we can create together."

The 37-year-old Dutch rider will join as a rider, targeting stage races and one-day races through to Paris-Roubaix Femmes in 2028, where a finish in the velodrome is planned to be a career finale. Then she will transition to a staff role for the German-based WorldTour squad.

"When the opportunity came along to potentially finish my road cycling career at Paris-Roubaix, I knew straight away that it was a chance I had to grab with both hands," she said.

"Over the last few years, I’ve noticed that my role as a rider has become more than just racing. In a way, I’ve already been taking on the responsibilities that a sports director might have, and I’ve discovered how much I enjoy that side of the sport.

"I really love working with young, ambitious athletes, sharing my experience, and helping them grow. It’s something I’d love to explore further and develop myself in. That’s why it was important for me to find a team that recognised those qualities and was willing to give me an opportunity to grow in that direction."

Canyon-SRAM adds new title sponsor Scalable Capital next year and the roster features half of the riders at 24 years old or younger, including 19-year-old Emily DIxon moving up form the development team. The team's Director of Sport Rolf Aldag said Brand was an "obvious choice" as a veteran to help the team grow.

"There are a lot of changes happening to our roster, and we’ll have quite a few younger riders, so we need to create the right mix of potential versus experience and leadership," Aldag said.

"Having Lucinda is as much about leadership as it is mentorship. But, it’s not all about race results, it’s also how she also lives and pays attention to all the smaller details that are critical for reaching the very top.

"So, I think she can mentor our younger riders really well, and then bring a lot of stability to the classics team, which is a strong sporting focus for the next two years. We believe that the addition of Lucinda will be a real game-changer for us.”

Brand began her career as a 19-year-old with a Dutch squad and moved to the powerful Rabobank-Liv team from 2013 to 2016, racing during that time with compatriots Marianne Vos, Anna van der Breggen, and Annemiek van Vleuten. After winning the Dutch elite women's road race ahead of her teammates that first year then winning GP de Plouay-Bretagne in 2014, her road career ignited the next season with four stage podiums, including two victories, at Giro d'Italia for women and a second Dutch road title.

The team structure at Canyon-SRAM, with a singular focus on women's cycling, was one of the great appeals to make this transition.

"I’ve spent the last years in a very big organisation, with different teams all under one roof, and that has been a great experience. But, I’m really excited about coming into a smaller environment, where the lines are shorter, communication is more direct, and everyone is working towards the same goal. What I really like is that Canyon-SRAM still has a whole pathway – from development to the pro team – but within an organisation that is fully built for women’s cycling," she added.

On the road she has amassed 28 victories, including Baloise Ladies Tour, Tour de Suisse Women, and Thüringen Ladies Tour while at Lidl-Trek. This year she competed at the Giro d'Italia Women for a 15th time, challenging from a breakaway to go second on stage 2 into Salice Terme.

She's had podiums at the most challenging one-day races - Dwars door Vlaanderen, Amstel Gold Race, Liège-Bastogne-Liège and Paris-Roubaix. And it was the cobbles of 'Hell of the North' where she wanted to leave her mark for road racing.

“I love the challenge, the way the race unfolds, and the toughness of the cobbles – riding over them is unique and not something everyone can do," she said about the 'Hell of the North', where she was third in 2022 and 10th in 2026.

"For me, Paris-Roubaix is the race where road cycling and cyclocross come together in a beautiful way. Every time I think about racing it, my heart beats just that little bit faster.”

This time of year Brand goes back to work on her highly-decorated cyclo-cross duties, where she begins a 10th season with a team directed by Sven Nys. On the volatile tracks that range from sand to dirt to mud, Brand has 77 career victories. She attributed Nys with helping her connect with Trek-Segafredo years ago to give her a renewed interest in top-level road racing.

"When I was losing my joy for cycling, Sven brought it back. His passion, energy and belief in me made me fall in love with the sport all over again," she wrote on Instagram, adding that she would "always look back on with a big smile and so much gratitude" as she moves on to her new chapter.

She recently extended her off-road commitment to Baloise Verzekeringen - Het Poetsbureau Lions squad for this season and the 2027-2028 CX campaign. She opened this season with five podiums, including wins on the first two rounds of HG Cross series and the Superprestige series opener in Overijse. Last year she won the UCI Cyclo-cross World Championships a second time and also won the UCI World Cup and X2O Badkamers Trofee series.

items.title: More Chinese brands in the pro peloton for 2027 as TotalEnergies swaps Cube for Pardus
items.author: thomas.wieckowski@futurenet.com (Tom Wieckowski)
items.content:
Team TotalEnergies has announced a new bike sponsor today in the form of the Chinese brand Pardus.

The two parties have announced a three-year partnership which will run from 2027 through to 2029.

In an Instagram announcement, they spoke of a 'strategic partnership based on technological innovation.'

This is the second bike sponsor announcement in recent weeks after Specialized and Soudal-Quick-Step parted ways after a long and successful partnership together. Incidentally, Total Energies raced on Specialized bikes prior to partnering with Enve.

The team also released a press release on its website containing a little more information. Pardus will become a 'material sponsor' for all of the team's squads, which include the UCI Pro Team and U19 and U23 squads.

Pardus bikes are raced by the Chinese National Team and were also used by Team Vini Fantini in 2025 at a high level in races like the UAE Tour.

The Total Energies teams will use the SPK EVO G4 and Robin EVO G3 road models, along with the Gomera Evo TT bike.

Those are models that may not be as familiar as those from more established brands, and Pardus represents another Chinese brand joining cycling's top flight. Although Total Energies is not a WorldTour team, they will be riding some of the world's biggest races on Pardus machines over the next three years.

"Working alongside the Chinese national team since the Rio Olympics, we have gained in-depth knowledge of the demands of elite competition and the expectations of riders.

"This partnership will be a fantastic opportunity to share our technical expertise throughout the season, continuously enhance our product ranges through interaction with athletes, and solidify Pardus' presence at the heart of European cycling culture," said Terry Gong, Deputy General Manager of Pardus.

The brand's aero model is the SPKG4 Evo (pictured below). This is the model we may well see the TotalEnergies riders racing on most of the time.

items.title: The best indoor cycling accessories for under £25 / $25
items.author: Tim Perkin
items.content:
Indoor cycling has significantly grown in popularity, offering riders the possibility to train year-round regardless of the weather or daylight. Creating a comfortable and effective indoor training environment can improve your experience.

Improving your setup doesn’t have to be expensive, with some of the most valuable additions being the simplest and cheapest.

A few well-chosen accessories can help you stay hydrated, manage sweat, protect your bike, and ride more comfortably, all without stretching your budget.

If you are looking to make a small investment to make your indoor training more enjoyable, here are five affordable accessories, priced under £25 / $25, that deliver practical benefits and are good value for money.

You don't need to buy everything at once, either. Start with the essentials and add to your setup as needed.

A water bottle is one of the first accessories every cyclist should buy, as indoor cycling is thirsty work!

Although bottles are relatively inexpensive, investing in one or two durable options is worthwhile, particularly during the indoor training season when you'll use them regularly.

Elite supplies nearly every WorldTour cycling team in the professional peloton with bottles, so they know a thing or two about them.

Elite’s Fly Tex bottle is one of the most-used bottles in cycling, so this would be my recommendation. It's made from recyclable materials and is BPA-free.

They come in multiple colours and three different sizes: 950 ml, 750 ml, and 550 ml.

Depending on your selection, prices start at $11.99, so for $25 you could buy a couple.

A towel is an essential accessory, as indoor cycling is a sweaty business. Fortunately, Elite has designed one that is fit for purpose. Measuring 1,300 x 300 mm and made from 100% natural cotton, it is a practical size to hang around your neck or drape over your handlebars.

Compact and soft, it's a practical addition to any indoor training setup, helping you manage sweat throughout your session.

A front wheel riser block is a simple accessory that can make indoor training more comfortable.

Placed beneath your bike's front wheel when using a compatible wheel-on or direct-drive trainer setup, it helps level the bike and provides a more stable riding position.

Riser blocks are available from numerous brands and are generally inexpensive. With prices starting at around $8.99, it's an affordable way to improve your indoor cycling setup.

Whilst you can use household objects to do the same job, they can be prone to moving under effort. A riser block is simply the best tool for the job.

Before buying, check that the block is compatible with your trainer and front-wheel setup, especially if you are running gravel tyres.

Muc-Off is renowned for its cleaning products. Its Sweat Protect spray is designed to help protect bike components from corrosion associated with sweat exposure.

Using a suitable protective product can help reduce the risk of corrosion and keep your bike in better condition over time.

If you want to safeguard your bike from the potential damage caused by heavy indoor use, this is a worthwhile investment. Always follow the manufacturer's instructions and check product compatibility before applying it.

Sweat can take a toll on your bike over time, particularly when it repeatedly drips onto the handlebars, frame, and components during indoor training.

The Wahoo Fitness Sweat Guard sits across your handlebars and attaches around the back of your saddle. It helps shield your bike from perspiration by catching sweat before it drips onto the frame and other components, where prolonged exposure can contribute to corrosion.

There are multiple brands on the market that sell these, but we like the Wahoo Fitness Sweat Guard.
