items.title: Abus Hyp-E helmet review: An urban e-bike helmet that's ready for anything
items.author: Simon Lock
items.content:
572g / 20.2oz (size M tested)

S, (51-55) M (54-58), L (57-61cm)

Signal Yellow, Champagne Gold, Volcano Titan, Gleam Silver, Jungle Green

2 hours on constant, 40 hours on flashing

USB-C

Abus may be better known for its D-locks and chains, but the German brand also has a nice line in helmets.

Founded in 1924 by August Bremicker, Abus has gradually built a helmet range that runs from race lids to kids' helmets, with a particularly strong urban line.

The Hyp-E is the brand's flagship e-bike helmet line, and it scooped a Eurobike Award in 2024. Where Abus' more basic Pedelec 2.0 helmet relies on a pull-out rain cap to fend off the elements, the Hyp-E goes one better with in-built sliding vent covers. It also goes all-in on visibility too, with integrated front and rear lights that act as indicators, triggered by a wireless remote on your handlebar.

Like its Pedelec stablemate, the Hyp-E carries Dutch NTA 8776 certification, which means it's been tested at the higher impact speeds you can reach with a motor under you, and it covers more of the head than a standard bike helmet.

The Hyp-E comes in three versions that all essentially use the same base helmet but come with increasingly flashy add-ons. The standard model reviewed here includes integrated lights, an indicator remote and a vent cover for when the weather turns. The ACE adds a magnetic flip-up visor and clip-on ear pads, and the BL.ACE adds a brake light remote on top of that. Those extras can also be bought separately, so the standard Hyp-E is effectively the base you can build up from.

I tested the standard Hyp-E on both electrically-assisted rides around town, as well as on my 40-minute, pedal-powered commute. Being early autumn, I enjoyed some warmer rides but was also faced with some biblical downpours, so the helmet got properly put to the test.

By design, the e-bike helmet is a bigger piece of kit than the everyday commuter helmet. The NTA 8776 certificate dictates that the shell needs to cover a larger proportion of the head. Add to that some integrated lights and vent covers and the size and weight is only going one way.

While the Hyp-E isn’t the bulkiest design on the market, it’s not exactly petite either. It’s not as streamlined as the Pedelec 2.0, but it’s not as big as some of the other smart helmet options, such as the Unit 1 Aura.

Abus calls the construction a multishell design, as part of the outer surface uses a tougher hard shell while the rest is a thinner in-mould polycarbonate layer. A polycarbonate strip also wraps the lower edge to protect against scuffs, which is welcomed by the tester as it will inevitably end up being knocked about a bit.

The lights are undeniably the stars of the show. Rather than clipping on as an afterthought, the front and rear LED strips are moulded into the shell, sitting flush with the contours. With the lights switched off, the helmet looks clean and tidy. With them on, you're highly visible.

The outer shell comes down lower at the temples and the back of the head than a standard helmet, as required by the NTA 8776 standard. Up top, the vents are generous by urban helmet standards, and the Hyp-E comes with a vent cover that slides over them when the weather turns.

Out of the box, the standard Hyp-E is the most stripped-back version of the three helmets in this range. There's no visor or ear pads to bulk it out, just the shell, the lights and a set of MagneticHub mounting points at the front. Those points are there so you can add Abus's magnetic visor, in clear, smoke or photochromic, and the clip-on Ear Pads (also sold separately). Add both and the Hyp-E takes on a distinctly motorcycle-like look, which personally feels a bit much, especially if you plan on using it on pedal-powered rides.

The standard Hyp-E also has the widest choice of colours in the range, giving you a choice between evocative names such as Champagne Gold, Jungle Green and Volcano Titan. The Midnight Blue that I tested had a nice matte finish across the shell, with a grey rear section housing the rear light, with some subtle touches of exposed EPS.

As soon as you pick up the Hyp-E, you’ll notice how robust it feels. Abus combines both in-mould and hard-shell production methods, which is why the helmet appears to have two distinct sections. The in-mould process fuses the EPS liner into a thin polycarbonate outer during production, while the hard-shell process involves manufacturing the liner and outer shell separately and then sticking them together. The in-mould process gives the Hyp-E its protective lower edge and rear section, while the hard shell allows for the slidable vents.

Safety is underpinned by NTA 8776, the Dutch e-bike standard that requires testing at higher impact speeds and extra coverage around the temples and back of the head. The helmet also carries CE and US CPSC certification. What it doesn't have is MIPS or any other rotational impact system, which is a notable omission at this price, and there's no Virginia Tech rating to back up the protection claims either.

The headline feature, of course, is the lighting. Rather than offering clip-on units, the front and rear LEDs are integrated into the shell, come with six modes – steady, power, flow, pulse, flash and eco – and boast an output of up to 50 lumens. Runtime ranges from a claimed minimum of two hours on the brightest steady setting to 40 hours in flashing mode, and the lithium-polymer battery takes around four hours to charge via USB-C. That's a welcome step up from the Micro-USB port and 10 lumens on the Abus Pedelec 2.0.

As well as providing a good source of visibility, the lights double as indicators, and the helmet comes with a wireless remote that straps to your handlebar. Pressing either button triggers a sequential sweep on the relevant side of the helmet, front and rear. Press both at once and you get a hazard-warning function. The remote is simple and connects via a radio link system, rather than Bluetooth, so there's no app to set up.

The standard Hyp-E doesn't include the brake light remote, which comes with the top-tier BL.ACE. Rather than relying on an accelerometer to guess when you're slowing down, Abus's brake light uses a rubberised cap that slips over your brake lever and fires when you pull it. It can be bought separately if you want to add it later.

Fit is handled by the Zoom Spin dial system, which uses a full headring and is height-adjustable, with an opening to accommodate ponytails. Abus's strap dividers lock in place below the ears, and they fasten with a magnetic buckle that can be opened one-handed.

Ventilation comes from three closable intakes on top of the helmet and two exhausts at the rear. The intakes are backed by bug mesh, and the included Vent Cover clips over them to block out rain, wind and cold. If you find you want more weather protection, the Hyp-E can be upgraded with the visor and ear pads that come with the Hyp-E ACE.

Even without those extras, the Hyp-E is no featherweight. At a claimed 580g for a medium, it weighs considerably more than the 350g Pedelec 2.0 and sits at the heavier end of the e-bike helmet category. That's the price you pay for high-quality integrated lights and battery.

I’ve been testing a lot of different e-bike helmets over the last six months, and picking my favourites for the best e-bike helmets has been a tough task. While the Hyp-E didn’t quite make the cut, it still performed extremely well in a range of conditions.

My top two criteria when researching helmets are safety and comfort. While I’m not paid nearly enough to put the Hyp-E’s safety credentials fully to the test, you can rest assured that some thorough testing has been carried out by people far more qualified than me. The NTA 8776 certificate is the gold standard when it comes to e-bike lids, and I would hesitate in recommending a helmet without it.

When it comes to comfort, there is of course an element of subjectivity, and to go some way to mitigating that, I did pass my Abus round a few friends for a second opinion. The consensus is that it is a pretty comfy piece of kit.

The Hyp-E uses a full 360-degree headring within the cradle, which means that any pressure that comes from tightening the dial adjust should be spread out, rather than being applied from the front or back, which can be the case with 180-degree rings. The fact that the rear section and dial adjust can be moved up and down only adds to the level of customisation when it comes to fit. It also allows for ponytails.

The strap doesn’t boast the reflective thread like the Pedelec 2.0, but otherwise it’s got some nice touches. The magnetic buckle is an advancement in fastening that I am fully on board with. Being able to unbuckle one-handed when you come crashing through the door after a wet and windy commute is the kind of small win I am here for. In addition, the soft chin guard beneath the buckle is held in place by Velcro, which saves you having to line it up every time you do the thing up.

For me, the two big plus points on the Hyp-E are the retractable vents and the integrated lights. Abus have clearly set out to make a line of e-bike helmets for all seasons and conditions. By including three big front vents, it has done what so many modern e-bike helmet manufacturers have failed to do, and allow sufficient airflow for warmer days. But by adding the slide-down covers, the design accounts for wet, cold and windy days, too. Abus has done this on the Pedelec 2.0 as well, although the cover comes in the shape of a tiny anorak which packs into a compartment at the rear of the shell.

In testing, the vents did exactly what they were designed to do, letting a decent amount of air in at the front and out through the rear. The vent covers are easy to close while riding, with a single slider fitted at the top of the shell.

Having tested this during early autumn, I was faced with a decision on those wet-but-still-warm rides. With the vents closed, the airflow is completely shut down, so it does get a bit warm. Honourable mention here to the Lazer Verde which has tried (with limited success) to create vents that both let air in but keep rain out. The Pedelec’s anorak should probably get another mention here, as that does at least allow some breathability.

With the nights starting to draw in, I was really glad to have the option of extremely effective integrated front and rear lights. At 50 lumens these aren’t the brightest (honourable nod to the Unit 1 Aura), but when it gets properly dark they really stand out. In addition, they wrap a long way round the shell, giving you a better chance of being seen by vehicles approaching from the side.

Once you get to know the button and the modes, it’s easy enough to operate whilst riding, and the USB-C charger means you’re not forever hunting through drawers for an old lead.

I’m a big fan of these lights, and while I’d always recommend pairing them with some decent bike lights as well, the extra visibility goes a long way. As far as the indicators go, I’m not fully convinced turn signals via a helmet light is something drivers are fully tuned into, but that will inevitably change if and when the technology becomes more widely used.

The indicators on the Hyp-E go produce a very clear flashing light on the right or left of the helmet, and the colour switches from red to yellow. This means anyone paying attention will see a pretty distinct signal, as opposed to mistaking it for just another mode. The handlebar-mounted switch was easily paired with the helmet in a matter of seconds, and also charges via USB-C.

I didn’t get a chance to fully put Abus’ claims around helmet battery life to the test, but the lowest output mode (which I assume gets you the maximum 40 hours of charge) is frankly pretty crap compared to the other settings. So I would assume the time between charges to be considerably shorter than that.

One drawback of the Hyp-E is that it’s pretty heavy, which is to be expected when you include such good lighting. It weighs a full 200g more than the Pedelec, which is ultimately one of the reasons its little cousin made it into the final list of favourites ahead of this one. While e-biking between school and nursery, I didn’t really notice it, as these are 20-minute rides and I sit more upright, but head down on my pedal-powered commute, I did notice the difference compared to my regular lid.

The Hyp-E currently retails at around £159, putting it just about in the top end when it comes to e-bike specific helmets. If you want to add the bells and whistles (not literally) you could fork out £199 for the ACE or £230 for the top-spec BL.ACE.

For that money, you get integrated front and rear lights, indicators with a handlebar remote, a vent cover, USB-C charging and NTA 8776 certification. That's actually quite a lot of tech for well under £200. The missing pieces are MIPS or any rotational protection, a Virginia Tech score, but you’re still getting a good return on your investment.

If you don't need indicators and you want to trim the weight, Abus's own Pedelec 2.0 costs around £150 to £160, weighs significantly less and has a clever integrated rain cap, but its 10-lumen rear light is a big step down.

The Smith Dispatch MIPS costs £155 and combines MIPS, Koroyd and NTA 8776 certification with an included clip-on rear light, all at 394g. Personally, I love the Dispatch, but it lacks the front light and vent covers. The Giro Camden MIPS costs around £120 and pairs NTA 8776 and MIPS with a big rear light and does have vents you can close.

The most direct rival is probably the Unit 1 Aura MIPS. At £200, it costs a little more but adds MIPS and a full five-star Virginia Tech rating to NTA 8776 certification. Its eye-catching 350-lumen front and rear lights charge via USB-C, and it also offers crash detection. It's heavier still at 610g, though, and the indicator remote isn't included as standard.

If being seen is your top priority, the Hyp-E is one of the most complete packages on the market at this price. Integrated front and rear lights, indicators and a remote all come as standard for less than many rivals charge for a helmet with a single rear light.

It also scores highly in the helmet-for-all-seasons category, with the large vents offering enough airflow on warm days and the retractable covers giving you the option of shutting out the elements.

Despite the weight, which is pretty significant, I also found it otherwise really comfortable, as did a few friends (albeit not for long periods). The full 360-degree headring (which isn’t a given at this price point) and adjustable rear section make finding a snug fit nice and easy.

Add to the mix the USB-C charging port and the magnetic buckle, and the Hyp-E is suddenly ticking a lot of boxes.

While it comes badged with the NTA 8776, the lack of MIPS is a real omission, and the Unit 1 Aura offers more independently verified protection for not much more money. But if visibility, ventilation and comfort matter most, the HYP-E makes a strong case.

Testing scorecard and notes

Great customised fit with 360-degree headring and adjustable height on the dial

Comes with NTA 8776 but lacks Virginia Tech rating and rotational impact protection

Great ventilation that can be shut off in cold or wet weather.

Good visibility with USB-C charging and indicator function.

A good looking lid although slightly on the bulkier side and weighs a lot.

Compared to the competitors you're getting decent value, with plenty of features for just under £160. Ultimately it depends how much value you put on things like indicators and vent covers.

items.title: Canyon Grail CF SLX review: More capable than ever before, but perhaps not quite as fun
items.author: thomas.wieckowski@futurenet.com (Tom Wieckowski)
items.content:
• $5,499 / £4,799 / €4,999
  • 9kg (S) out of the box with sealant, computer mount, cages, storage bag and tools.
  • SRAM Force XPLR - 10-46T / 40T
  • Strawberry Shake / Metallic Acid / Monochrome

The Grail has been in the Canyon range since 2018 and is the brand's racier, performance-oriented model.

Gravel bikes designed for competition are becoming more aerodynamic, race-focused, and are getting bigger clearances; this latest update sees Canyon take the Grail down that path further still.

The new machine is more aero, lower, racier and now has 57mm tyre clearance. The previous Grail had 42mm clearance, so this is a big jump. That smaller clearance number was probably the key weak spot in the 2nd-gen bikes' armour as gravel machines progressed at pace.

Canyon said it took its time with this update, and wanted to keep the Grail feeling like a Grail. I can understand that; the previous bike was one of the best gravel bikes and was pretty much universally regarded as a strong all-rounder.

This time around, I have tested the CF SLX 8 AXS, the model I also tested last time, in the eye-catching 'Strawberry Shake' colourway. The price for this second-tier CF SLX model is $5,999 / £4,799 / €4,999.

You can see the outgoing Grail up above and compare the visual differences, but let's cover what exactly has changed first.

Tyre clearance has really been boosted from 42mm up to 57mm, and that new number is a big talking point when it comes to the new Grail.

Canyon has achieved this by using a thin but solid section of driveside chainstay and by growing the rear chainstays by 10mm. Up front, a revised fork provides plenty of clearance. 57mm + 4mm either side in line with ISO guidelines.

The new frame is a little heavier; my Gen 2 CF SLX 8 weighed in at 8.2 kg out of the box. This time we were at 9kg on my scales. If you're a racer, the increased aero will probably make you faster, depending on speed, but as a general gravel bike for an everyday rider, I think the added weight at times makes the bike feel just a touch less nimble.

The frame has some deeper tube profiles and more aero overall shapes; you can read about Canyon's claims regarding aero performance in our Grail news piece.

On the aero topic, there's also a new, more aerodynamic seatpost, the SP0093 VCLS. Canyon says it offers 25% more vertical compliance than a rigid unit.

The front end is more aggressive; it's now 15mm lower, but Canyon is speccing shorter stems on models. Small to large bikes come with an 80mm stem as well as an adjustable 390-440cm bar. The stem has been pretty much ideal for me, but bigger riders or those wanting a long reach may want or need a longer front end.

On the geometry, the Grail has received some slight tweaks, but on paper things are very similar to the old bike. For a small, my size, the head tube angle of 71.5 degrees stays the same, and the seat tube angle steepens slightly, going from 73.5 to 73.9 degrees.

The chainstays have grown by 10mm, and the wheelbase is 5mm longer. The stack is 15mm lower, whilst the reach number is the same.

That stem is part of the adjustable CP0048 integrated handlebar with width-adjustable Control bar drops. You can buy alternate drops or handlebars, but you will have to pay extra to do it.

The CF SLX model also has full fender mounts, something the race-focused CFR model doesn't. If you choose to use the Canyon FAST Fender system, you won't be disappointed; it's very easy to use and provides excellent protection in bad weather. Don't forget you may need to come down in tyre size with them depending on what you are running.

Canyon has also produced some new frame storage bags for the bike in partnership with Cyclite; these are lightweight options and integrate neatly. They are available separately for $119.99 for the big bag, and $69.99 for the top tube option.

The CF SLX 8 arrived with a solid range of equipment. There's an excellent SRAM Force XPLR groupset with a left-hand power meter. Stock cranks are also 165mm in length, very on-trend.

The wheels are carbon fibre DT Swiss GRC 1400s, a hardy and aerodynamic option. They are wrapped in 45mm Schwalbe G One RS tyres. Some may criticise the decision not to fit a 50mm+ tyre from the off, but there is nothing wrong with the stock 45mm tyres.

I'm constantly impressed by just how capable a good gravel bike is these days. They can do so much, so well. The Grail CF SLX is no exception; it's performed well everywhere.

It goes fast on the flat and on smoother gravel and broken tarmac. I often leave the road behind on my to-go loop and enter a short descent into a long, straight gravel track; I get the Grail up to speed there, and it just eats the road up.

That lower front end helps a touch, but the bike doesn't feel aggressively low; it's a measured change. I like it.

The bike is stable at speed and under hard braking in the drops, and handles rough technical sections well. There's no doubt this is a hugely capable bike; I haven't found it wanting in any one area. The bar has been raised wholesale with modern gravel bikes; the differences are finer and more specific now, I find.

The Grail is undoubtedly more race-oriented; however, I don't find the CF SLX super stiff, and it doesn't feel quite as agile and, dare I say it, as fast as the Argon 18 Anti Matter I rode in the summer did.

It's a calmer experience with the Grail; it has not put a foot wrong on any terrain during my testing, but at times the ride feels a little muted.

Perhaps it's the capability of the overall package that just makes things feel calmer, or the longer chainstays, bigger rubber and slightly heavier wheelset (1600+ grams) on this model reducing some playfulness.

I started on the stock Schwalbe G One R 45mm tyres, then switched to big 2.2" Continental Dubnital tyres in their fastest version, and went back to the 45s, and I think I had more fun on the 45s at home riding solo.

The big tyres fit comfortably, and part of the reason for switching was to verify the bike's clearance myself. It's there, and the bike's proportions still look very normal. Canyon has executed it very well.

It's heartening to know that big clearance is there for when you need it, but a 45 or a 50mm tyre is still very capable, and the bike feels a little more nimble and exciting to ride, in my opinion. I'd maybe go big where needed if I was racing a gravel calendar, and run a 45 or 50mm tyre at home.

My standard advice now is to shop for a gravel bike with a SRAM XPLR 1x groupset if you are looking for a gravel bike. They are fantastic groupsets for off-road riding. I have no complaints about the drivetrain performance, and the brakes are fantastic for scrubbing off speed off-road.

At times my knees have scuffed the Cyclite top tube bag; I've found the bag material quite rough, sharp on the edges, even. It's my problem, but long term I'd probably need a different bag, or even no bag, to prevent knee grazing.

The strong speccing continues through the CF SLX 8 model; the drivetrain is excellent, and the wheel and tyres package is great; the Schwalbe G-One tyres are excellent all-rounders. The wheelset is a touch on the heavier side in its 50mm version; perhaps some lighter wheels may help boost the feeling of acceleration and nimbleness.

Aside from some rough bag material, the Grail has performed perfectly. No mechanical issues of any kind, which is always good.

Maintenance and servicing

We're heading into winter here in the UK, and my thoughts are already turning to winter maintenance. I've had to hose down a muddy Grail a few times already.

At risk of sounding like a broken record, the key maintenance area to watch here is the integrated handlebar and stem assembly. You can't remove the stem easily, so trapped water and dirt will stay inside the headset/head tube area. A full strip-down for replacements will be expensive. Look after it by minimising aggressive hosing, and consider a front fender in some conditions.

Elsewhere, I'd recommend staying on top of the seatpost clamp assembly, thru-axles, and AXS rear derailleur sleeve in general. There's also a press-fit bottom bracket, which shouldn't cause too much of a headache, really. Though, of course, creaks do arise sometimes.

You're starting in a competitive place immediately with Canyon's direct pricing.

This bike costs $5,999 / £4,799 / €4,999 at RRP. The SRAM Force XPLR-equipped Factor Sarana I tested in the summer costs $2,500 more than this bike. Though you can spec your desired bar width and stem length at checkout with the Factor.

There's a solid spec with no gaps here, and any and all spare parts or hardware you might need are easily found on the Canyon site. The Grail range also has several cheaper bikes with this, and in my experience, Canyon bike specs are generally solid.

As ever with Canyon models, it would be nice to get the computer mount included with the bike, and you will, of course, need to buy any accesories you need separately, such as the frame storage bag, frame bags, or mudguards.

The latest Canyon Grail is a massively capable bike that will handle pretty much whatever you throw at it; it's a tank.

Canyon has given it a thorough update and improved the areas that were seen as the weaknesses of the old bike, namely the conservative tyre clearance. Riders and racers alike can now go as large as they want depending on preference or the demands of a course, that's to say nothing of mud clearance.

As I said in my first ride piece, the Grail still largely feels like a Grail; performance and capability have increased. I'll hammer the point home: this is a massively capable gravel bike, but it isn't quite as lively as the previous bike.

Perhaps this is where gravel bikes are now heading; if you're a racer looking for the most capable aero race bike with big clearance, you can just get on and race, then step this way.

Very nice, I think the frame looks very 'normal' for the big 57mm clearance, and the frame looks agressive and purposeful. I like the 'Strawberry shake' paint too.

Very solid, excellent groupset, solid wheels and tyres and Canyon's equipment works wekk. The wheels are a little on the heavier side, and may not help acceleration.

Super capable and fast in any terrain. Clearance provides more tyre choice than ever before. The ride feel does feel a little muted at times. I don't feel the seatpost adds much in the way of comfort.

9kg for a small out of the box without pedals, and with accesories. Not superlight, in line with other competitor models.

Very good, a solid spec and overall build. As ever with Canyon, it would be nice to get the computer inluded.

items.title: 'Still so much I want to achieve' – Jay Vine commits future to UAE Team Emirates-XRG with 2029 contract extension
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
After a season blighted by poor luck and injury, Jay Vine has committed his long-term future to UAE Team Emirates-XRG, extending his contract until the end of the 2029 season.

This will bring the Australian time trial champion's time on the Emirati team to a total of seven seasons, having joined in 2023. Since then, he has developed into an elite time trialist, breakaway hunter, and fine domestique, contributing to others’ successes while still able to take his own opportunities.

Vine, 30, began his time at UAE with overall victory at the Tour Down Under, bagging the first of two general classification successes in his home race. He followed that with stage wins at the Vuelta a España, where he has twice won the mountains classification, the Tour de Romandie, Coppi e Bartali and the Vuelta a Burgos.

Despite beginning his 2026 season by winning a stage and second GC title at the Tour Down Under, his 2026 has been far from plain sailing. On stage five of that very race, he was hit by a kangaroo which jumped into the peloton, sustaining a broken bone in his wrist, though was still able to finish and take the GC.

Returning for the Volta a Ciclista a Catalunya, he crashed out on stage three, before being one of two UAE riders forced to abandon the Giro d’Italia after a huge crash on wet roads during stage 2, this time leaving him with a fractured elbow and concussion.

There was more bad fortune at the Vuelta a Burgos, where he again crashed out, before illness forced him out of the Vuelta a España. However, he bounced back to close his season with second place at the Chrono des Nations, behind a rampant Remco Evenepoel (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe).

"I’m really happy to be continuing with the team until 2029," Vine said in a team statement. "I couldn’t imagine a better fit, and I’m incredibly grateful for the trust and support I’ve been shown here, both in the good times and the more difficult ones. That support means a lot to me and is something I really value about this team.

"I’m already building towards the 2027 season and can’t wait to get started. There’s still so much I want to achieve, and I’m excited to keep working alongside some genuine friends, and see what we can accomplish together over the coming years."

items.title: After three-decade gap, Basque company Etxeondo joins forces again with Movistar as apparel sponsor
items.author: Alasdair Fotheringham
items.content:
Movistar have confirmed that Basque company Etxeondo will once again be their apparel sponsor from 2027 onwards, reviving a collaboration that lasted through much of the historic Spanish team's 'golden age' of the 1980s and early 1990s.

Etxeondo last sponsored Movistar back when it was the Reynolds squad, beginning in 1983 through to the mid 1990s, by which time the team's main backer was the Spanish bank, Banesto.

During that time, Reynolds/Banesto became a pioneering force for Spanish cycling in the Giro d'Italia and Tour de France as the country bounced back from its lacklustre era of the late 1970s. The team won the Tour with Pedro Delgado in 1988 and then Miguel Indurain from 1991 through to 1995, with Indurain also claiming the country's first-ever victories in the Giro in 1992 and 1993.

The return of Etxeondo as clothing sponsor for Movistar covers both the men's and women's teams, although the actual design of the new kit for both squads will likely only be revealed in early 2027.

"We are renewing a relationship that goes all the way back to the Reynolds years," Movistar said in a team press release. "It's a new phase which unites history with the development of race-competition apparel."

"Aerodynamics, comfort and protection in different kinds of weather will be the main focus points of our collaboration."

"The knowledge gained will have benefits beyond professional cycling. Etxeondo will transfer what is learned in the team to the development of its products to improve the experience of those who enjoy cycling every day."

Founded in the Basque Country in 1976, Etxeondo has spent the last five decades dedicated to the design and development of cycling clothing. It currently has two bases, in the towns of Irura (Gipuzkoa) and Castejón (Navarre).

items.title: Mads Pedersen among group of Danish athletes suing HBO over use of their images for advertising
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
Mads Pedersen is among a group of Danish athletes suing streaming service HBO Max over unauthorised use of their images.

Cyclists Amalie Dideriksen, Mikkel Bjerg, and Sebastian Fini Carstensen are also part of the lawsuit, which encompasses 13 athletes requesting 2 million Danish Kroner (DKK) – around £224,000 – in compensation.

In the lawsuit, the group of athletes, including athletes from other sports, are claiming 50,000 DKK (£5,600) per image HBO Nordic used in the run-up to the Paris Olympic Games in 2024.

Pedersen appeared in court via video link on Monday.

"It's difficult to sell my name and image to others if it's used for free," he said, according to .

"I believe without a doubt that it was for the purpose of selling a product. It has been harmful to the extent that I try to sell my picture and image to others.

"There are other companies that pay large sums of money for that. And I did not give HBO permission to use those photos."

Pedersen pointed to several of his own brand advertising deals. He noted that workwear brand Airtox is paying him 3.4 million DKK (£380,000) for a two-year deal to use his image, while Lidl-Trek's clothing sponsor Crivit is paying him 19 million DKK (£2.1 million) over five years.

Lawyers representing the group claim images of the athletes were used on HBO Max's website, Facebook and Instagram accounts and on a large banner advert in Copenhagen,

HBO's counterclaim is that its use of images should be considered in an editorial context, according to TV2.

Pedersen is claiming 150,000 DKK (£16,800) in compensation for three uses of his image. Other athletes in the lawsuit, badminton player Victor Axelsen and handball player Mathias Gidsel, have larger compensation claims of 450,000 DKK (£50,000).

items.title: UCI Gravel World Series: Former junior champion steps up to claim elite women's win at a muddy Gravelista while rowing Olympic medallist sails away for elite men's victory
items.author: simone.giuliani@futurenet.com (Simone Giuliani)
items.content:
The first 2027 Australian qualifier of the UCI Gravel World Series, Gravelista, crowned two very different first time series winners. The 19-year-old Ruby Taylor claimed the elite women's victory and an Olympic silver medallist in rowing, Great Britain's Harry Leask, won the elite men's category.

They both, however, crossed the line solo in muddy and wet conditions after the race, for a second year, was hit by a cool turn in the spring conditions. That resulted in a shortening of the original 135km course to 97.1km with 1,154m of elevation gain.

Taylor excelled in the conditions to take her first UCI Gravel World Series elite victory in dominating style. The young rider, who won the junior Australian gravel title two years ago, crossed the line after three hours, eight minutes and 36 seconds with a margin of nearly nine minutes to the closest women's competitor, Laura Tomlinson, who was riding in the 19-34 year old age-group category.

The 40-44 rider Belen Lopez Morales, who from 2011-13 claimed the Spanish time trial title on the road, was next over the line and it was then a group of six, including Great Britain's Hayley Simmonds, at nearly 11 minutes that fought for the next places in the overall and the remaining two spots on the elite women's podium.

The 35-39 category rider Philippa Birch won that sprint and then elite women's category riders Karoline Risager Schmidt – who finished in the top 30 at the UCI Gravel World Championships in Nannup – and Amanda Poulsen took the next two positions. In the process, Risager Schmidt and Poulsen also came second and third in the elite category.

For Taylor the top step was the continuation of a year where she hasn't just been easing her way out of the junior ranks, but blasting into a new category with victories that have often left her older and more experienced rivals leagues behind.

The run of successes has crossed disciplines and includes two stage wins at the three-stage ProVelo Super League round of the Tour of Tasmania plus an U23 Australian XCO Mountain Bike title that not only saw her shed her category rivals but also make up the one minute deficit at the start line to nearly all the elite women out on the course, the only exception being elite victor Rebecca Henderson.

In the men's elite race at Gravelista, which started and finished in Seymour in Victoria, the field included former Australian gravel champions Mark O'Brien and Connor Sens as well as past UCI Gravel World Series race winner Tasman Nankervis but Leask had also marked himself out as a potential threat with second at Devils Cardigan earlier this year.

Leask, who after rowing also became a cyclor in the America's Cup, made a crucial early move with Nankervis and O'Brien.

"Another wet and muddy race. Managed to get away 3 up after the main climb at 30k, then was able to get a gap in the last 6/7k to come across the line solo," said Leask in a post on social media.

The British rider crossed the line in two hours, 31 minutes and 16 seconds, which was 23 seconds ahead of second-placed Nankervis. O'Brien, a further four seconds back, claimed third in the elite category. It was then more than three minutes later when a group of four riders crossed the line to fight for fourth place, with Oliver Johnston leading them over.
